publicationDetails.detailsText: Jabri, M. (2026). Digital Disruption Adaptation Theory: Explaining Decision Function Restoration Following Family Disruption. Zenodo. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21778989.

detail.abstract: Family disruption such as divorce, bereavement, or separation fundamentally alters household structures and the routines underpinning everyday consumption. While existing literature explores fragmented outcomes of these transitions, theoretical understanding of how consumers reconstruct purchase decision-making remains limited. The rapid digitalization of commerce introduces algorithmic recommendations, artificial intelligence (AI), and online communities as alternative decision resources. This paper advances the Digital Disruption Adaptation (DDA) framework into a middle-range theory by introducing Decision Function Restoration (DFR) as its central explanatory mechanism. DFR posits that consumers adapt to family disruption by actively restoring three core disrupted household decision functions: information gathering, validation, and coordination. Through six theoretical propositions, this paper establishes a nomological network detailing how function deficits motivate consumers to utilize digital and human marketplace resources based on "Function-Resource Fit." This paper contributes to consumer behavior literature by providing a falsifiable, capability-centered theory of postdisruption adaptation, offering a robust agenda for future empirical research.

The secondary evidence assessed in Section 5 is drawn entirely from publicly available publications by the ILO, the World Bank, the IMF, and academic authors.

detail.abstract:
Algorithmic decision systems can act only on information that has been codified. This paper argues that in emerging-market commerce a structurally significant share of decision-relevant information is never codified at all, and it names that residue the uncodified margin. The margin is not a temporary data-coverage gap that better infrastructure will close. It is an equilibrium outcome in informal and semi-formal economies: counterparties operating outside formal credit, tax, and contracting regimes have positive incentives against creating a durable record, and information carried through trust networks derives part of its value from restricted circulation. Three properties follow. The margin is decision-specific rather than market-specific; it persists under improving data coverage wherever non-codification is incentive-driven; and it sets the ceiling on how much autonomy any system can responsibly be granted over a decision.

The argument is developed from eighteen years of direct field operation across five emerging markets, namely Gujarat (India), Ethiopia, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Uganda, in petrochemicals, FMCG, and agricultural trading. Four dated cases document formal data systems that were accurate about what they measured and simultaneously silent on what determined the commercial outcome: informal trucking substitution during the 2024 Red Sea shipping disruption; a rumour-driven 20 percent collapse in Ethiopian teff prices that propagated through social messaging ahead of any price feed; contractual failure from payment terms denominated in a fiscal calendar the counterparty did not operate on; and counterparty-specific credit judgment during Uganda's mid-2024 liquidity crunch. Each case is stated as a falsifiable proposition rather than an anecdote, and the framework is grounded in the established literatures on tacit knowledge, institutional voids, and economic embeddedness.

The paper then assesses its own February 2025 prediction against the subsequent empirical record. The joint ILO and World Bank background study for the World Development Report 2026 finds generative AI employment exposure of 34 percent in high-income countries against 11 percent in low-income countries across 135 economies, supporting the paper's claim of transformation rather than replacement, and supporting it for the specific structural reason the original advanced. Two risks the 2025 framing did not anticipate are reported alongside: sharply uneven exposure by gender and by career stage, and a developing-economy sequencing risk in which disruption may arrive faster than augmentation gains. A closing section derives design rules for organisations building market-intelligence systems that operate near the margin.

Relative to the 2025 original, this version restates the field cases with the sourcing and case-study method made explicit, adds the literature grounding, adds the retrospective assessment described above, and adds the applied section on design consequences. Readers seeking the original February 2025 formulation should cite the earlier working paper.

title: Improving Consumer Finance Measures: Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data
affiliations: Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management, Maastricht University, Catholic University Eichstatt-Ingolstadt and Maastricht University

detail.title: Improving Consumer Finance Measures: Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data
detail.abstract: Consumer finances are a central construct in marketing research, yet measurement practices remain fragmented, with limited guidance on when objective versus subjective measures are most appropriate. To address this empirically, we use a unique dataset linking household survey data on subjective financial well-being to observed household income from high-quality administrative tax registries. Across the domains of consumption behavior, financial vulnerability, and wealth accumulation, we find that subjective financial well-being explains more variance in subjective outcomes (including affordability perceptions, hardship indicators, and retirement adequacy) while objective income explains more variance in objective outcomes directly constrained by resource levels (such as actual expenditure, formal debt, and net wealth). This pattern, which we term financial measure-outcome alignment, holds across alternative operationalizations of subjective financial well-being, the inclusion of demographic controls and response tendencies, and measurement timing. We further show that the findings extend beyond administrative tax data to self-reported survey-based income measures when common sources of measurement error are addressed, suggesting that the observed pattern reflects construct differences rather than data quality. We translate these findings into a practical decision framework to guide researchers in selecting appropriate financial measures based on their research objectives and data availability.

title: Prevention is Better than Cure: A Crime Triangle Analysis of Art NFTs and Financial Crime
affiliations: Independent, The University of Sydney,  and Charles Sturt University

detail.title: Prevention is Better than Cure: A Crime Triangle Analysis of Art NFTs and Financial Crime
detail.abstract: Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) bring many opportunities for artists, investors, and creators, but they also have a dark side with significant potential for use in financial crimes. Vulnerabilities include their non-fungible nature, the decentralised nature of blockchain technology, the ease of creating NFTs, their financial value, and limited regulation. Drawing on relevant caselaw, a systematic review and topic modelling of literature, we map common examples of NFT-related crime, including fraud, money laundering, theft, and market-related offences. This empirical review lays the groundwork for the core contribution of this article, that is, application of the ‘crime triangle’ to NFT-related crime. Recognising heterogeneity in NFT-related crime, we detail five scenarios where such crime can occur and analyse these in the context of the crime triangle (inner and outer). This enables us to identify potential gaps and vulnerabilities in current crime prevention strategies. Given challenges in policing cybercrime, and specifically NFT-related crime, we argue that the crime triangle provides a useful heuristic tool for understanding the nature of NFT-related crime and for preventing such crime from happening.

title: Stochastic Choice with Advertising
affiliations: and

detail.title: Stochastic Choice with Advertising
detail.abstract: We study how advertised products (e.g., "Top Picks," "Recommended," "Featured") affect consumer choice on digital platforms and retail interfaces by extending the Luce (1959) (or multinomial logit) model. A consumer either focuses on the advertised items or considers the full menu, then chooses among the considered alternatives according to the Luce/logit rule. We characterize this model and show that its underlying primitives are uniquely identified from choice data. We also study a managerially important advertisement-design problem, in which a platform or retailer chooses the advertised subset to maximize expected profit, and we derive implementable design rules. We then introduce a richer framework in which advertising can influence both attention and preference. For this more general model, we provide a characterization and show how choice data can be used to separate the attention effect from the preference effect.

title: Knowledge Panels and Person Entity Confidence in the AI Search Era: A Signal, Traffic, and AI-visibility Audit of 1,005 US Personal Injury Attorneys and Law Firms

detail.title: Knowledge Panels and Person Entity Confidence in the AI Search Era: A Signal, Traffic, and AI-visibility Audit of 1,005 US Personal Injury Attorneys and Law Firms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the Founder and CEO of Rank Brilliance, a Semantic SEO agency that provides search engine optimization and entity-recognition services to clients across multiple verticals, including legal services. The research was conducted independently and does not involve any client data, proprietary engagements, or commercial partnerships with the 1,005 personal injury law firms or their managing partners included in the study sample. All analyzed websites and Knowledge Panel data were collected from publicly available Google Search results and the Google Knowledge Graph API. The author declares no other financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the findings reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or personally identifiable information requiring informed consent. The research is based on publicly accessible Google Search results, Knowledge Graph API responses, and publicly available website content. Managing partner names were identified from publicly available firm website and Google Search data. No ethics approval was required as the study does not fall under the scope of human subjects research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was self-funded and conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: The Google Knowledge Panel has evolved from a rich-snippet convenience into the visible surface of an entity-resolution machinery that also feeds Google AI Overviews and third-party generative answer engines. In the personal injury (PI) legal vertical, where practice is name-driven and commercial intent is dense, the practical question is whether a firm's managing partner has crossed the Knowledge-Graph confidence threshold that Google requires before rendering a Person-template Knowledge Panel. This study audits the Knowledge Panel status of the managing partner or firm owner of 1,005 top-ranking US personal injury law firms across 51 markets, classifies returned panels into a three-class taxonomy (Person Entity Panel, Local Business Panel, and Minimal or Other), and measures corpus and on-page signals associated with each class. We find that 21.3% of firms surface some Knowledge Panel when the managing partner's name is queried, split into 3.5% Person Entity Panels, 16.4% Local Business Panels, and 1.4% Minimal panels. Among the 35 Person Entity Panel holders, 67.6% anchor on a Wikipedia article as the canonical description source and 59.5% exhibit recent national-publisher media coverage versus a matched control rate of 32.7%. Schema-markup adoption does not meaningfully predict Person Entity Panel presence: Attorney/Person schema shows a 0.99x lift, and the only signal with measurable positive lift is Person-nested-in-Organization at 1.54x. Ten firms deploy the full entity-signal schema stack (SCI ≥ 17) yet still have no Person Entity Panel, evidencing that schema completeness is necessary hygiene rather than sufficient signal. Merging monthly organic-traffic estimates into the panel table reveals that Person-Entity-Panel firms carry a 2.95x traffic multiplier (Mann-Whitney p = 0.0003) after controlling for SERP rank, appearance frequency, and schema completeness, while Local-Business-Panel firms carry a 32% traffic deficit (multiplier 0.68x, p = 0.0023), consistent with zero-click cannibalization. A qualitative audit of six queries across Google AI Overviews and third-party generative answer engines shows Person-Entity-Panel attorneys are cited by name with unhedged verbs and grounded in Wikipedia and national-tier media, while a schema-heavy no-panel control is cited only to self-attested firm content. We argue that the confidence-threshold construct we term Person Entity Confidence, together with the practitioner discipline we term Brand Context Optimization, is the correct frame for legal-vertical AI Visibility in 2026 and beyond.

title: Hyperconnectivity and Personal Branding in Enhancing MSME Business Performance: The Mediating Roles of Product Innovation and Online Credibility
affiliations: Sam Ratulangi University, Sam Ratulangi University, Sam Ratulangi University and Sam Ratulangi University

detail.title: Hyperconnectivity and Personal Branding in Enhancing MSME Business Performance: The Mediating Roles of Product Innovation and Online Credibility
detail.abstract: This study investigates the effects of Hyperconnectivity and Personal Branding on MSME Business Performance by examining the mediating roles of Product Innovation and Online Credibility. The research aims to explain how digital connectivity and entrepreneurial branding contribute to business performance in the context of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). A quantitative research approach was employed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyze the relationships among the proposed constructs. The findings reveal that Personal Branding, Product Innovation, and Online Credibility have significant positive effects on MSME Business Performance, whereas Hyperconnectivity does not exert a significant direct effect. However, Hyperconnectivity indirectly enhances business performance through Product Innovation, while Personal Branding improves business performance through Online Credibility. These results suggest that digital connectivity alone is insufficient to improve business performance unless it is transformed into innovation and strengthened by customer trust. The study contributes to the digital entrepreneurship literature by providing empirical evidence on the mechanisms through which digital capabilities influence MSME performance. Practically, the findings offer valuable insights for entrepreneurs and policymakers to strengthen innovation capability, build online credibility, and develop effective personal branding strategies to enhance the competitiveness and sustainability of MSMEs in the digital economy.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Power, Productivity, Employment and the Global Balance Sheet

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Power, Productivity, Employment and the Global Balance Sheet

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No study with patients nor participants.
declarations.funderStatement: Self funded.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is reshaping the global energy system, transforming labour markets, and rebalancing economies at a speed few anticipated. This paper synthesises current data from the International Energy Agency, the World Economic Forum, Goldman Sachs, McKinsey, the IMF, the OECD, and Anthropic's Economic Index to assess five linked questions: (I) the current and projected energy consumption of AI and data centres; (II) efficiency and productivity gains by industry sector; (III) employment displacement from repetitive and cognitive task automation; (IV) an integrated net balance sheet of costs and benefits; and (V) country-by-country estimated effects across EU Member States, the UK, the US and China. We find that global data centre electricity demand is on course to roughly double to approximately 945 TWh by 2030, driven overwhelmingly by AI workloads, while AI is simultaneously delivering measurable productivity gains-a median 30% improvement in targeted tasks-and the WEF projects 78 million net new jobs globally by 2030 alongside 92 million displaced. We argue that the net effect is likely positive at the global level, but that the distribution of costs and benefits across countries and skill groups is highly uneven, and that the policy challenge lies in managing the transition between fossil-fuel dependence and clean energy, between automation and augmentation, and between economic gains and their equitable distribution.

title: Impact of User-Generated Content (UGC) Marketing on Consumer Buying Decision

detail.title: Impact of User-Generated Content (UGC) Marketing on Consumer Buying Decision

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved an anonymous, voluntary online survey of adult respondents. No personally identifiable information was collected. Participants were informed of the study's academic purpose before responding, and completion of the questionnaire was taken as consent to participate. No formal institutional ethics board review was required or sought for this undergraduate research project.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted as part of the author's undergraduate thesis at IIS (Deemed to be University), Jaipur.

detail.abstract: In the digital era, consumers increasingly rely on user-generated content (UGC)online reviews, ratings, testimonials, and social media postsrather than traditional brand advertising when making purchase decisions. This study examines the impact of UGC on consumer buying decisions, with particular attention to the role of customer trust as a link between the two. Primary data were collected from 130 respondents in India through a structured questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale, and analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and linear regression in SPSS. The results show a strong positive correlation between UGC and consumer buying decision (r = 0.671, p < 0.01) and between UGC and customer trust (r = 0.706, p < 0.01), while trust is moderately correlated with buying decision (r = 0.507, p < 0.01). Linear regression confirms that UGC is a statistically significant predictor of consumer buying decision (β = 0.671, F = 104.67, p < 0.001), explaining 45.0% of the variance (R² = 0.450). These findings indicate that UGC exerts a strong, statistically significant, and positive influence on consumer buying behavior, operating in part through the trust it builds with consumers. The study offers practical implications for marketers seeking to leverage authentic consumer content in digital marketing strategy, and contributes empirical evidence from the Indian market to the broader literature on UGC and consumer behavior.

title: The Impact of Social Media on Brand Building: A Consumer Perception Study

detail.title: The Impact of Social Media on Brand Building: A Consumer Perception Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any individual or organization that could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Participation in the survey was voluntary and anonymous. Respondents were informed of the study's academic purpose before completing the questionnaire, and no personally identifiable information was collected. As this study did not involve vulnerable populations, sensitive personal data, or physical/psychological risk, formal institutional ethics board approval was not sought, consistent with standard practice for undergraduate survey-based consumer research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was self-conducted as part of the author's undergraduate coursework.

detail.abstract: This study examines how social media shapes consumer perceptions of brands, focusing on trust, engagement, and purchasing behavior. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered to 102 respondents, including students, working professionals, freelancers, and business owners across a range of age groups. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple linear regression were used to analyze ten survey items covering brand discovery, trust, engagement, and purchase intent. Results show an overall positive perception of social media's role in brand building, with the strongest agreement recorded for its general contribution to brand image (M = 4.26, SD = 0.92). A regression model confirmed that the combined set of social media perception factors significantly predicts overall brand-building outcomes (F = 2.797, p = 0.006, R² = 0.215), with purchasing influence and brand responsiveness emerging as the strongest individual predictors. Influencer collaborations and user-generated content did not show significant independent effects, suggesting their influence may operate indirectly or depend on context. These findings carry practical implications for brand managers refining digital engagement strategies, while underscoring that brand building remains a multidimensional process shaped by factors beyond social media alone.

title: The Unmonitored Dependency: Human Supervisory Capacity as a Blind Spot in Frontier AI Safety Frameworks

detail.title: The Unmonitored Dependency: Human Supervisory Capacity as a Blind Spot in Frontier AI Safety Frameworks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper was written entirely in a personal capacity, draws only on publicly available sources, and does not represent the views of any employer. The author has no financial interest in any AI laboratory discussed beyond incidental exposure through diversified retirement funds that the author does not direct.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this work. The research was conducted independently, on the author's own time and equipment.

detail.abstract: Frontier AI safety frameworks measure model capability with increasing rigor and rely on competent human oversight as a primary safeguard. The second half of that arrangement rests on an unmonitored assumption. A clause-level analysis of five current frameworks — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta, and xAI — coded every provision in which human judgment is the operative control and every provision addressing the competence of the person exercising it. All five specify that decisions are reviewed and approved; they vary in how far they name the office that reviews and in what they require of whoever holds it, but none contains an operative provision measuring whether those reviewers remain competent. The boundary falls in the same place in all five. One names erosion of human supervisory capacity as a potential catastrophic risk but classifies it as too nascent to evaluate; its preparedness report evaluates the model-side emerging risks in that category and reports nothing on the human-side one, while resting its determination on expert rubrics whose authors are documented as disagreeing. Evidence from software engineering, medicine, education, and consulting, though early and heterogeneous, indicates that AI assistance can degrade or fail to build the capacities oversight depends on, often invisibly. Aviation answered a version of this problem by treating manual proficiency as a maintained resource, not a stable trait; European law already requires competence of those overseeing high-risk AI systems, but that obligation does not reach frontier models. The paper proposes the same treatment for supervisory capacity, showing each framework already holds governance provisions through which such a requirement could enter. The inference from individual-level effects to oversight failure is offered as a hypothesis these frameworks cannot detect or rule out, not as an established finding.

title: The Person Entity Confidence Gap: A Knowledge Panel Taxonomy Across 1,005 US Personal Injury Attorneys and Law Firms in the AI Search Era

detail.title: The Person Entity Confidence Gap: A Knowledge Panel Taxonomy Across 1,005 US Personal Injury Attorneys and Law Firms in the AI Search Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the Founder and CEO of Rank Brilliance, a Semantic SEO agency that provides search engine optimization, entity-recognition, and Knowledge Graph onboarding services to clients across multiple verticals, including legal services. The research was conducted independently and does not involve any client data, proprietary engagements, or commercial partnerships with the 1,005 personal injury law firms or their managing partners included in the study sample. All analyzed data were collected from publicly available Google Search results, Google Knowledge Graph API responses, Wikipedia's public MediaWiki API, Google Books' public API, and publicly accessible law firm websites. The author declares no other financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the findings reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or personally identifiable information requiring informed consent. The research is based on publicly accessible Google Search results, Knowledge Graph API responses, Wikipedia articles, Google Books listings, Google News results, and publicly available law firm website content. Managing partner names were identified from publicly available firm website content and Google Search data. All data sources used in this study are public-facing and freely accessible. No ethics approval was required as the study does not fall under the scope of human subjects research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was self-funded and conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: The transition from ranking-based search to entity-based retrieval has changed what "visibility" means for a personal injury law firm on Google. A firm can rank on Page 1 for its target keywords while its managing partner remains absent from Google's Knowledge Graph as a first-class person entity. This paper audits the state of Person Entity recognition across the top-ranking US personal injury legal vertical and quantifies the business consequences. Using a sample of 1,005 top-ranking firms across 51 US markets, we identify the managing partner of each firm via LLM-assisted disambiguation of Google SERP results, audit whether a Knowledge Panel surfaces at the partner-name query, classify each panel into a Person Entity Panel, a Local Business Panel, or a minimal-attribute panel, and enrich each result with external corpus signals (Wikipedia article presence and size, Google Books authorship, national-publisher news coverage) plus each firm's schema-completeness score. We further merge in third-party monthly organic-traffic estimates for the same 1,005 firms and test whether Knowledge Panel class predicts firm-site traffic under rank-controlled and multivariable-regression conditions. Only 3.5% (35 of 1,005) of the firms surface a Person Entity Panel with biographical attributes; 16.4% (165) surface a Local Business Panel keyed to the partner's name; the remaining 80% surface no panel. Among the 35 Person Entity Panel holders, 67.6% anchor on a Wikipedia article as the canonical description source and 59.5% show top-10 news hits from a major national publisher, versus 32.7% for a matched no-panel control. Schema markup adoption does not meaningfully predict Person Entity Panel presence; the strongest on-page schema signal is Person nested inside Organization at 1.54x lift. Ten of the most schema-complete firms in the sample deploy the full entity-signal schema stack and still have no Person Entity Panel, only one of them has a Wikipedia article for the managing partner, and even that one has no panel. Person Entity Panel presence is associated with a 2.95x organic-traffic multiplier under rank and schema controls (Mann-Whitney p = 0.0003), while Local Business Panels are associated with a 32% organic-traffic deficit versus no-panel firms at the same rank tier (Mann-Whitney p = 0.0023), the zero-click cannibalization effect made visible for the legal vertical. We locate these findings inside Google's own patent record on Knowledge Panel triggering (US-9268820-B2 and family) and corroboration (US-8682913-B1), formalize a Brand Context Optimization maturity model that maps observed corpus-signal patterns onto expected AI Visibility outcomes, and offer a prioritized recommendation set for firms targeting Person Entity Confidence and AI Visibility across Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Claude research surfaces.

title: Does AI Have a Voice? Measuring and Controlling Machine Writing Style in Marketing Communications
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Whitewater

detail.title: Does AI Have a Voice? Measuring and Controlling Machine Writing Style in Marketing Communications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests. The study evaluates language models developed by Anthropic; the author has no financial, employment, or advisory relationship with Anthropic beyond the purchase of standard API access at public rates, and Anthropic had no role in the design, execution, analysis, or reporting of the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The research involving human participants (Study 2, in which anonymous adult raters evaluated marketing texts in an online survey) was reviewed by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Wisconsin-Whitewater and approved as Exempt under Category 2(i), protocol IRB-FY2026-2027-2. All participants provided informed consent before beginning the survey. Sessions that declined consent or reported an age under 18 were terminated without data collection. The remaining studies analyzed machine-generated text and archival public web text and involved no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Firms increasingly delegate customer-facing writing to large language models. Applying the writing-style traits framework, we ask whether a language model has a measurable voice, whether instruction can control it, and whether the model can describe it. Three models from one provider wrote 9,600 documents across four marketing registers under bare-API conditions, scored against a balanced subset of a matched 2,684-document pre-2022 human corpus. The models share a ten-marker structural signature, and readers separate the sources and identify machine authorship above chance, though an individual’s judgment that a text was human-written is unreliable when most texts are machine-generated. Popular tells point the wrong way: AI buzzwords run below the human marketing baseline, and the voice concentrates in structure and rhythm, where banned habits comply partially but can invert. Instructed to imitate a brand voice, the models remain almost perfectly separable from the brand’s held-out text on style-only instruments. Asked to predict their own style, every model missed more often than it hit. A brand generating copy with a language model inherits a register-dependent voice it did not choose; managing it takes measurement, not word lists or the model’s self-report.

title: Flexible Selling and Leasing Contracts for Interdependent Durable Goods
affiliations: and

detail.title: Flexible Selling and Leasing Contracts for Interdependent Durable Goods
detail.abstract: In many industries, firms offer products composed of multiple interdependent components and increasingly adopt ownership models that combine the sale and lease of individual parts of the product. Motivated by such practices, we investigate how a firm should design its optimal selling and leasing strategy when distributing products that generate value only when their parts are consumed jointly. This paper focuses on how the market is segmented across different ownership models and how it is influenced by component durability and asymmetry, cost structure, retailer structure, pricing, and consumer behavior. In our model, consumers are heterogeneous and make two-period decisions. Each component can be sold or leased, with durability governing how value depreciates over time. The retailer incurs procurement and maintenance costs, and components may differ in durability, valuation, and costs. We begin with a centralized setting in which a single retailer sets all packages and prices, and then extend the analysis to decentralized retail structures with independent retailers. Some major findings include: (1) The market may be segmented, with consumers of different valuations selecting different ownership arrangements. In addition, mixed ownership can arise as an optimal strategy for some consumers in which the two components are offered under different ownership models. (2) Component durability and its connection with the maintenance costs play significant roles in shaping the optimal ownership. For cases with maintenance costs not influenced by product durability, stronger durability encourages the sales model. However, if higher durability mitigates maintenance, the lease model is more attractive. (3) Finally, retailer decentralization introduces the classic double marginalization problem, as expected. What is interesting is that this decentralization makes leasing more attractive and also reduces the likelihood of full market segmentation.

title: The Transition of Ethiopia's Treasury Bill Market: From Administrative Controls to Market-based Monetary Policy
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Transition of Ethiopia's Treasury Bill Market: From Administrative Controls to Market-based Monetary Policy

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was granted an exemption of ethics approval due to the retrospective use of fully anonymized data.

detail.abstract: Ethiopia has experienced one of the most significant monetary policy reforms in its recent economic history. For decades, monetary policy relied on direct instruments, including administrative credit controls, regulated interest rates, and central bank financing of government deficits. These policies constrained financial market development and weakened monetary policy transmission. In 2024, the National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) initiated comprehensive monetary and financial sector reforms to establish an interest-rate-based monetary policy framework. A central component of these reforms was the modernization of the Treasury bill (T-bill) market. During the transition period, a temporary credit growth cap was introduced to contain inflation while the market-based framework was being developed. Following the removal of the credit cap in 2026, Treasury bills became the principal instrument for liquidity management and open market operations. This article reviews the evolution of Ethiopia's Treasury bill market across the pre-reform, transition, and post-transition periods and discusses its implications for monetary policy and financial market development.

title: The U.S.-China Engagement Paradox: Integration, Productive Centrality, and the Changing Architecture of Power

detail.title: The U.S.-China Engagement Paradox: Integration, Productive Centrality, and the Changing Architecture of Power

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Hormuz Group, an independent market intelligence platform. The author declares no other competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or experimental research requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
U.S.-China engagement is now frequently described as a strategic failure: the United States opened relations with China, supported its integration into the world economy, and expected economic liberalisation to moderate Chinese behaviour or encourage political convergence, only to help create its principal strategic competitor. An opposing account treats China's rise as the execution of a patient long-term strategy that used Western markets, capital, and technology to accumulate power. Both interpretations impose more continuity on the past than the historical record can bear.

This paper offers a different account. It treats engagement as a sequence of bargains whose purposes changed over time. The opening initiated under Richard Nixon was primarily geopolitical, exploiting the Sino-Soviet split to improve the American position in a triangular balance. China's post-1978 reforms then converted diplomatic access into developmental access to foreign capital, technology, knowledge, and markets. WTO accession deepened that process by increasing the predictability of China's participation in the global trading system. Yet integration did more than subject China to existing rules. Combined with domestic reform, infrastructure, investment, and industrial policy, it enabled production to reach a scale at which dense industrial ecosystems became difficult to replace.

The paper distinguishes three analytically different forms of structural power: institutional power, derived from influence over rules and organised relationships; gatekeeping centrality, derived from control or jurisdiction over critical nodes through which others must pass; and embedded productive centrality, which arises when production becomes organised around an ecosystem whose replacement is costly even in the absence of a formal gate. The United States and China possess all three forms, but in different combinations. American power remains unusually strong in global finance, security alliances, advanced-technology chokepoints, and institutional access. China has acquired exceptional embedded centrality across important parts of manufacturing, battery supply chains, mineral processing, and industrial production.

The emerging order is therefore neither a simple continuation of American hegemony nor a completed transition to Chinese hegemony. It is a layered system in which different forms of indispensability increasingly reside in different states. Contemporary U.S.-China competition can accordingly be understood as a struggle to preserve one's own centrality while reducing dependence on the other's.

title:
Fossil-Energy Premium in War and Peace:
Energy Firms and Global Equity Returns during the Iran-US/Israel Wars in 2025 and 2026
affiliations: , University of Giessen, Justus-Liebig-Universität Gießen and Justus-Liebig-University Giessen

detail.title:
Fossil-Energy Premium in War and Peace:
Energy Firms and Global Equity Returns during the Iran-US/Israel Wars in 2025 and 2026
detail.abstract: We study the relationship between the Iran and Israel/US wars and the pricing of global equities. Focusing on energy firms, we conduct event studies of the 2025 12-Day War and several events of the 2026 war. We find that abnormal returns of non-energy firms declined by 2.8% at the outbreak of the 2026 war, while energy firms earned 4.3% abnormal returns. At the outbreak of the 2025 12-Day War, energy firms earned 2.4% while non-energy firms lost 0.7%. These findings are substantiated by four additional escalation and de-escalation events, where the premium reversed at each de-escalation and returned when escalation resumed in July 2026. Positive abnormal returns for energy firms are concentrated among oil and gas and oil-services firms and increase with Brent exposure. Energy returns are larger where headquarters-country dependence on Gulf crude imports is lower, although this association is not robust.

title: Trademark Law's View of the Image: A Computational and Empirical Analysis
affiliations: New York University School of Law,  and Vanderbilt University - Vanderbilt Law School

detail.title: Trademark Law's View of the Image: A Computational and Empirical Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: New York University Law Review, Forthcoming

detail.abstract:
Trademark law maintains a remarkably primitive, incoherent, and unexamined approach to images, even as the number and importance of image marks has grown dramatically. The law has viewed image marks as unanalyzable. In practice, trademark law also privileges representational meaning over visual appearance when searching for similar image marks, but it reverses that priority when assessing image mark distinctiveness. It has additionally long assumed that businesses can draw from an effectively limitless supply of "image synonyms"-different images that convey the same meaning.

This Article presents the first large-scale computational and empirical analysis of image marks. We focus on the 2.9 million image mark applications filed at the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (PTO) from 1985 through 2023. Drawing on advances in marketing theory and computational approaches to image analysis, we use machine learning models as a diagnostic tool to show that the PTO's adjudication of image marks is systematically inconsistent and incomplete. Specifically, we show that the PTO routinely refuses registration of applied-for image marks on the basis that they are confusingly similar with already-registered marks even though the PTO has allowed the registration of numerous other marks more confusingly similar to those already-registered marks than the applied-for mark. We further show that registered image marks have become increasingly descriptive or generic of their associated goods and services but distinctiveness refusals remain exceptionally rare.

We propose three reforms. First, image similarity should be assessed under an explicit "sight and meaning" test that gives weight to both the representational meaning and visual appearance of image marks. Second, image mark inherent distinctiveness should be assessed under a hybrid of the two differing approaches that courts currently use. Third, trademark law must investigate, rather than assume, that the supply of image synonyms is inexhaustible. Throughout, we urge that trademark doctrine learn from computational methods of image analysis, seeking to demonstrate how these methods can serve trademark law's overarching goal of facilitating fair and efficient competition.

detail.abstract: This paper presents the Doctrine of Directed and Ethical Intelligence, a developmental‑ethical framework that conceptualises intelligence as a functional capacity requiring direction, constraint and socio‑emotional integration. Drawing on empirical research in adolescent moral development (Malti et al., 2021; Killen & Smetana, 2022), cognitive maturation (Steinberg, 2005; Casey et al., 2005) and the ethics of psychological influence (Haidt, 2001; Bandura, 1986), the doctrine argues that formative decisions made during adolescence establish enduring principles governing the responsible use of cognitive power. The framework synthesises findings from developmental psychology, moral reasoning and social‑cognitive theory to articulate a unified model in which intelligence becomes constructive only when normatively guided, culturally grounded and ethically regulated.

title: The Price of Fear: Uncertainty, Trade, and Economic Welfare in International Commodity Markets during the Black Sea Grain Initiative

detail.title: The Price of Fear: Uncertainty, Trade, and Economic Welfare in International Commodity Markets during the Black Sea Grain Initiative
detail.abstract: The Black Sea Grain Initiative reopened Ukraine's seaborne grain exports under an agreement signed in July 2022, and although grain flowed for a year, the market never stopped questioning whether the corridor would hold, until it collapsed in July 2023. Because the price of grain over this period reflected both the grain that was physically missing and the market's fear that shipments would be cut off again, this study sets out to separate the two, treating the second as the price of corridor risk itself. To measure that risk, a two-regime Markov switching model of daily wheat and maize futures recovers a market-implied probability that the corridor is under stress, and this probability follows the events of the Initiative closely, rising from near zero before the war to 0.7625 around the invasion and 0.4860 around the collapse. Over the year the corridor was open, when grain was moving freely, a shift from calm to stressed belief raised the wheat price by 0.4790 log points, an effect that holds at the one percent level and across specifications. This fear premium fell most heavily on developing economies, which bore 65.6 percent of the added import cost, and as the crisis wore on the grain itself moved toward wealthier buyers, with the high-income share of Ukrainian exports rising from 29.8 to 59.7 percent.

title: When Consensus Acquits Capture and the Defence of Collective Judgment
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Government

detail.title: When Consensus Acquits Capture and the Defence of Collective Judgment
detail.abstract: Collective judgment can be captured. A court, a jury, a committee can be swept or suborned to deliver the verdict a power wants. We distinguish two ways this is done. A bench can be forced to agree-the show trial, the acclamation, the manufactured unanimity. Or it can be packed to control the outcome while dissent goes on the record. The two threats call for different defences. Against the first, the optimal defence reads agreement against itself: a captured bench manufactures consensus, so consensus becomes the sign of capture, and the rule that defends the court refuses to convict on it. We characterise this defence and show its sharp form is a rule that looks perverse-where capture is likely and concentrated on consensus, a bench that convicts unanimously acquits the accused (Sanhedrin 17a). A family of devices follows as complements: a tilt toward acquittal, an order of voting that denies deference, benches that grow with the gravity of the charge. The Sanhedrin's capital procedure assembles them all, and we read it as the clearest instance of the design. Where a body decides not a hidden fact but a removal, as in Athenian ostracism, there is no count to read against itself, and the defence falls back on breadth and a mild, reversible penalty. Against the second threat, that bench needs entrenchment, not suspicion. We sort the institutions of collective judgment by the capture they fear and the count they can read.

title: Translational Decision Intelligence (TxDI): Foundations of a Game-Theory-Informed Decision Science Approach for Healthcare AI

detail.abstract: Technical performance does not by itself determine whether a health system should adopt an AI-enabled pathway or how an AI output should change action. This methodological paper introduces Translational Decision Intelligence (TxDI), a game-theory-informed decision science approach for translating healthcare AI outputs into decision-ready evidence. TxDI was developed through a purposive integrative conceptual synthesis of three bodies of scholarship: strategic decision science, including medical decision science, game theory, and information economics; health-system value assessment, including decision modeling, simulation, health technology assessment, and economic evaluation; and AI implementation and lifecycle evaluation, including implementation science, learning health systems, and AI evaluation guidance. No empirical dataset was analyzed. TxDI centers two connected decisions: whether a health system should pilot, adopt, continue, scale, modify, restrict, pause, redesign, or stop an AI-enabled pathway; and, if the pathway is used, how its outputs should inform clinical, population-health, operational, resource-allocation, coverage, governance, or policy action. The framework comprises seven linked stages: system problem; technology/analytics; decision and value framing; action specification; implementation or pilot deployment; realized consequences and value; and learning loop. It further distinguishes the narrower task of output-to-action mapping from broader strategy evaluation, anticipated from realized value, and model performance from pathway value. A lightweight stakeholder-and-incentive diagnostic operationalizes the game-theoretic backbone, while stylized signaling and hidden-action models illustrate how information asymmetry and incentive compatibility can be formalized when the decision problem is sufficiently specified. TxDI does not replace established AI evaluation, implementation, economic, equity, or governance methods; rather, it organizes their use across the pathway from adoption decisions and AI-informed actions to realized consequences and lifecycle learning.

detail.title: The Special-Dividend Drift: Six Decades of Unmeasured Post-Announcement Returns

detail.abstract: For forty years, research on special dividends has stopped one day after the announcement. I extend the window and document that declaring firms continue to earn abnormal returns of about 1.2% over the following month (trading days +2 to +20; declaration-month clustered 𝑡 = 6.03) on 5,246 U.S. declarations from 2003 to 2024-and that the same drift, at nearly the same magnitude, is present in the 7,986 declarations from 1962 to 2002 that no prior study examined: an anomaly hiding in plain sight for six decades. A second, sharper finding explains why the literature missed it: the information in a special dividend lives after the jump, not in it. Firsttime specials drift roughly twice as much as specials the firm has declared repeatedly-precisely the pattern implied by the DeAngelo, DeAngelo, and Skinner (2000) argument that predictable specials lose their information content, an implication those authors probed at the announcement window, found insignificant, and left untabulated. The drift is not earnings-announcement drift in disguise: it is unchanged after controlling for the most recent earnings surprise, holds when no earnings announcement falls anywhere near the window, and the conclusion covers seventy percent of events once the surprise is rebuilt from Compustat fundamentals. It is not explained by factor exposure-a calendar-time portfolio earns a five-factor-plus-momentum alpha of 14.7% per year (𝑡 = 3.90) during the drift window and none afterward, with unchanged loadings-and it holds against size-and momentum-matched control firms. It survives realistic bid-ask and price-impact costs outside microcaps. The drift concentrates where arbitrage is costly: the illiquid half of events drifts nearly three times the liquid half, which also explains how the effect survived six decades unexploited-under pre-decimalization spreads it was too expensive to trade away. A simple net-of-cost portfolio grows one dollar into roughly six and a half over 2003-2024. I discuss deployment limits-thin books, modest standalone Sharpe ratios, and the boundaries of the recurrence result under matched-control adjustment-explicitly.

detail.abstract: Egocentric errors in the director task become more common across later adulthood, but descriptive error curves do not identify how the underlying interpretive process changes. We reanalyzed the open behavioral data of Bradford et al. (2023) using a choice-level projection of Heller et al.’s (2016) probabilistic mixture model — in which a weight α indexes the egocentric contribution to interpretation — with a Beta–Binomial participant hierarchy and a publicly frozen robustness protocol. The age-dependent model estimated a contrast of Δα = +0.127 between ages 25 and 75, with a 95% participant-bootstrap interval of [+0.062, +0.196]. It also predicted entirely held-out participants completing the same task and items better than the fitted constant-α model in all 20 cross-validation repetitions. However, a prespecified parametric predictive check failed among younger adults: 18 participants aged 20–37 made exactly one egocentric error, exceeding the model’s 99% predictive interval of [1, 11]. Thus, an age-varying mixture weight provides a robust and predictively useful description of behavioral differences across adulthood, but a single mixture process does not reproduce the full distribution of observed errors. Because final choices cannot distinguish probabilistic weighting from an equivalent lapse process, all psychological interpretations of α remain conditional on the assumed response rule.

detail.abstract: Since March 2020, the massive global outbreak of novel coronavirus (COVID19) pandemic has disrupted the Gulf industries, severely impacting the living and working conditions of the vast majority of foreign expatriates in the urban Gulf. 1 By closely examining the two key Gulf economic centres-Dubai and Jeddah-during the initial wave of COVID19 pandemic (March-August 2020) via a mixed-method approach (n=117), the study aims to analyze the complex and multilayered effects of COVID19 pandemic on the three largest foreign expatriate communities in these selected Gulf cities, specifically Filipinos, Egyptians, and Pakistanis. 2 The study specifically explores how COVID19 has affected foreign workers' economic and welfare status in both Gulf cities mainly on the following thematic areas: working conditions, living conditions, access to medical services and dispute resolution system, remittance contribution, and current and future employment and security perceptions both in the Gulf and home country labour markets. 3 Key highlights of the study include the following:-Unemployment among foreign workers across various industries (except healthcare, pharmaceutical, selected food delivery, and digital sectors among others) has become pervasive during the initial wave of COVID19 pandemic, which has significantly impacted both of their income levels and remittance contributions.

title: Bangladesh: Between Economic Miracle and Graduation Crisis A Macroeconomic and Sociological Synthesis

detail.title: Bangladesh: Between Economic Miracle and Graduation Crisis A Macroeconomic and Sociological Synthesis
detail.abstract: This study conducts a comprehensive empirical synthesis and theoretical integration of Bangladesh's macroeconomic trajectory as it prepares to formally graduate from the United Nations Least Developed Country (LDC) category on November 24, 2026. While aggregate growth over the past five decades has been heralded as a developmental "miracle"marked by a sevenfold increase in per capita income and significant improvements in life expectancy-this paper exposes severe, systemic vulnerabilities that threaten to undermine these achievements. We analyze the dual growth engines of Readymade Garments (RMG) and migrant remittances, evaluating the impending "tariff cliff" of 2029 when preferential access to the European Union market expires. To understand these macro-micro disparities, we integrate advanced empirical and theoretical frameworks from Al Mayen (2026a, 2026b, 2026c, 2026d). Using fixed-effects panel econometrics, we formalize a consumption-inflation model proving that unanticipated CPI inflation operates as a highly regressive shock, compressing annual household consumption per capita by $42.56 (p ¡ 0.001). Furthermore, we model income inequality (the Gini coefficient) as a developmental "friction coefficient" that severely degrades the translational efficiency of GDP growth into human welfare (β =-0.28, p ¡ 0.001), shedding light on the structural rot that fueled the siphoning of $234 billion in capital flight and the spike in system-wide non-performing loans (NPLs) to a world-record 35.73%. We examine the student-led July 2024 Revolution through a sociological critique of the "false promises of social mobility," showing how a rigid public-sector quota system shattered the meritocratic expectations of a generation suffering from a 30% youth NEET rate. Finally, we implement an interactive epidemiological model showing that economic crises account for a 34.3% Population Attributable Risk (PAR) of clinical depression, demonstrating that public Active Labor Market Program (ALMP) spending can completely neutralize recession-induced suicide mortality once it crosses a critical threshold of $208.42 per capita. We outline a comprehensive policy roadmap for newly elected leader T.K. Rahman to navigate the post-graduation transition and stabilize the fragile state.

detail.abstract:
Working paper / preprint — not peer-reviewed. This paper proposes a theoretical policy framework and is not an empirical study. Drafting and formatting were AI-assisted; some figures and country-specific statistics have not been independently re-verified and may contain errors. Findings are conditional on the framework's stated assumptions and should be read as structural illustrations, not real-world predictions or forecasts. This is not financial, investment, or legal advice. Corrections, critique, and independent replication are welcome — contact mo_barakatm@yahoo.com.

The global financial system relies overwhelmingly on interest-bearing debt. With global public debt exceeding $102 trillion, this paper examines whether debt-compounding dynamics are a structural feature of interest-based finance, and proposes an alternative architecture — "Economic Sovereignty" — built on interest-free financing.

The framework rests on four pillars. First, a zero-interest policy intended to remove the compounding-debt mechanism as a driver of cost-push inflation. Second, profit-and-loss-sharing (PLS) finance, which replaces debt contracts with equity-style investment, so that financial returns are tied to real economic performance rather than fixed obligations. Third, a 2.5% asset-based tax replacing income and corporate taxation, designed to discourage capital hoarding and encourage productive circulation. Fourth, a dynamic monetary stability mechanism intended to anchor money supply to the real economy and absorb supply-side shocks.

detail.abstract:
Working paper / preprint — not peer-reviewed. This is a companion simulation study to Aly (2026), Economic Sovereignty: Engineering the Interest-Free System [https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=7253121]. Simulation code and validation modules were AI-generated; the economic framework under test is the author's original work. All results are conditional on the model's specific parametric assumptions and should be read as structural properties of a stylised theoretical model, not empirical predictions about real-world economies.

This paper presents a comparative macro-simulation of two financial architectures — a conventional interest-based system ("Legacy") and a profit-and-loss-sharing system ("Sovereign") — across ten macroeconomic stability tiers, using a Monte Carlo framework (200 runs per tier, 4,000 total paths, 30-year horizon, seed=42 for full reproducibility). Two metrics are introduced: the Kinetic Efficiency Index (KEI), integrating growth, inflation deviation, and debt burden, and a state-space Divergence Metric, D(t), quantifying structural separation between the regimes over time.

Under the model's parameterisation, the Sovereign architecture shows lower debt-crisis probability in low-to-moderate stress environments, while both architectures converge toward high failure rates under severe stress, with the Sovereign system's primary vulnerability shifting to a money-velocity-driven inflation channel above moderate stress levels. An internal validation exercise (formula verification, ±25% sensitivity analysis, cross-model comparison against Domar, Fisher, Taylor-rule, and stock-flow-consistent frameworks) is reported alongside the main results, including limitations: the model's policy-rate rule is intentionally sub-stabilising relative to the Taylor principle, shock sequences are not strictly identical across regimes in a given run, and the transition simulation assumes a frictionless institutional shift not present in real-world monetary reform. These limitations are discussed in full in the paper's validation appendix.

Corrections, critique, and independent replication are welcome — contact mo_barakatm@yahoo.com.

title: A Machine Learning Framework for Comparative Housing Valuation and Listing Price Fairness Assessment
affiliations: K. N. Toosi University of Technology

detail.title: A Machine Learning Framework for Comparative Housing Valuation and Listing Price Fairness Assessment
detail.abstract: Deciding whether a listed housing price is fair, relatively high, or relatively low is an important practical problem for buyers and sellers. Conventional automated valuation approaches typically frame housing valuation as a price-prediction task, producing an estimated price from a property's characteristics. This paper instead considers the complementary problem of assessing an observed listing price relative to a model-implied reference value. A polynomial regression estimator is used to estimate a reference housing price from property characteristics, with particular attention to the methodological risks associated with encoding location-based variables. The resulting reference value is compared with the observed listing price through a Price Deviation Index (PDI), which measures the relative difference between the two values. The framework therefore provides a simple data-driven mechanism for identifying listings whose asking prices are relatively higher or lower than the estimated market-consistent value of comparable properties. The proposed approach is intended as an interpretable complement to conventional housing price prediction and comparative market analysis rather than as a substitute for professional property appraisal.

detail.abstract: Social disconnectedness has emerged as a critical public health and socioeconomic challenge with farreaching implications for mental and physical health, labour productivity, social cohesion, and overall wellbeing. Although a growing body of literature documents its adverse consequences, comparatively little empirical evidence examines the demographic, socioeconomic, and behavioural factors that shape social disconnectedness, particularly in developing countries such as India. Existing studies have largely adopted psychological or public health perspectives, with limited attention to the role of socioeconomic conditions and digital behaviour within an integrated analytical framework. This study investigates the determinants of social disconnectedness using primary survey data collected from 150 adults in India. Social disconnectedness is measured using the Social Connectedness Scale developed by Lee and Robbins (1995), with responses reverse-coded to construct a Social Disconnectedness Score. Guided by Social Capital Theory, the Capability Approach, and Behavioural Economics, the study employs Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression to estimate the association between demographic characteristics, socioeconomic status, digital engagement, and social disconnectedness. The findings indicate that age, religion, place of residence, family size, household income, occupation, and daily screen time are significant determinants of social disconnectedness. Respondents aged 20-60 years, individuals from larger households, urban residents, and those belonging to higher-income households exhibit significantly lower levels of social disconnectedness. Conversely, business owners, homemakers, respondents from minority religious groups, and individuals reporting four to six hours of daily screen time experience higher levels of social disconnectedness. Gender, caste, disability status, educational attainment, and mere social media presence do not demonstrate statistically significant associations after controlling for other explanatory variables. The study contributes to the emerging interdisciplinary literature by shifting the focus from the consequences of social disconnectedness to its underlying determinants within the Indian context. By integrating demographic, socioeconomic, and behavioural perspectives into a unified econometric framework, it demonstrates that social disconnectedness is shaped by structural inequalities, family and occupational circumstances, and patterns of digital engagement. The findings provide important policy insights for designing interventions that strengthen social capital, promote healthy digital behaviours, enhance community participation, and reduce socioeconomic barriers to social inclusion.

title: Responsibility for the Future: Hans Jonas and the Philosophical Foundation of the Precautionary Principle
affiliations: NATIONAL KAPODISTRIAN UNIVERSITY OF ATHENS

detail.title: Responsibility for the Future: Hans Jonas and the Philosophical Foundation of the Precautionary Principle
detail.abstract: Hans Jonas's ethics of responsibility is among the most influential philosophical attempts to respond to the unprecedented temporal and spatial reach of modern technological power. This study examines whether, and in what sense, Jonas can provide a philosophical foundation for the precautionary principle in environmental law. It argues that Jonas should not be treated as the author of a legal precautionary rule. Rather, his work supplies a normative grammar for precaution: the expansion of responsibility beyond contemporaries, the priority accorded to avoiding irreversible catastrophe, the epistemic significance of uncertainty, and the duty to preserve the conditions for genuine human life. The study compares this philosophical structure with Principle 15 of the Rio Declaration and Article 191(2) TFEU, while addressing objections concerning indeterminacy, paralysis, proportionality and conflicts with present interests.
