detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Targeting, and the Enduring Uncertainty of Membership in an Organized Armed Group

publicationDetails.detailsText: Transnational Law & Contemporary Problems, Volume 35, No. 2.

detail.abstract: Persistent uncertainty over the lethal targeting of members of organized armed groups (OAGs) challenges the ability to develop and deploy lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS).  These challenges arise, in part, from insufficient specification of OAG membership in international humanitarian law.  This article highlights these challenges by comparing three methods of determining OAG membership: a formal approach adapted from the United States' pre-9/11 individual belligerent framework, the International Committee of the Red Cross' continuous combat function framework, and the United States' post-9/11 conduct-based framework.  It establishes the United States' historical, individual belligerent framework, and critiques both the functional and conduct-based frameworks.  It also describes each framework's operational limitations for ensuring IHL compliance for the development and deployment of LAWS.

title: Repeated States are not Trajectories: The Identification Limits of Snapshot Inference in Survey Economics
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Repeated States are not Trajectories: The Identification Limits of Snapshot Inference in Survey Economics
detail.abstract: Repeated measurement is often treated as evidence of dynamics. This paper argues that the inference is generally invalid. A sequence of observations of population states, (P_t(y)), does not by itself identify the individual trajectories or transition law that generated them. Distinct processes involving delayed detection, heterogeneous memory, reinforcement, threshold response, or rapid belief revision may remain observationally equivalent at the sampling times. The resulting limitation is not primarily statistical. It is structural: greater sample size, improved representativeness, and more sophisticated estimation can increase the precision with which successive states are measured without identifying the dynamics connecting them. The argument is developed through the case of Stantcheva and Tham's study of public attitudes toward the 2025 U.S. tariffs. Their four-wave design provides unusually rich evidence on changing distributions of tariff-related beliefs, yet it also illustrates the distinction between repeated snapshots and trajectory identification. This distinction extends an earlier critique of Stantcheva's treatment of perceptions and zero-sum thinking: the substantive domain and empirical design have changed, but the underlying inferential architecture remains state-based. The paper identifies three classes of information required once beliefs are treated as trajectories rather than isolated states: heterogeneous detection lag (\Delta t), memory weighting (K(t-\tau)), and stability overhead (SO(T)). These quantities are introduced not as components of a competing theory of public opinion but as methodological coordinates for determining whether persistence, revision, and resistance to perturbation are empirically identifiable. The broader conclusion is that repeated states and trajectories are different mathematical objects. When dynamic explanations are inferred from measurements that identify only the former, multiple transition mechanisms remain compatible with the same empirical record. The central methodological question therefore precedes estimation: does the observable contain enough information to identify the process being explained?

title: The Budget-maximizing Peacemaker: The Success Paradox of Peace-through-strength Defense Policy

detail.title: The Budget-maximizing Peacemaker: The Success Paradox of Peace-through-strength Defense Policy
detail.abstract: This paper develops a general theory of defense bureaucracies as budget-maximizing institutions whose internal incentives can distort their stated missions. While defense bureaus are tasked with preserving peace and security through the maintenance of military strength, their need to justify budgets and maintain relevance generates what this paper terms the Success Paradox: the bureaucratic pursuit of peace may create incentives to manufacture conflict to justify continued funding and to suppress real conflict that later erupts into prolonged and destructive wars. Therefore, defense policy is not necessarily the neutral pursuit of peace and security that it is stated to be. The analysis builds on Niskanen's model of bureaucratic behavior to explain how these incentives operate across institutional contexts. Historical and contemporary cases are analyzed to illustrate variation in how defense bureaus amplify or manufacture conflict, suppress genuine tensions, or are constrained by institutional conditions that prevent the Success Paradox from activating.

title: Goods Movement and Environmental Justice Policy Pathologies
affiliations: and University of Southern California

detail.title: Goods Movement and Environmental Justice Policy Pathologies
detail.abstract:
The goods movement industry, as it spreads across the Inland Empire, San Joaquin Valley, Bay Area, and other regions, presents a newer version of a longstanding tension in environmental protection, namely between enforcing air quality standards under the Clean Air Act and addressing localized or neighborhood-scale effects under civil rights law. Through on-site emissions and “indirect” emissions from heavy-duty truck traffic that makes its way to and from a region’s warehouse footprint, goods movement contributes to ozone, particulate matter, and other air quality challenges. In regions that attract area sources such as warehouses and distribution centers and, indirectly, high concentrations of truck traffic along freight corridors, the modern air pollution control system breaks down. 

Specifically, the cumulative impact of mobile (e.g., truck traffic) and underregulated area sources can result in poor air quality, even as facilities comply with existing air quality and emissions standards. These impacts, particularly in overburdened communities, raise the stakes for balancing regional air quality and localized impacts further. Fortunately, there are underutilized areas of law, including Section 110 of the Clean Air Act, that can address both regional nonattainment with existing air quality standards and the neighborhood-scale, disparate impacts of industry operations and practices.

This report considers the rise and renewal of Indirect Source Review (ISR), its basis in law, its design and enactment in the San Joaquin Valley and Southern California, and its promise for adoption in other regions across the country. We find that ISR is not only a legal imperative, but also an opportunity for regional air districts, state regulators, and communities to rebalance the benefits and costs of land use, including public health benefits and equity concerns, and to overcome the presumption, adopted by regulators years ago, that air quality in a surrounding community should be considered protective in areas that comply with air quality standards.

title: On the Ordering of Vine Copula Construction for Risk Measures Forecasting and Asset Allocation
affiliations: and University of Campinas

detail.title: On the Ordering of Vine Copula Construction for Risk Measures Forecasting and Asset Allocation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was financial in part by the coordenação de Aperfeiçoamento de pessoal de Nivel Superior - Brasil (CAPES) - Finance code 001, grant 88887.711369/2022-00; the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development (CNPq), grant 409630/2024-1; and the São Paulo Research Foundation (FAPESP), grants 2023/02538-0, 2023/01728-0, 2025/06131-7, and 2025/08502-2.

detail.abstract: Vine copulas are well-established and commonly used tools for modelling and forecasting financial time series, largely, favoured for their flexibility in capturing complex dependence structures among multiple time series. However, despite their strong empirical performance, the construction of vine copulas can become computationally demanding in moderate and high-dimensional settings, partly, because ordering procedures are typically required to mitigate the combinatorial complexity of model specification. In this paper, while acknowledging the importance of ordering in vine copula construction, we investigate its practical impact on risk measures forecasting and portfolio allocation. Specifically, we evaluate whether the widely adopted R-vine ordering algorithm proposed by Dissmann et al. (2013) offers significant advantages over a less demanding alternative: a D-vine copula based on an arbitrary ordering. Through Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical applications, we show that, after appropriate marginal modelling and pairs copula selection, the specific ordering of series plays a limited role in forecasting risk measures, but remains relevant for portfolio construction.

title: On a Simple Relationship Between Order Imbalance, Skew and Width in Over-the-Counter Trading

detail.title: On a Simple Relationship Between Order Imbalance, Skew and Width in Over-the-Counter Trading

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We consider a market maker who can only obtain and dispose of inventory by responding to a sequence of sealed-bid enquiries, and whose customers arrive with imbalanced intent: sellers more often than buyers, or the reverse. Under the assumption that the best competing response is exponentially distributed around a commonly discerned fair price, we observe a symmetry in the steady state solution that compresses the imbalanced problem onto the perfectly balanced one. Order imbalance is absorbed, exactly, by a translation of the market maker's skew, a widening of her quotes, and a multiplication of her effective cost of carry. The adjustment is simple even though the solution it adjusts is not, and it involves no free parameter beyond the observable market width. The exponential assumption is needed only locally, at the quotes actually made, and the width that enters is the locally observed one. Among the consequences: a market maker with zero inventory should still skew; skew responds to imbalance at first order whereas width responds only at second order; and the popular "constant width, linear skew" heuristic is recovered as the small-skew solution in the special case of balanced flow and quadratic holding cost.

title: Misalignment and Reconstruction of the Scientific Research System and Talent Assessment Mechanism from the Perspective of Practical Labor
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Misalignment and Reconstruction of the Scientific Research System and Talent Assessment Mechanism from the Perspective of Practical Labor
detail.abstract: Practical labor constitutes the origin of scientific knowledge generation and technological innovation evolution. Many frontline industrial technical practitioners accumulate tacit knowledge through long-term on-site production practice and can independently carry out incremental innovative activities such as process optimization and equipment retrofitting. Nevertheless, this group generally struggles to interpret highly modeled and abstract academic literature. Meanwhile, most researchers lack prolonged experience in frontline production conditions, making it difficult for them to comprehend practical constraints within industrial scenarios. A distinct discourse barrier thus emerges between academic circles and industrial sites. Against the backdrop of China s continuous reform to break the evaluation criteria of four overemphases (overemphasis on papers, academic credentials, professional titles and awards), two structural contradictions persist: the detachment of academic research from industrial reality and the formalization of talent assessment. Constrained by prevailing research evaluation incentives, some academic studies prioritize research directions with controllable experimental conditions and convenient academic output, rather than long-standing on-site technical bottlenecks in industries. Talent assessment mechanisms gradually deviate from the original goal of realizing scientific person-post matching and degenerate into hierarchical screening tools, triggering practical problems including mismatches between job requirements and academic threshold standards and oversimplified evaluation criteria. Adopting a dialectical research perspective, this paper acknowledges the instrumental value of academic theories, academic papers and standardized assessment systems. Drawing on Polanyi s tacit knowledge theory, industry-university-research collaborative innovation theory and Schumpeter s innovation theory, this paper identifies two differentiated innovation paths: experience-driven innovation and theory-driven innovation. Combined with typical manufacturing cases, the study systematically analyzes internal incentives for the separation of research systems and talent assessment mechanisms from practical labor, and clarifies cognitive misunderstandings stemming from binary opposition between theory and practice. The research reveals that the rupture of innovation chains mainly arises from high knowledge encoding and conversion costs between two types of knowledge systems, the absence of regular interaction channels, and evaluation frameworks biased excessively toward explicit written achievements. Accordingly, this paper proposes systematic reconstruction approaches from three dimensions: macro policy guidance, corporate talent management, and coordinated industrial and educational cultivation. The research aims to promote research rooted in real industrial scenarios, align talent evaluation criteria with practical job requirements, bridge communication gaps between academic communities and frontline practitioners, and provide references for high-quality innovative development of the real economy.

title: Paying for Pessimism: Verification, Escrowed Commitment, and Informational Black Holes

detail.title: Paying for Pessimism: Verification, Escrowed Commitment, and Informational Black Holes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could have influenced this work. The paper was produced by a team of AI agents under the author's sole direction; the division of labor is stated in the paper's disclosure appendix, and the complete production record (every prompt and interaction) is appended to the paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. AI model usage costs were paid personally by the author.

detail.abstract: Primary markets must sometimes pay an investor to say that a deal should stop. We study how that payment can be made when reports are costly, contracts are limited by deal cash flows, and the mechanism must survive the coalitions and renegotiations it creates. In the lead-veto contracting class we characterize, three currencies buy pessimism: a verification lottery that wastes surplus, a stake that rewards correct silence but leaves information rent, and relationship capital that pays across histories. We derive the exact rent-verification frontier and the general capacity condition. A co-investor veto contract eliminates verification waste when its cancellation fee is exactly calibrated, escrowed with a payer outside the side-contracting coalition, and the relevant history cannot be relabeled; otherwise coalitions can farm the fee. Sufficient credible capacity closes the information loss identified by Axelson and Makarov, while failures of enforcement, history integrity, or coalition discipline leave an institutional residual. The model yields testable predictions for break fees, syndication, repeat intermediaries, collateral, and costly review.

title: Macro-Monetary Policy, Cost of Capital, and the Corporate Control Cycle (1985-2025)

detail.title: Macro-Monetary Policy, Cost of Capital, and the Corporate Control Cycle (1985-2025)
detail.abstract: The market for corporate control remains an unresolved empirical paradox: mergers and acquisitions (M&A) consistently fail to create net economic value for acquiring form shareholders, yet takeover volumes cluster in massive, synchronized macroeconomic waves of consolidations and de-consolidations. This study resolves these gridlocks by revealing the relationship between merger waves and cyclical adjustments in the 3-Month U.S. Treasury bill rate. I demonstrate that an upward shift in the risk-free rate disproportionately inflates the cost of capital for large-cap firms, most of which are characterized by below-unity betas. To balance their weighted average cost of capital (WACC) and realign their debt-to-equity ratios, corporate executives rationally engage in large-scale asset acquisitions. Parallel to this, I develop a mathematical model proving that 3-month Treasury bill rate hikes paradoxically expand the aggregate money supply. Adhering to the Cantillon effect, the larger portion of new money is isolated within the upper echelon of the financial ecosystem. Large-cap giants may exploit this concentrated pool of new, cheap credit lines to fund cash-financed takeover waves. Once the risk-free rate recedes, large-cap firms likely divest their previously acquired assets, whose expected returns decline along with a decrease in the Treasury bill rate. Empirically tested via an Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model under Newey-West (HAC) robust estimation using a deflated U.S. corporate dataset (1985-2025), the results of this paper confirm that periodic oscillations of the 3-month Treasury bill rate operate as a deterministic pendulum driving the corporate control cycle.

title: Teachers and Inequality in Student Performance - Estimating Value Added and Sorting Under Endogenous Mobility
affiliations: Aarhus University and Aarhus University

detail.title: Teachers and Inequality in Student Performance - Estimating Value Added and Sorting Under Endogenous Mobility
detail.abstract: This paper deals with issues related to estimating the causal impact of teachers on student test scores. The central challenge is that students and teachers are matched non-randomly. To deal with this, we propose an extension of the standard teacher value-added model that is more robust to such endogenous mobility bias than conventional models. We then apply and extend recent innovations in bias correction of variance components to quantify the overall importance of teachers and estimate patterns of sorting and segregation. We find that teachers in Denmark are more important for student inequality than the conventional approaches would suggest. Further, we document a novel pattern of negative sorting that is driven by compensatory school investments through the within-school matching of high-value-added teachers to low-ability students. We also show that high-value-added teachers tend to be more experienced and educated and that they are particularly skilled at classroom management. Finally, we present suggestive evidence that these teachers also promote student non-cognitive skills and well-being.

title: A Priori Power Analysis Wizard: A Guided Interface for Choosing and Justifying Sample-Size Calculations in Behavioral Science

detail.title: A Priori Power Analysis Wizard: A Guided Interface for Choosing and Justifying Sample-Size Calculations in Behavioral Science

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This work received no funding, grant, or financial support from any organization.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This manuscript describes software and does not report a study involving human participants, their data, or biological material.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or funding from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Power analysis is now expected by most journals and funders, but the tools researchers are pointed to (chiefly G*Power and the pwr R package) assume the user already knows which test to run, which effect-size metric it uses, and how to translate a research question into a defensible input. That assumption is reasonable for an experienced methodologist and a genuine barrier for anyone running a power analysis for the first time, who, in our experience, more often falls back on an under-justified Cohen's-convention default than works through a principled, study-specific decision. We present the A Priori Power Analysis Wizard, an open-source tool that treats choosing the right analysis and justifying its effect size as part of the software rather than a prerequisite for using it. A plain-language decision helper routes first-time users to one of sixteen closed-form analysis families, including designs in which participants interact rather than act independently. Every effect size is justified through one of three explicit branches: Cohen's conventions, a previous estimate corrected by the safeguard-power procedure of Perugini and colleagues, or a directly stated smallest effect of interest. Distributed under the MIT license as a static WebAssembly build, the tool runs entirely in the browser with no installation or server, making it usable directly in teaching. We describe its design and validate the closed-form methods behind each family against pwr and Monte Carlo simulation; formal evaluation of its effect on users' actual decisions is left to future work.

title: A New Era for Labor Migration in the GCC?
affiliations: and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: A New Era for Labor Migration in the GCC?
detail.abstract: The six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), are among the most dependent on foreign workers to fill private-sector jobs. A combination of lower oil prices and rapid native labor force growth has given new impetus to efforts to diversify GCC economies away from oil and encourage natives to fill private sector jobs. This article summarizes the current status of foreigners and foreign workers in GCC countries and considers several scenarios, including maintaining the status quo, improving protections for foreign workers in countries of destination (CODs) and countries of origin (COOs), and changing the current migration system to employ fewer and more skilled workers.

title: Typed SSA NativeIR for Semantics-Preserving JIT and Static AOT in Gray

detail.title: Typed SSA NativeIR for Semantics-Preserving JIT and Static AOT in Gray
detail.abstract: This paper presents Gray's typed NativeIR, a bounded control-flow representation used to compile an eligible numeric subset of Gray bytecode to native code on Linux x86-64 and Apple-silicon AArch64. The initial representation records typed values, basic blocks, predecessors, terminators, source locations, runtime exits, calls, relocations, and cancellation obligations. A selective local-to-SSA pass computes local liveness, inserts explicit Phi nodes at joins, rewrites promotable loads and stores, removes trivial Phis, compacts value identities, and revalidates the result. The same verified function then feeds architecture-specific emitters for Live JIT execution or is serialized into a Static artifact and loaded without startup compilation. Unsupported signatures, bytecodes, control-flow shapes, calls, targets, and resource bounds reject the whole function to the existing VM; Static artifacts retain bytecode for the same fallback and for explicit GRAY_JIT=0 execution. Fresh Apple-silicon verification at source commit 4283424 passed IR, builder, allocator, control-flow, double, direct-call, bounded-fallback, leaf, main-region, class-method, layout, and four-policy cancellation gates. Four seeded differential fixtures contain 2,051 fixed or generated source-level calls per policy and produced identical observable output in Live JIT, Live VM, Static AOT, and Static VM modes. Two deterministic AArch64 Static builds of an 18function fixture were byte-identical; the native bundle contained 1,408 bytes of function code and five relocations. A separate 31-round measurement placed complete Static artifact construction at a 6.201 ms median on this host. Retained, CPU-pinned Linux evidence passed the corresponding x86-64 IR and differential gates. A shared exactreduction proof applied on both targets provides an extensibility case study, not a general language comparison. Gray does not yet provide a formal semantic-preservation proof, a general owned-value IR, AArch64 Linux emission, or a NativeIR-fed standalone-native publisher. The contribution is a portable, refusal-safe compiler backend for a declared subset, rather than a collection of untracked benchmark accelerators.

title: A Geopolitical Shock to Bank Assets and Monetary Policy Transmission
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank, Deutsche Bundesbank and Deutsche Bundesbank - Research Centre

detail.title: A Geopolitical Shock to Bank Assets and Monetary Policy Transmission
detail.abstract: Geopolitical shocks are typically modeled as supply shocks that monetary policy should look through. Exploiting the 2022 Russian invasion as a shock to euro area bank assets, and transaction-level deposit and loan data, we identify a countervailing financial channel. Banks with prewar exposure to Russian and Belarusian borrowers pay higher deposit rates, lose their largest depositors, and cut credit; firms dependent on these banks cannot fully substitute and reduce borrowing, employment, and investment. Before any policy action, this silent tightening was equivalent, for the customers of highly exposed banks, to a 61 basis point rate hike, about 7.6 basis points economy-wide and stable between 5 and 10 basis points across definitions requiring material exposure. Once the ECB began hiking, the same banks transmitted each 100 basis point increase by 20 (deposits) to 30 (loans) basis points more strongly than non-exposed banks. Geopolitical shocks are thus not pure supply shocks: they tighten bank-intermediated monetary conditions before and beyond any policy action, and central banks that look through them misread both the stance and its transmission.

title: Introducing Strategic Decision Space (SDS): An Integrative Conceptual Framework for Sovereign Strategic Capacity

detail.title: Introducing Strategic Decision Space (SDS): An Integrative Conceptual Framework for Sovereign Strategic Capacity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: the author declares that there are no financial interests, personal relationships, or competing interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: The ability of states to make sovereign strategic decisions has become increasingly important in an era of geopolitical fragmentation, economic interdependence, and intensifying strategic competition. Existing scholarship explains state behaviour through concepts such as balance of power, hedging, strategic autonomy, and state capacity. Although these perspectives offer important insights, none provides an integrated explanation of a state's practical capacity to formulate, implement, and sustain sovereign strategic decisions under the simultaneous influence of domestic constraints and external pressures. This paper introduces Strategic Decision Space SDS as a distinct integrative conceptual framework for assessing sovereign strategic capacity. Strategic Decision Space (SDS) as a conceptual framework for assessing sovereign strategic capacity. Strategic Decision Space is defined as the practical capacity of a state to formulate, implement, and sustain sovereign strategic decisions while managing the interaction between internal institutional conditions and the external strategic environment. Rather than treating political, institutional, economic, security, and geopolitical factors as independent variables, the framework conceptualises them as interdependent dimensions that collectively determine the scope of sovereign strategic choice. The paper concludes by outlining the theoretical implications of the proposed framework and establishes a foundation for its future operationalisation, empirical measurement, and comparative cross-national application.

title: Beyond “China + 1”: FDI Rebalancing, Regionalization, and the Reconfiguration of Asian Global Production Networks, 2020–2025
affiliations: University of Buckingham and Mewar University

detail.title: Beyond “China + 1”: FDI Rebalancing, Regionalization, and the Reconfiguration of Asian Global Production Networks, 2020–2025
detail.abstract: The primary purpose of this study is to find out whether the rising inflow of FDI in South-East Asia, which is accompanied by decreasing inflows to China, indicates the separating of these two regions structurally or if it simply reflects the process of restructuring production networks in Asia. Instead of seeing the “China + 1” phenomenon as simply relocation, this research uses theoretical approaches focusing on such concepts like eclectic paradigm, global value chains, global production networks, real-options theory, dynamic capabilities, and regional strategy of multinational companies to evaluate the case. The data for analysis has been recently obtained from UNCTAD regarding inward FDI flow in South-East Asia for the years 2020-2024 with the forecast data for the year 2025 for the identification of three empirical facts. First, the FDI inflows to South-East Asia increased from $113.1 billion to $225.3 billion while the inflow of investments into China decreased from $149.3 billion to $116.2 billion resulting in the increase of the ratio between the South-East Asia FDI and that of China from 0.76 to 1.94. Second, it has been demonstrated that Singapore accounted for more than 62-66% of the total inflow of FDI to South-East Asia that proves that FDI is influenced by factors like financing structure and ownership structure much more than relocation of production facilities. Finally, in 2024, the manufacturing FDI inflow into ASEAN countries in general increased significantly thus indicating that significant real production activities took place in the region along with the shift in investments.

title: Digitalization and the Environmental Kuznets Curve: Does ICT Moderate the Income-Carbon Emissions Relationship in 107 Countries?
affiliations: University of Zambia (UNZA)

detail.title: Digitalization and the Environmental Kuznets Curve: Does ICT Moderate the Income-Carbon Emissions Relationship in 107 Countries?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no competing interests to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable as no human subjects were involved in the study
declarations.funderStatement: No specific funding was received for this study

detail.abstract: This study investigates whether information and communication technology (ICT) moderates the relationship between economic growth and carbon dioxide (𝐶𝑂2 ) emissions across a panel of 107 countries from 2010 to 2022. Grounded in the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) framework and endogenous growth theory, the empirical strategy employs Principal Component Analysis to construct a multidimensional ICT adoption index from eight core digital infrastructure and trade variables. To address cross-sectional dependence, slope heterogeneity, and endogeneity, the analysis uses Driscoll-Kraay fixed-effects regressions and two-step System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimators. The findings confirm the baseline EKC hypothesis, revealing a robust inverted U-shaped relationship between real GDP per capita and 𝐶𝑂2 emissions per capita. Furthermore, the interaction terms between the ICT index and economic growth terms indicate that digital adoption significantly flattens the emissions trajectory during the industrialization phase. Marginal effects analysis demonstrates that higher ICT penetration reduces the positive income elasticity of emissions, allowing digitally advanced economies to decouple economic output from environmental degradation earlier in their developmental cycle. These results highlight the dual role of the digital economy as both an energy-consuming sector and a structural moderator for decarbonization.

title: Triangulated Best-Judgement Assessment as Constrained Estimation: Conservation Structure, Corridor Operators, and the Statistics of Evidentiary Standing
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Triangulated Best-Judgement Assessment as Constrained Estimation: Conservation Structure, Corridor Operators, and the Statistics of Evidentiary Standing

keywords: Generating response  Copilot said: Indirect Assessment

detail.abstract: This paper supplies the mathematical foundations of the two-pathway indirect audit framework of MWP-2026-02 and derives, from those foundations, the forensic properties that Commonwealth evidence law demands of a best-judgement assessment. The audited project is modelled as a control volume whose internal capital accumulation is bound by conservation to fluxes across instrumented boundaries — customs, banking, withholding, payroll and trade surfaces — so that each evidence stream is a boundary measurement inducing an upper bound on true cost. The supportable-cost determination is formalised as a corridor operator on these bounds and shown to be antitone in state-side evidence, isotone in taxpayer substantiation, idempotent, and 1-Lipschitz: an error in any single input propagates to the determination at most one-for-one. The stochastic analysis quantifies the downward (anti-taxpayer) bias of the minimum of noisy ceilings via order statistics, and converts the framework's graduated stringency into an explicit Bonferroni coverage guarantee and an asymmetric-loss quantile choice, giving the "known error rate" that Daubert-style admissibility analysis requests. Escalation is treated information-theoretically: corridor tightening is a monotone submodular set function of the evidence streams, so the platform's greedy request-next protocol is near-optimal with the classical (1 − 1/e) guarantee. Digit-distribution evidence is derived from scale invariance, and its forensic role is confined, by construction, to reliability and culpability. A final section maps each legal standard — the Trautwein rationality requirement, the civil balance of probabilities, the Makita exposure rule, the Daubert factors — onto a specific theorem, statistic or disclosed parameter of the framework, closing the distance between the mathematics and the courtroom. All numerical illustrations use the synthetic reference case; no real taxpayer data is used.

title: Optimization of Financial Inclusion and Digital Finance to Enhance Foreign Direct Investment in Algeria: An Empirical Analysis for the MENA Region (2000–2024)
affiliations: Hohai University and Hohai University

detail.title: Optimization of Financial Inclusion and Digital Finance to Enhance Foreign Direct Investment in Algeria: An Empirical Analysis for the MENA Region (2000–2024)
detail.abstract: Financial inclusion and digital finance have become central pillars of development strategy across the MENA region, yet their aggregate effects on foreign direct investment (FDI) remain empirically underexplored particularly for resource-dependent economies such as Algeria. This paper constructs a composite Financial Inclusion and Digital Finance Index (FIDFI) and embeds it within a threshold-based econometric framework to identify conditions under which financial inclusion enhances FDI attraction, treating disaggregated FIDFI sub-components as a pseudo-panel across seven financial-access dimensions over 2000–2024. The study employs panel unit root and cointegration tests, Hansen threshold regression, and Windmeijer-corrected Blundell-Bond System GMM, triangulated with CART, Random Forest, and regularized XGBoost with SHAP-based interaction decomposition. Data combine World Bank WDI, IMF IFS, ITU, and Worldwide Governance Indicators.Results indicate that Algeria's FDI-to-GDP ratio averaged 0.90% well below the MENA median with volatility driven by commodity price cycles and institutional fragility. A threshold effect emerges at an internet penetration rate of 38–42%, above which FDI sensitivity to financial inclusion turns positive; CART corroborates this at 41.2%. The complementarity between financial inclusion and digital payment infrastructure is positive only where regulatory quality and government effectiveness exceed sample median levels. The paper yields policy prescriptions for Algeria's 2021–2025 Economic Recovery Plan and contributes a replicable threshold-complementarity framework for comparable resource-rich economies.

title: Detection Without Enforcement: The Ukraine Facility and the Domestic Limits of the Protection of EU Financial Interests

detail.title: Detection Without Enforcement: The Ukraine Facility and the Domestic Limits of the Protection of EU Financial Interests
detail.abstract:
On 29 February 2024, the European Union enacted the most substantial funding commitment it has ever made to a state outside its own borders. Regulation (EU) 2024/792, the Ukraine Facility, commits up to €50 billion in stable and predictable financing to Ukraine by 2027, covering the country's recovery, reconstruction, and the reforms tied to its EU accession path, disbursed while the country remains at war. Alongside this commitment sits one of the developed financial-interestprotection institutions the EU has built: the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF), the European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO), a purpose-built Audit Board, and a 2024 EU-wide asset confiscation regime. EU financial-interest law was built, provision by provision, on the assumption that the conduct it targets, and the assets it seeks to recover, occur inside a Member State's territory, reachable by a Member State's police, prosecutors, and courts, or by an EU institution acting with a Member State's cooperation. The Ukraine Facility asks that same architecture to protect the EU's financial interests on the territory of a state that is not a Member State. 

This paper raises the question: when the EU detects fraud, corruption, or misappropriation affecting Ukraine Facility funds, does that detection convert into the prosecution of the individuals responsible? The thesis defended here is that it generally does not, and that the reason lies not in any deficiency of EU legislative drafting but inside Ukraine's own legal order. The EU-side architecture examined in this paper, the PIF Directive, the EPPO Regulation, the 2024 Confiscation Directive, and the Ukraine Facility Regulation itself, is built to detect irregularities and to correct them financially, by reducing or recovering EU funding. It is not built, and by its own jurisdictional limits cannot be built, to prosecute conduct committed by Ukrainian nationals, on Ukrainian soil, using funds already disbursed. That task depends on two domestic Ukrainian institutions performing functions no EU body can perform for them: the State Audit Service, acting as Ukraine's Anti-Fraud Coordination Service (AFCOS), and the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) together with the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO). Where either institution's capacity is compromised, and this paper shows that both have been, the enforcement chain breaks, however well the EU-side apparatus performs its own, narrower function. No forthcoming EU legislation closes that gap because the missing power was never the EU's to grant in the first place.

title: Do brown assets hedge green assets, or merely co-move with them? Regime-dependent evidence from listed power generators
affiliations: Prague University of Economics and Business and Prague University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Do brown assets hedge green assets, or merely co-move with them? Regime-dependent evidence from listed power generators
detail.abstract: Investors in power generation are widely advised to retain brown generation assets alongside green ones on the grounds that the two hedge each other, and a growing empirical literature supports that advice by showing that measured hedging effectiveness rises sharply during market stress. We ask whether the inference follows from the measurement. Using nine technology-pure pairings of listed, predominantly European power generators — solar, wind and biomass peer groups set against coal-fired, gas-fired and nuclear peer groups — we estimate autoregressive distributed-lag models on daily returns from 2015 to 2024 and compute variance-minimising hedge ratios and Ederington hedging effectiveness in a full-period window and in separate calm and crisis windows. Measured effectiveness rises in crises by factors of up to 28.9, reproducing the established pattern. We then show, analytically and numerically, that when the hedge ratio is held constant within an estimation window the Ederington statistic is algebraically identical to the squared brown–green return correlation; across our 27 pairing-by-regime cells the two agree to within 2.8e-14 percentage points. The crisis increase therefore records rising co-movement, which is what a hedge is meant to avoid, and cannot be read as evidence of crisis protection. We further show that the cross-sectional spread of the hedge ratios tracks relative volatility rather than dependence: biomass pairings exceed 1.0 while solar pairings fall below 0.7, with no matching ordering in effectiveness. Brown assets here supply variance scaling, not diversification, and constant-ratio effectiveness should not be used to justify retaining brown generation exposure.

title: The Evolution and Diversification of Stock-Flow Consistent Modelling: A Bibliometric Review
affiliations: Universidad Central del Ecuador, Students, Facultad Latinoamericana de Ciencias Sociales (FLACSO) - Ecuador, Students,  and Facultad Latinoamericana de Ciencias Sociales (FLACSO) - Ecuador, Students

detail.title: The Evolution and Diversification of Stock-Flow Consistent Modelling: A Bibliometric Review
detail.abstract: This paper presents a bibliometric analysis of the Stock-Flow Consistent (SFC) literature from 1975 to 2026. The corpus includes 479 publications from Scopus, Web of Science, and expert-guided screening. Building on the classification proposed by Nikiforos and Zezza (2017), using keyword-based classification and manual validation, the paper maps the evolution of five major research areas: extensions of the core SFC framework, open-economy models, empirical SFC models, ecological SFC models, and SFC-agent–based models. The results show a clear expansion of the literature after the Global Financial Crisis, followed by further acceleration after 2017. Recent growth is especially visible in empirical and ecological SFC applications, as well as in works combining multiple research areas. The journal mapping also shows that, while SFC research remains strongly rooted in heterodox economics outlets, it has increasingly expanded into interdisciplinary and non-traditional journals. The paper contributes by updating the 2017 survey and documenting the diversification and broader diffusion of SFC research.

title: Chemistry-Contingent Incentives and Upstream Mineral Output: Evidence from Indonesia's Nickel-Battery Value Chain
affiliations: Padjadjaran University - Faculty of Economics and Business

detail.title: Chemistry-Contingent Incentives and Upstream Mineral Output: Evidence from Indonesia's Nickel-Battery Value Chain

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Does a downstream incentive conditioned on battery chemistry raise upstream mineral output? Using a recursive-dynamic CGE model of Indonesia calibrated to the 2020 Input-Output Table, we simulate nickel-contingent electric-vehicle incentives to 2060. Battery output rises 99 percent by 2050, yet nickel output is invariant, changing by under 0.01 percent. Two conditions bind. Ore reaches batteries only indirectly, through smelting, giving an effective linkage coefficient of 0.224 percent; and capacity constraints remove even that. Quadrupling capacity yields 0.234 percent, matching the input-output prediction. A technology-neutral incentive of equal size delivers identical vehicle output at no chemistry-specific fiscal cost.

title: Local Non-Bossiness and Improvements over Deferred Acceptance
affiliations: University of Southern California

detail.title: Local Non-Bossiness and Improvements over Deferred Acceptance
detail.abstract: In school choice, the student-proposing deferred acceptance mechanism (DA) is stable and strategy-proof, but it may be Pareto inefficient for students. Duque-Rosas, Pereyra, and Torres-Martínez (2026) show that DA is locally non-bossy: a student who changes her report and keeps her school cannot change who else is assigned to that school. We ask whether mechanisms that Pareto improve upon DA inherit this protection. Any improvement over DA preserves the size of every school and the set of unassigned students; hence, when schools have a single seat, every mechanism that improves upon DA is locally non-bossy. With multi-seat schools the conclusion fails: we exhibit an environment in which no Pareto-efficient mechanism that improves upon DA is locally non-bossy. Efficiency adjustments can therefore give a student leverage over her classmates even when they give her none over her school.

title: Privacy by Architecture: Protecting Sensitive Data in AI-Powered Intake Systems
affiliations: FiftyOne AI, Stafford Moore PLLC, FiftyOne AI, Howard University School of Law and Howard University School of Law

detail.title: Privacy by Architecture: Protecting Sensitive Data in AI-Powered Intake Systems
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming intake processes for advocacy organizations, legal aid providers, healthcare systems, and community groups, with the potential to close the service gaps that leave vulnerable communities without adequate help. Yet AI-powered intake creates a critical privacy paradox: the individuals and communities most in need of these services are often those most endangered when their personally identifiable information (PII) is processed by cloud-based AI systems. A single breach, a single rogue employee, or a single government subpoena to a platform provider can expose the data of thousands of people who sought help from the organizations they trusted. This paper presents V.E.I.L. (Verified Entity Isolation Layer), a privacy architecture deployed in the JustAsk AI-powered form builder. The Protection Layer runs entirely on the respondent's device with zero download, identifying and stripping PII through pre-normalization, regex detection, and heuristic NER before any data leaves the browser. By default, this prevents AI services from ever accessing identifiable information. Organizations handling especially sensitive data can activate zero-access encryption: the full response is encrypted on the device with the deploying organization's public key, and the platform stores only ciphertext it cannot decrypt, rendering it mathematically unable to produce readable data under subpoena. No one and no entity between the user and the intended recipient can access the information. In a pre-publication evaluation of the live V.E.I.L. provider path on a 702-sample fabricated test set containing 2,146 labeled sensitive entities, spanning baseline intake, multicultural name and location cases, adversarial red-team examples, and focused remediation cases, V.E.I.L. achieved 89.8% recall and 82.2% F1 overall, with structured identifiers performing strongest: 100.0% F1 for email addresses, 95.4% F1 for A-numbers, 93.4% F1 for SSN and ITIN, and 93.1% F1 for phone numbers on the multicultural corpus. The Protection Layer maintains an average detection latency of 0.004 ms with less than 0.1 KB of bundle overhead. We ground our analysis in Fourth Amendment jurisprudence, the right to encrypted communication, ABA Model Rule 1.6, GDPR Article 25, and the disparate impact framework from civil rights law. V.E.I.L. is, to our knowledge, the first production form-builder system to combine client-side PII isolation with zero-access encryption for AI-powered intake in a deployment accessible to non-technical organizations.

reference: CESifo Working Paper No. 12897
title: Alternative Insurance: Gig Work and Social Insurance Participation
affiliations: Kean University and Brigham Young University

detail.title: Alternative Insurance: Gig Work and Social Insurance Participation
detail.abstract: Flexible gig opportunities provide a new means for workers to self-insure against negative economic shocks. Exploiting the roll-out of Uber, we use difference-in-differences, staggered treatment timing methods, and a survey experiment to show that access to flexible gig arrangements reduces participation in public assistance programs like Social Security Disability Insurance, Supplemental Security Income, and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. To some extent, this new private self-insurance crowds-out traditional social insurance. However, the effect of gig opportunity access on program participation is attenuated in weak local labor markets, meaning gig work does not replace social programs when insuring against aggregate, macroeconomic risks.

title: The Double-Edged Sword of AI Public Domain Myth: When Generative AI Arming Intellectual Property Against Culture Assets
affiliations: Fordham University, School of Law and Fordham Law School

detail.title: The Double-Edged Sword of AI Public Domain Myth: When Generative AI Arming Intellectual Property Against Culture Assets
detail.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has introduced a “limitless” capacity for data extraction that fundamentally threatens the integrity of Indigenous cultural heritage. While culture serves as the authentic imprint of community identity, it is currently being treated by AI developers as “raw material” for training models[1], justified by the legal concept of the public domain. This paper examines how GenAI industrializes cultural misappropriation[2], transforming the slow erosion of heritage into automated, high-scale erasure[3]. It analyzes how current intellectual property frameworks, specifically U.S. copyright law, fail to restrain this technology, often acting not as a shield for Indigenous works but as a mechanism that facilitates their extraction[4]. To prevent the hallucinations of AI from replacing authentic heritage, the paper proposes a “Fair Source” doctrine and a new legal mechanism, “Community-Embedded Authorship” (CEA), to ensure technology serves cultural sovereignty rather than extractivism.

title: The Cloud Compute Question in U.S. Export Controls, 2009–2026

detail.title: The Cloud Compute Question in U.S. Export Controls, 2009–2026
detail.abstract: Between 2009 and 2026 the question of whether U.S. export controls reach the provision of computational capacity was answered four times by advisory opinion, once by rule, and once by statute. This paper reads that record in the order it was produced and follows the form each answer took. The four advisory opinions issued by the Bureau of Industry and Security between 2009 and 2014 answered within the categories the agency already had, and the January 2009 opinion recorded that the access restriction at section 740.7(b)(2) could not be applied because it was written for individual systems whose access could be identified, whereas grid and cloud computing draw on a combination of systems out of a larger set at any one time. The interim final rule of October 2023 acknowledged that infrastructure as a service could be used to reach the capability the controls were aimed at, adopted an end-use control of a familiar kind attaching to hardware transfers and sorted by corporate headquarters, and asked providers how they would identify a customer developing a model of concern. Two trade associations answered in January 2024 that several of the rule’s criteria named facts their members do not hold, and proposed that those criteria be rewritten in values the members already compute. The Remote Access Security Act, passed by the House in January 2026, does not extend the export category to remote access. It adds remote access to the definitions section of the Export Control Reform Act as a fourth term alongside export, reexport, and in-country transfer, grants a separate authority to regulate it, and amends the statute’s references to export control so that they read as references to control. The paper describes this progression from interpretation to rulemaking to the creation of a new category. It does not assess whether the controls achieve what they are for.

title: Retrospective Amendments in Tax Law cannot Befall Penal Consequences: Supreme Court of India Ushers 'Fairness' in Fiscal Laws
affiliations: Supreme Court of India

detail.title: Retrospective Amendments in Tax Law cannot Befall Penal Consequences: Supreme Court of India Ushers 'Fairness' in Fiscal Laws
detail.abstract: Traditionally the judicial construction of fiscal paradigm in India has been postulated only a single monochromatic premise; ‘equity not a consideration in tax’; rather ‘equity and tax are strangers’. In 2014, however, a unanimous decision of larger bench of five-judges of the Supreme Court ushered a new theme. It explicitly introduced the ‘doctrine of fairness’ as new pivot in the interpretation of taxation laws. However, the decision was limited in effect; retrospectivity cannot be implied in fiscal legislations to the detriment of the taxpayers. In a recent decision the Supreme Court of India has extended the protection by declaring that (notwithstanding the legislative power to enact or validate a retrospective tax legislation) the courts must prevent retrospective tax laws “from assuming a punitive character”. The decision rules out levy of interest and penalty on back-dated tax levies, marking another critical pivot in tax jurisprudence and protecting taxpayers against hard levies.

title: On the Moments of a Noncentral Wishart Matrix: A Fast Exact Recursion
affiliations: University of Southampton, University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management and

detail.title: On the Moments of a Noncentral Wishart Matrix: A Fast Exact Recursion
detail.abstract: Hillier and Kan (2021) posed the problem of computing the moments of a noncentral Wishart matrix W recursively, rather than through combinatorial expansions of intractable size. We solve this problem. The key step is a new closure operator, obtained from Stein's identity, that turns the term created by the nonzero mean into a simple two-rule rewriting operation on symbolic expressions in the covariance and noncentrality matrices. The resulting recursion computes every moment E[W^k] and, more generally, the expectation of any product of powers and traces of powers of W in exact integer arithmetic, at a cost that in practice grows linearly with the size of the output: the tenth moment, whose published computation required days, is obtained in about ve seconds on a single core, together with the entire moment family of the same degree. The numerical coecients produced by the recursion are nonnegative integer polynomials in the degrees of freedom, and the formulas remain valid for noninteger degrees of freedom. We also establish a symmetry law for the resulting coecients and extend the theory to the complex noncentral Wishart distribution.

title: ADAM: A Governed Operating Machine for AI-Native Software and Multi-Agent Systems

detail.title: ADAM: A Governed Operating Machine for AI-Native Software and Multi-Agent Systems
detail.abstract: Large language models are rapidly moving software development from code completion toward workflow-level agency. Contemporary coding agents can inspect repositories, formulate plans, modify files, execute tools, diagnose failures, and revise implementations. Yet the ability to perform these activities does not establish that the resulting system is authorized, accountable, reproducible, or safe to operate inside consequential software environments. The central problem is no longer whether a model can generate a plausible patch. It is whether a software engineering system can preserve the relationship between human intent, model reasoning, execution authority, observed evidence, and accepted change throughout the entire development transaction. This article introduces ADAM, the Adaptive Development and Assurance Machine, and its central reasoning architecture, Governed Multimodel Reasoning, or GMR. ADAM separates reasoning, authorization, enforcement, and execution into distinct system responsibilities. Models may interpret objectives, propose plans, generate candidate changes, and critique evidence, but they do not possess an inherent right to execute tools or alter repositories. Every consequential action must cross an external assurance surface that evaluates objective scope, policy, model eligibility, tool permissions, execution context, evidence requirements, and approval state. The separation is enforced structurally rather than behaviorally: the reasoning layer holds no write path to external state, and this absence is a property of the build rather than a promise of the prompt. The article reports findings from a longitudinal action design research program in which ADAM was developed through progressively more capable experimental phases. The experiments advanced from deterministic transactions and live model planning to governed repository reads, signed worker grants, isolated patch execution, human approval workflows, durable state, model passports, validation ledgers, and real-repository collaboration. Several failures were especially informative. ADAM rejected a seemingly useful plan because it introduced an unauthorized credential-checking tool outside the approved objective. It rejected reviewer narratives containing invalid evidence references. It failed closed when live credentials were unavailable. These outcomes demonstrate that refusal, containment, and bounded incompleteness are not secondary error states. They are positive properties of an accountable engineering system. The findings suggest that reliable agentic software engineering requires a change in architectural emphasis. Intelligence should remain flexible, plural, and replaceable. Authority should remain narrow, typed, externally granted, observable, and revocable. The article proposes a ADAM: A Governed Operating Machine Surendra Reddy framework for evaluating governed engineering systems across objective fidelity, authorization correctness, evidence integrity, execution integrity, reversibility, reviewability, and adaptation discipline. It concludes that the transition from coding assistant to engineering coworker will not be completed by more capable models alone. It will require systems in which reasoning can expand without allowing authority to expand with it.

title: A Multi-Layer, Institution-Centric SOSM-NIS Framework: Structuring Innovation Challenges Through Problem Structuring Methods

detail.title: A Multi-Layer, Institution-Centric SOSM-NIS Framework: Structuring Innovation Challenges Through Problem Structuring Methods
detail.abstract: National Innovation Systems (NIS) research has expanded significantly over the last four decades. However, the field still lacks a structured conceptual foundation for distinguishing between different types of innovation challenges and for selecting appropriate analytical tools. This paper develops an institution-centric, multi-layer conceptual model that integrates the System of Systems Methodologies (SOSM) proposed by Jackson (2019) with the National Innovation System (NIS) framework of Freeman (1987), Lundvall (1992), and Nelson (1993). By decomposing NIS into micro, meso, and macro layers and mapping each layer onto SOSM categories, the model identifies the nature of innovation problems and the Problem Structuring Methods (PSMs) suitable for each context. Developed through conceptual modelling on the basis of a systematic review of existing PSMs, the framework incorporates key stakeholders and institutions-including firms, universities, innovation agencies, ministries, regulatory bodies, and national policy structuresand aligns them with PSMs based on the philosophical foundations articulated by the original developers of each method. The model's diagnostic value is illustrated through an application to Iran's national innovation system. The model advances NIS theory by clarifying the structure of system complexity and contributes to policy and practice by offering a systematic approach for diagnosing coordination failures, institutional misalignments, and systemic lock-ins. The paper concludes with implications for policymakers, intermediaries, and firms, and outlines directions for future research.

title:
After the Offshore Trust Turn 
How China's 2026 Legal Changes Will Affect Insurance-Backed Offshore Liquidity
affiliations: University of Groningen, Faculty of Law

detail.title:
After the Offshore Trust Turn 
How China's 2026 Legal Changes Will Affect Insurance-Backed Offshore Liquidity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: China's July 2026 offshore-trust tax measures meet insurance-backed offshore liquidity (IBOL) when a Hong Kong insurance asset begins to serve as collateral, trust property or both. A Mainland resident may acquire a cash-value policy, borrow against it offshore and later transfer the policy or its proceeds to a trustee. The fiscal consequences now follow more of that history. Contribution to a resident-funded trust may be taxable, income can be attributed annually before distribution, and a non-resident-funded trust may produce a taxable benefit when its property supports a resident's borrowing. Filing obligations also require a record from which funding, control, value and economic enjoyment can be reconstructed. Private-law distinctions remain important, but the stages of an IBOL arrangement are less informationally separate than before. Valuation and documentary continuity will therefore matter earlier. The outbound-investment regulation adopted in the same summer reinforces that shift, although detailed rules for resident individuals are still to come. IBOL is unlikely to disappear; it is more likely to divide between arrangements whose history can be explained coherently and those whose utility depended on gaps between remittance, policy, credit and trust.

title: The Immunocompromised Economy : Has Three Decades of Crisis Intervention Weakened America's Resilience to Recession?

detail.title: The Immunocompromised Economy : Has Three Decades of Crisis Intervention Weakened America's Resilience to Recession?

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study as it utilizes publicly available, anonymized aggregate data and did not involve human participants or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: The research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Since 2001, the United States has responded to recessions with escalating government intervention. This paper examines whether this escalation has coincided with a decline in the economy's capacity for creative destruction, the process by which recessions clear out failing firms and reallocate labor and capital toward more productive uses. Using Census Bureau Business Dynamics Statistics data, this paper compares job creation, job destruction, firm exit, and establishment entry across the 2001, 2008-2009, and 2020 recessions and their subsequent recoveries. The reallocation rate rose 13 percent above its pre-recession baseline through the 2001 recovery, the only episode without large-scale, targeted intervention, but fell 14 percent below baseline through the 2008-2009 recovery and moved only marginally in 2020. The mechanism behind this decline differed by episode: weak firm entry in 2008-2009, and weak firm exit in 2020, corresponding to the differing designs of the interventions involved. A secular trend regression confirms a statistically significant decline in reallocation of 0.29 percentage points per year since 1990, independent of any single recession. The empirical evidence shows that post-recession reallocation failed to recover during high-intervention cycles, pointing to a strong correlation and an important structural tradeoff for policymakers to consider.

title: Optimal Cognitive Capacity: Choosing How Precisely to Choose
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Center for Neuroeconomics, The University of Sydney - School of Economics and New York University (NYU)

detail.title: Optimal Cognitive Capacity: Choosing How Precisely to Choose
detail.abstract: Why do nonlinear utility and stochastic choice persist when both reduce earnings? We answer by endogenizing cognitive capacity in a model of repeated riskless choice. In our model, objective prizes are encoded as bounded, noisy subjective utilities. Higher capacity improves discrimination and reduces errors but is costly. The model captures diminishing returns to cognitive capacity and predicts endogenous and environment-specific optimal capacity and utility curvature. Changes in the range and shape of the prize distribution, as well as the number of possible prizes, and the size of the choice set influence optimal capacity and utility. We conclude that utility curvature and choice stochasticity need not reflect fixed preferences or irrationality. They can emerge jointly as an optimal response to costly cognition and the expected economic environment.

title: Divergent Paths: Corporate Governance and Sustainability Regulation in the United States and Europe, 2026

detail.title: Divergent Paths: Corporate Governance and Sustainability Regulation in the United States and Europe, 2026

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with the organizations or entities discussed in this paper that could be perceived to influence its findings.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding

detail.abstract: The year 2026 marks a visible bifurcation in how the world's two largest regulatory blocs treat corporate sustainability and governance obligations. In the United States, a combination of federal deregulation, a withdrawn Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) posture toward shareholder-proposal exclusion requests, and state-level uncertainty has produced a governance environment in which formal rules have loosened even as procedural volume has, paradoxically, increased. In the European Union, the long-anticipated Omnibus simplification package has narrowed the scope of flagship due-diligence and reporting directives without abandoning the underlying mandatory-disclosure architecture. This paper synthesizes primary regulatory developments, shareholder-proposal voting data, and governance-advisory research published between January and August 2026 to characterize this divergence, examine its proximate causes, and consider its implications for multinational companies, institutional investors, and corporate boards. The analysis finds that procedural deregulation in the United States has not reduced governance activity so much as redistributed it-toward governance-topic proposals, litigation, and board-level oversight of strategy, artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity-while European simplification has concentrated compliance obligations on a smaller set of very large firms. The paper concludes that the practical effect for globally active companies is convergence on a de facto minimum standard, driven less by any single jurisdiction's ambition than by the operational necessity of managing two moving regulatory targets at once.

title: Trading the Jump in Prediction Markets

detail.title: Trading the Jump in Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: Prediction-market prices are quoted as probabilities, but the object high-speed traders race to discover is the tradable value of the claim, and the two can diverge. I model public-news trading as a race between jump traders and market-maker cancellation, then estimate the model by maximum likelihood on 2,046 contract-announcement events around scheduled U.S. macroeconomic releases. Maker cancellation wins five of six stale-quote races, so the race burns thirty percent of stale rents, identified from the trader-win share alone. With twenty-two minute adjustment half-lives, faster price discovery worsens probability accuracy after valuation-only news. Counterfactuals price maker defense, batching, and quote withdrawal.

title: Does Momentum Survive Transaction Costs in Korea? Survivorship-Free Evidence Net of a Time-Varying Securities Transaction Tax

detail.title: Does Momentum Survive Transaction Costs in Korea? Survivorship-Free Evidence Net of a Time-Varying Securities Transaction Tax
detail.abstract: I test whether cross-sectional price momentum is profitable in the Korean equity market once realistic frictions and standard biases are removed. Using a survivorship-free universe of 3,361 securities from Compustat Global Security Daily over 2010-2026-including every firm that delisted during the sample-I evaluate twelve long-only momentum specifications and the value-weighted winner-minus-loser (WML) spread against a true buy-and-hold benchmark, net of Korea's statutory securities transaction tax (STT), commissions, and slippage. The WML spread is 6.0% per year gross but statistically indistinguishable from zero (t = 0.60), and it is insignificant in every sub-period examined. No long-only specification beats buy-and-hold net of costs; the most concentrated variants lose up to 19% per year. None survives White's (2000) Reality Check for data-snooping (p = 0.67). A cost decomposition shows the shortfall is driven primarily by the weakness of the underlying signal rather than by the transaction tax: even with all costs set to zero, momentum underperforms buy-and-hold, while the STT contributes roughly one percentage point per year. The results reinforce and modernize earlier findings of weak or negative momentum in Korea (Chui, Titman, and Wei, 2000; Chae and Eom, 2009), using survivorship-free data, a time-varying statutory cost schedule, and multiple-testing corrections.

title: Optimal Tax Depreciation Rules under Limited Classes
affiliations: and BI Norwegian Business School

detail.title: Optimal Tax Depreciation Rules under Limited Classes
detail.abstract: Tax depreciation systems apply a limited number of statutory rules to a heterogeneous set of capital assets. A common approach is to match economic depreciation as closely as possible for each asset. We show that this principle is generally not aligned with efficiency maximization under the given constraint. By assigning statutory depreciation rates, the tax depreciation system affects relative user costs and thereby the economy-wide allocation of capital across assets. Efficiency therefore depends not only on asset-specific deviations from true user costs, but also on interactions among tax-induced wedges and the economic importance of the affected assets. As a result, optimal policy departs from asset-by-asset accuracy. Instead, it prioritizes coordinating user-cost wedges among interacting assets and allocating more precise treatment to economically important inputs. This perspective yields several implications. Assets with identical economic depreciation may optimally receive different tax treatment, and even when a first-best depreciation rate is available for an asset, it need not be optimal to assign it to that class. Conversely, assets with different depreciation rates may be optimally grouped together. Moreover, improving the accuracy of a given asset in isolation can increase overall inefficiency if it worsens the pattern of wedges across interacting inputs. In fact, there exist cases in which a policy that is strictly less accurate for every asset generates lower efficiency loss by better coordinating wedges across the production system.

title: The Thermodynamic Cost of Attention: A Landauer-Bounded Model of Rational Inattention
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Thermodynamic Cost of Attention: A Landauer-Bounded Model of Rational Inattention
detail.abstract: Rational inattention models (Sims, 2003) posit that agents optimally choose how much information to acquire about payoff-relevant states, subject to a cost proportional to the Shannon mutual information between the state and the agent's signal. The proportionality constant-the "shadow price" of attention-is standardly left as a free, unmodeled parameter. This paper proposes a structural micro-foundation for that cost function using two results from the physics of computation: Landauer's (1961) principle, which establishes a lower bound on the energy dissipated per bit of information processed, and the theory of finite-time thermodynamic dissipation, which shows that any information-processing protocol executed faster than quasistatically incurs an additional cost that grows with the square of the information processed and inversely with the time allotted. Combining these two results yields a cost function that is linear in information at the margin but convex in the rate of information acquisition, generating a testable speed-accuracy trade-off in economic decision-making that is absent from the standard linear-cost specification. We derive the agent's optimal attention choice, characterize comparative statics with respect to decision stakes, time pressure, and a "cognitive temperature" parameter, and discuss, with appropriate caution, how the model's structure-as distinct from its literal physical constants-can be disciplined and tested empirically.

title: Uncertainty in Refinancing Costs for Foreign-Currency Sovereign Bonds Issued by Developing Country Governments -An Empirical Analysis Based on Issuance Yield Estimation and Spread Decomposition-

detail.title: Uncertainty in Refinancing Costs for Foreign-Currency Sovereign Bonds Issued by Developing Country Governments -An Empirical Analysis Based on Issuance Yield Estimation and Spread Decomposition-
detail.abstract: This study examines uncertainty in the refinancing costs of foreign-currency sovereign bonds issued by developing-country governments, distinguishing between the short-term predictability of issuance yields and longer-term changes in market conditions. It first estimates yields on new issues and refinancing transactions using secondary-market yields, comparing the Nelson-Siegel model, cubic spline interpolation, and the Nelson-Siegel Approach with Local Interpolation (NS-LI). The results show that issuance yields can be estimated with reasonable accuracy using market information available immediately prior to issuance. The estimated issuance yields are then decomposed into the benchmark rate, a spread common to developing-country sovereigns, and the marginal spread per rating notch. The results indicate that refinancing costs are strongly influenced by exogenous factors, particularly U.S. interest rates and global risk appetite. During risk-off episodes, borrowing costs for lower-rated sovereigns tend to rise through an increase in the marginal spread. By quantifying the sources of refinancing-cost uncertainty, this study highlights the need for developing-country governments to manage issuance volumes, maturity structures, foreignexchange reserves, and redemption profiles while accounting for changes in U.S. interest rates, global risk appetite, and rating-dependent spreads.

reference: Journal of Economics and Business Issues, Volume 6, No. 2, pp. 15–29 (2026).
title: Risk-Related Expenditure Pressure and Urban-Rural Consumption Structure in China: Provincial Evidence
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Risk-Related Expenditure Pressure and Urban-Rural Consumption Structure in China: Provincial Evidence

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Economics and Business Issues, Volume 6, No. 2, pp. 15–29 (2026).

detail.abstract: This study examines whether provincial rural-urban differences in medical and health care expenditure shares are associated with differences in education, culture, and recreation (ECR) expenditure shares in China. It develops household shock-absorbing capacity as an analytical distinction from subjective risk preference: observed willingness to accept risk may depend not only on preferences but also on whether income, liquid resources, and social protection allow a household to withstand failure. Using a balanced panel of 31 provincial regions from 2015 to 2024, the study estimates two-way fixed-effects models with controls for provincial GDP per capita, the rural-urban disposable-income ratio, urbanization, and the share of the population aged 65 and above. In the preferred specification, a one-percentage-point increase in the ruralurban medical expenditure-share gap is associated with a 0.224-percentage-point decline in the rural-urban ECR expenditure-share gap. The coefficient remains negative when the old-age dependency ratio replaces the aging control and under both province-clustered and Driscoll-Kraay inference. However, amount-based, compositional log-ratio, first-difference, and lead-placebo specifications do not support a strong causal or absolute crowding-out interpretation. The evidence is therefore interpreted as a provincial-level association in consumption composition. Implications for demand composition and innovation are presented as bounded theoretical extensions rather than directly tested outcomes.

title: An Evaluation of the Adequacy of Ghana's Legal Regime for the International Carriage of Goods by Sea: Alignment with International Standards and Capacity to Regulate Emerging Maritime Technologies

detail.title: An Evaluation of the Adequacy of Ghana's Legal Regime for the International Carriage of Goods by Sea: Alignment with International Standards and Capacity to Regulate Emerging Maritime Technologies
