declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable.

detail.abstract: A bill of lading plays a crucial role in the international sale and carriage of goods using the maritime artery, particularly the sea. The document serves as a receipt for the goods shipped, a document of title, and evidence of the contract of carriage. Ghana enacted the Bills of Lading Act, 1961 (Act 42), which incorporates specific provisions, subject to certain statutory modifications, of the International Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules of Law Relating to Bills of Lading, signed at Brussels on August 25, 1924, commonly referred to as the Hague Rules. Act 42 revoked the Carriage of Goods by Sea Ordinance (Cap 242) and the operation of the United Kingdom Bills of Lading Act, 1855. However, 64 years after the enactment of Act 42, the Hague Rules have been revised twice through the Hague-Visby Rules (1968) and the 1979 Additional Protocol. The amendments introduced changes in maritime transport practices, such as containerization and bulk cargo transportation and refined the liability regime in the Hague Rules. Additionally, at a time when countries such as the UK are recognising trade documents, including bills of lading and bills of exchange, in electronic form, Ghana has yet to update its 64-year-old law. The paper discusses the limitations inherent in Act 42 in light of international standards and trends. It recommends amending the law to incorporate electronic bills of lading.

title: The Two-Layer Economy of Intelligence IV: The Frontier as an Escape Hatch — Payload Cost and the Projection of the Two-Layer Structure into Orbit

detail.title: The Two-Layer Economy of Intelligence IV: The Frontier as an Escape Hatch — Payload Cost and the Projection of the Two-Layer Structure into Orbit
detail.abstract: The first three installments of this series established a two-layer economy of intelligence—a commoditizing Base Layer and a scarcity-preserving Apex Layer (Paper I)—traced electricity cost as a physical constraint on that structure (Paper II), and showed that the diminishing returns of scaling laws are bounded by the finitude of terrestrial "specific factors": electricity, data, semiconductors, cooling, and land (Paper III). This paper (Paper IV) asks whether expansion beyond Earth—to the orbital frontier—relaxes that limit, and if so, whether it disperses or concentrates the two-layer structure. Borrowing Frederick Jackson Turner's frontier thesis (1893) as an ideal type—the frontier as a "safety valve" that disperses tension and power—we test two rival hypotheses against the pivotal empirical variable of payload (launch) cost and the 2025–2026 orbital-datacenter race. Launch cost has fallen roughly 97% (Space Shuttle ~$54,500/kg to reusable Falcon 9 ~$1,500/kg), but the next order-of-magnitude drop depends entirely on Starship, whose $67–200/kg target remains unproven. We read SpaceX/xAI's "Starmind" constellation and "AI1" satellite—a private, vertically integrated actor backed by a record $75-billion IPO—against China's state-led Three-Body Computing Constellation, as embodiments of the "integration" and "sovereign" poles projected into orbit. Our conclusion: the orbital frontier is not a safety valve. Because orbital constellations require trillion-dollar or state-scale capital, the frontier raises entry barriers by orders of magnitude and concentrates rather than disperses—a double inversion of Turner's thesis (a competitive-arena extension rather than a safety valve; concentration rather than dispersion). The two-layer structure is not dissolved but projected into orbit and sharpened. We are explicit that this is anticipation, not prediction: the claims rest on unproven launch economics and early-stage ventures.

title: Beyond Visibility: Measuring the Impact of Strategic Communications on the Sustainability of UN-Led Development Programs

detail.title: Beyond Visibility: Measuring the Impact of Strategic Communications on the Sustainability of UN-Led Development Programs
detail.abstract: Within the United Nations system, strategic communications have historically been marginalized as a peripheral public relations function rather than recognized as a core operational instrument of development efficacy. This paper investigates the empirical and theoretical nexus between structured strategic communication frameworks and the long-term sustainability of multilateral development interventions. By aligning strategic communication with the revised 2019 OECD-DAC evaluation criteria-specifically Relevance, Coherence, and Sustainability-and examining multi-country project execution frameworks across agencies such as the IAEA, the International Trade Centre (ITC), and UNCTAD, we demonstrate that proactive stakeholder engagement, bilingual visibility campaigns, and institutional transparency directly mitigate project implementation risks and enhance local ownership. We introduce the Strategic Communication Efficacy Index (SCEI), a novel evaluative framework designed to quantify the correlation between communication investments and post-project sustainability across developing and fragile economies.

title: Regimes Matter: Regime-Based Dynamic Asset Allocation Using Neural Networks
affiliations: , University of Connecticut - Department of Finance, Old Dominion University - Department of Mathematics and Statistics and Disciplined Alpha

detail.title: Regimes Matter: Regime-Based Dynamic Asset Allocation Using Neural Networks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We study Merton's optimal portfolio problem in a market responsive to macroeconomic regimes, as characterized by VIX. Instead of solving the traditional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, we train an artificial neural network (ANN) to learn the optimal allocation as a feedback function. Our regime-specific strategy using a simple ANN with one hidden layer, benchmarked against the classical Merton portfolio, shows superior performance subject to realistic diversification constraints with borrowing/short selling excluded. A 35-year backtest (1990-2024), including 17 out-of-sample years, on a diversified portfolio of twelve assets plus cash, reveals that accounting for regime shifts improves both expected utility and average returns.

title: AI Assistance, Labor Demand, and Stability in Matching Markets
affiliations: Université Paris-Saclay

detail.title: AI Assistance, Labor Demand, and Stability in Matching Markets
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can raise productivity while also reshaping employment patterns and the organization of work. We study AI assistance in matching markets with contracts, where hospitals may add an AI-assisted term to contracts offered to doctors. Although all previously available contracts remain available, every doctor may become strictly worse off at every stable allocation. We identify observable aggregate-demand displacement, a restriction on hospital choice that prevents this welfare reduction at the doctor-optimal stable allocation. We then introduce preference restrictions governing how AI changes doctors' choices across hospitals and the doctors represented in hospitals' chosen sets, and derive comparative-statics results for cumulative offer processes. Building on these comparative statics, we characterize the maximal domain on which no doctor is harmed. We also identify conditions under which offering AI assistance benefits hospitals under the side-optimal stable mechanisms.

title: Memoranda on Competition (Amendment) Bill (National Assembly Bill No. 4 of 2026) on Digital Market Competition Regulation in Kenya
affiliations: Technische Universität München (TUM)

detail.title: Memoranda on Competition (Amendment) Bill (National Assembly Bill No. 4 of 2026) on Digital Market Competition Regulation in Kenya
detail.abstract: Since independence, the Kenyan market economy has shifted from a state-controlled to an open and competitive market. In 2010, Kenya enacted a modern competition legislation to replace the 1989 Restrictive Trade Practices, Monopolies and Price Control Act. The established Competition Authority of Kenya (CAK), in its enforcement activities, especially in the banking and telecommunication sectors, has enhanced business competitiveness in Kenya and increased foreign direct investment. During this period, the CAK has worked closely with regional competition authorities, such as the COMESA Competition and Consumer Commission (CCCC), to address regulatory challenges, including jurisdictional conflicts, conflicts of law, and inconsistent decisions, to enhance business investment. The 2026 Kenyan Competition (Amendment) Bill (the Bill) seeks to amend the 2010 Competition Act (Cap. 504) to broaden CAK’s mandate to address anti-competitive conduct in digital markets and unfair market conduct arising from the abuse of a superior bargaining position. This submission, drawing on domestic, regional, and global developments in the regulation of competition in digital markets, seeks to draw the Kenyan Parliament's attention to the important policy and economic consequences of the Bill for business investment, innovation, and international cooperation with international partners, including big tech companies.

title: Dynamical Systems: The Four Quadrants Version 8
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, City University of New York (CUNY) - Department of Real Estate

detail.title: Dynamical Systems: The Four Quadrants Version 8
detail.abstract: This note offers a pedagogic approach to understanding dynamical systems, emphasizing the connections between discrete time and continuous time, and between deterministic and stochastic systems. Many people find discrete-time stochastic processes much more intuitive than their continuous-time analogs. This note shows that the two are in fact very similar, and that the continuous-time versions become far easier to understand when read alongside their discrete-time counterparts. The organizing device is a 2 × 2 table. One dimension is time: discrete or continuous. The other is randomness: deterministic or stochastic. We work through all four quadrants with the same running example-a mean-reverting process-so that the only thing changing from cell to cell is the modelling apparatus, never the economics. We then replace the driving randomness with jumps and ask which results survive. Terms are defined precisely, and then again in plain language, before they are used. Every result stated in the main text is derived line by line in the appendix.

title: Where the Risk Lives: Exchange-Rate Pegs, Dollar Debt, and Debt Deflation
affiliations: Chuo University

detail.title: Where the Risk Lives: Exchange-Rate Pegs, Dollar Debt, and Debt Deflation
detail.abstract: A country whose firms owe dollars is told to fear floating: if depreciation would imperil dollar-indebted firms, fix the exchange rate. This advice misidentifies where the risk lives. Because the real burden of dollar debt moves with the terms of trade (depreciation minus domestic inflation), a peg cannot make revaluation risk disappear; it only relabels it as debt deflation. A world interest-rate shock forces the peg to tighten sharply to defend the parity, while an inflation targeter barely moves rates, so roughly half the revaluation survives as deflation. We then add the strongest countervailing force against the anti-peg result, remittances, whose domestic value rises with depreciation: in a two-agent New Keynesian small open economy at second order, they cushion the peg's cost but do not overturn the ranking. In the benchmark calibration, domestic-inflation targeting dominates for both groups, and above a threshold hand-to-mouth share the peg loses local stability.

title: The Accountancy Cartel: How a Model Law, the State Boards, and the IRS Managed Out an Equivalent Competitor

detail.title: The Accountancy Cartel: How a Model Law, the State Boards, and the IRS Managed Out an Equivalent Competitor
detail.abstract: The 2015 Supreme Court case of N.C. State Board of Dental Examiners v. FTC (NC Dental) set forth precedent that licensing boards run by market participants are vulnerable to antitrust liability and that such boards must have active supervision by the state in order to maintain state action immunity from antitrust lawsuits. However, as it relates to public accountancy licensing, there are two things that heighten that vulnerability: the first of which is the federal cascade where state-level CPA and non-CPA distinctions in practice scope play a role in federal practice rights and exclusions via the IRS's Circular 230, known as parity determination. The second of which is the class-mortality finding, where such determinations are predicated upon whether the non-CPA class is that of a perpetual or a dying class, and not based on true competency, which the existing public protection rationale does not explain. Across thirty Office of Chief Counsel memoranda covering twenty-nine states, Delaware alone presented an open, scope-equivalent class, and Delaware alone was denied. The foundational framework from which this article makes its core argument is based on the Uniform Accountancy Act (UAA), which was drafted by the profession itself: American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) and National Association of State Boards of Accountancy (NASBA), two influential active market participants. This article applies to the accountancy profession the board-capture framework as explained by Edlin and Allensworth, documenting two mechanisms that have not been located in prior research works. It documents a theory of competitive harm and a roadmap for enforcement; it does not claim to establish a violation.

title: Quantifying the Financial Risk of Online Gambling Using Mathematical Modeling
affiliations: , Unaffiliated Author, Unaffiliated Author, Unaffiliated Author and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Quantifying the Financial Risk of Online Gambling Using Mathematical Modeling

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used publicly available data and mathematical modeling. No human participants, identifiable personal data, or animal subjects were involved; therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a mathematical and statistical framework for quantifying the financial risk associated with online sports gambling. Rather than evaluating gambling outcomes solely by winnings and losses, the model defines financial harm relative to disposable income after taxes and essential expenditures. Parallel disposable income models are developed for the United States and the United Kingdom using publicly available demographic, taxation, and expenditure data. Building on this foundation, annual gambling outcomes are modeled as a stochastic process incorporating betting intensity, loss-chasing behavior, income variability, and sportsbook house edge. Monte Carlo simulation is used to estimate insolvency risk, defined as annual gambling losses exceeding disposable income. The framework is then extended to evaluate population-level effects, including aggregate debt burden, financial fragility, and long-term wealth erosion. Results indicate that gambling-related financial harm is disproportionately concentrated among lower-income individuals and those exhibiting high-risk behavioral patterns, particularly loss-chasing. The proposed framework provides a quantitative approach for assessing gambling-related financial vulnerability and may inform future research on consumer finance, behavioral economics, and public policy.

title: Bridging the Disability Digital Divide: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Accessibility and Inclusion
affiliations: Berhampur University and Berhampur University

detail.title: Bridging the Disability Digital Divide: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Accessibility and Inclusion
detail.abstract: Despite increasing recognition of disability rights, persons with disabilities (PwDs) continue to experience structural exclusion from the digital sphere. This exclusion restricts access to education, employment, healthcare, and civic participation, thereby reinforcing broader social inequalities. This study conducts a systematic review and meta-analysis of literature on the disability digital divide published between 2015 and 2025. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted across Scopus, PubMed, and Google Scholar using keywords such as digital accessibility, disability digital divide, disparity, and welfare schemes. Out of 453 records initially retrieved, 74 peer-reviewed studies met the eligibility criteria and were included for analysis. Data were synthesised thematically to identify recurring barriers, enablers, policy interventions, and gaps. Findings show that inaccessible digital infrastructure, affordability constraints, and limited digital literacy remain persistent barriers. These challenges are especially pronounced in rural and low-income contexts, where exclusion is compounded by socio-economic disadvantage. At the same time, enabling factors such as assistive technologies, inclusive ICT design, and community-led initiatives were shown to promote meaningful digital participation. Government efforts, including India’s Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016 and the Accessible India Campaign, represent important milestones but remain limited by weak enforcement, low awareness, and fragmented implementation. The review also highlights regional disparities, with research concentrated in the Global North and emerging but uneven contributions from the Global South. Digital inclusion for PwDs is not only a technological imperative but a matter of equity, justice, and human rights. Strengthening accessible ICT ecosystems through enforceable policies, universal design, and sustainable community-driven practices is essential for bridging the divide. Such measures are critical for advancing the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and SDG 16 (Inclusive Institutions).

title: The No Salt Policy: A Preventive Framework for Ethical Independence and Anti-Corruption Governance

detail.title: The No Salt Policy: A Preventive Framework for Ethical Independence and Anti-Corruption Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial, commercial, institutional, or personal conflicts of interest that could have influenced the preparation, interpretation, or presentation of this conceptual research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This manuscript is a conceptual research paper and does not involve human participants, patients, personal data, clinical procedures, animal studies, surveys, interviews, or experiments. Accordingly, institutional ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was independently conceived, researched, and prepared by the author without financial support from any governmental agency, commercial organization, research sponsor, or grant provider.

detail.abstract:
A substantial literature explains why corruption occurs: reciprocity norms create psychological indebtedness even from small, unsolicited exchanges (Cialdini, 1984; Gouldner, 1960; Mauss, 1925); conflict-of-interest scholarship documents how personal relationships compromise official judgment; and behavioral ethics shows that decision-makers often drift into wrongdoing through incremental, self-serving rationalization rather than deliberate choice (Bazerman & Tenbrunsel, 2011). What this literature explains less fully is a simple, preventive behavioral discipline that individuals and institutions can apply before obligation forms — a gap between diagnosing the mechanism of corruption and offering an individual-level practice addressing it at the point of formation, prior to and beneath the threshold of what legal and disclosure-based instruments are designed to regulate.
This paper proposes the No Salt (Paraya Namak) Policy (NSP) as a conceptual framework addressing that gap: a preventive ethical discipline against seeking, asking for, accepting, or accumulating unnecessary obligation-based benefits, paired with the Auto Integrity Lock (AIL), a model of internalized ethical restraint developed through sustained practice and adapted conceptually from skill-acquisition and habit-formation research (Dreyfus & Dreyfus, 1986; Wood & Neal, 2007; Lally et al., 2010). The paper's core normative claim, stated formally in Section 4.2, is that ethical independence is best secured by declining to form obligation in the first instance, rather than by managing it once formed.
The framework is positioned as a conceptual and interpretive model within behavioral ethics, anti-corruption governance, and Indic ethical thought, and is compared against existing anti-corruption and governance instruments — UNCAC, the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention, ISO 37001, the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, the UK's Nolan Principles, and standard gift/hospitality disclosure regimes — to clarify where it complements rather than duplicates them. The paper expressly acknowledges that NSP/AIL is not yet empirically validated and requires future pilot testing; it offers the Integrity Activation Scale as a heuristic for that future research, not as a validated psychometric instrument, and presents NSP/AIL as a supplement to, not a substitute for, legal and institutional anti-corruption systems.

title: From Impact Intent to Financial Consequence: An Information-value Conversion Framework for Sustainable, Impact, and Development Finance
affiliations: University of Technology Sydney (UTS) - Institute for Sustainable Futures

detail.title: From Impact Intent to Financial Consequence: An Information-value Conversion Framework for Sustainable, Impact, and Development Finance
detail.abstract: Sustainable, development and impact finance increasingly seek to allocate capital according to real-world performance. Yet improvements in measurement, disclosure and assurance have not consistently translated into financial decisions that generate better real-world outcomes. Existing research has focused primarily on the production, credibility and financial consequence of non-financial information, with limited theoretical explanation of the causal processes involved. This paper explores under what conditions information about real-world outcomes becomes financially consequential. Drawing on information economics, disclosure theory, transaction cost economics and market microstructure, the paper develops an integrative Information-Value Conversion Framework. The framework identifies four serially complementary conversion conditions: performance representation capacity, financial legibility, financial value recognition and financial actionability. It distinguishes these conditions from the resulting financial consequence and the subsequent appropriation of value by the actors responsible for producing the performance and information. Failures across the information-value conversion process produce three distinct forms of breakdown. Reach failure arises when actors cannot produce or verify information in the forms finance requires. Response failure occurs when financially legible performance lacks sufficient private, regulatory, contractual or mission value to influence financial outcomes. Appropriation failure arises where the costs of producing credible performance information are borne by actors unable to capture sufficient resulting financial value, weakening incentives for future information production and superior real-world performance. The framework identifies the informational and institutional conditions under which finance can more effectively reach and reward superior real-world outcomes. Highlights-Credible performance information may remain financially inert.-Reach failure may exclude capable actors despite strong underlying performance.-Response failure leaves verified performance financially inconsequential.-Appropriation failure weakens incentives to produce credible performance information.-Information requirements can improve integrity while increasing exclusion.

title:
The Blonde Device
Sexuality, Spectacle, and Patrimonial Suspicion in Argentine Politics, 1983-2026

detail.title:
The Blonde Device
Sexuality, Spectacle, and Patrimonial Suspicion in Argentine Politics, 1983-2026
detail.abstract: In Argentine political scandal the sexualized woman does not operate as fact but as evidence. The figure journalistically constructed as blonde, showgirl, model, or influencer works as an evidentiary shortcut: it renders visible and verifiable, before an audience, a prior suspicion about the man holding power, namely that he commands money, time, and bodily access whose origin is undeclared. This paper states that hypothesis with enough precision for it to fail, and examines a corpus of high-salience episodes between 1983 and 2026. Four categories that coverage tends to fuse are separated: spectacularized romantic relationship, contradiction between private conduct and public position, scandal with patrimonial derivation, and sexual or gender-based violent crime. The fourth does not belong to the device and is treated apart, not out of prudence but because including it would destroy the hypothesis. The Insaurralde-Clerici-Cirio case serves as the core, since there sexual exhibition precedes and produces the patrimonial opening. The rumor linking Pedro Pompilio to Jésica Cirio, denied and judicially sanctioned, functions as a negative control: the device survives intact with no fact beneath it. The conviction of Ezequiel Guazzora fixes the outer limit, where the vocabulary of scandal stops describing and begins to conceal. On Peronist overrepresentation the position taken is restrictive: it cannot be asserted without building a denominator of institutional exposure, and that denominator is specified.

title: AI Driven Automated Valuation Models AVMs and Climate Devaluation in Commercial Real Estate CRE Asset Backed Financing
affiliations: and Georgia Institute of Technology

detail.title: AI Driven Automated Valuation Models AVMs and Climate Devaluation in Commercial Real Estate CRE Asset Backed Financing
detail.abstract: Commercial real estate (CRE) markets are experiencing a fundamental transformation as artificial intelligence (AI), automated valuation models (AVMs), and climate risk analytics become increasingly integrated into property assessment and asset-backed financing decisions. Traditional real estate valuation approaches have historically depended on expert judgment, comparable transactions, income capitalization analysis, and market-based indicators. While these methods remain important, they often face limitations in rapidly changing environments where climate-related risks, technological disruption, and evolving market conditions create new sources of uncertainty. This research examines the role of AI-driven AVMs in identifying and measuring climate-related devaluation risks within commercial real estate assets and explores their implications for asset-backed financing structures. The study develops a conceptual framework that combines machine learning-based valuation methods, climate intelligence, property-level characteristics, and financial risk assessment mechanisms. AI-driven AVMs are examined as advanced analytical systems capable of processing large-scale structured and unstructured data, including market transactions, geographic information, building characteristics, environmental exposure indicators, and operational performance metrics. The research investigates how these systems can improve the detection of climate-induced depreciation patterns that may influence collateral values, financing decisions, and long-term investment performance. The findings suggest that AI-enhanced valuation frameworks provide significant advantages over conventional valuation models by improving predictive accuracy, identifying complex relationships between environmental conditions and property performance, and supporting more dynamic asset valuation processes. Climate devaluation is shown to operate through multiple channels, including physical damage exposure, regulatory changes, shifting tenant preferences, insurance constraints, and changes in investor perception. Therefore, valuation systems that exclude climate-related factors may underestimate future asset impairment risks. The research further highlights the importance of combining AI capability with transparency, governance, and professional valuation expertise. Although automated valuation models can improve efficiency and consistency, their effectiveness depends on data quality, model interpretability, cybersecurity protection, and appropriate human oversight. Emerging approaches involving multimodal AI, computer vision, blockchain-supported data sharing, and machine learning-based forecasting indicate significant potential for improving CRE valuation resilience. This study contributes to the sustainable finance and real estate technology literature by demonstrating how AI-driven AVMs can support climate-aware commercial real estate financing. The integration of climate intelligence into valuation processes can enhance lending decisions, improve investor risk assessment, and support the development of more resilient real estate markets capable of responding to environmental and economic uncertainty.

title: Used Vehicle Price Differences in the Four Corners Area

detail.title: Used Vehicle Price Differences in the Four Corners Area
detail.abstract: This study examines the factors that influence used vehicle pricing throughout the Four Corners region of New Mexico, Colorado, Arizona, and Utah. The purpose of the research was to determine why similar vehicles often have significantly different prices depending on whether they are sold by a dealership or a private seller. The project applies several core microeconomic concepts, including supply and demand, consumer choice theory, market competition, price elasticity of demand, information asymmetry, and value-added services. Vehicle information was collected from Don Reeves Auto Center, competing dealerships, Facebook Marketplace, Kelley Blue Book, and Edmunds. Vehicles were compared based on year, make, model, mileage, asking price, condition, financing availability, warranty coverage, and seller type. The analysis found that dealership vehicles generally carry higher asking prices because dealerships provide additional value through inspections, vehicle reconditioning, financing options, warranties, vehicle history reports, and customer support. These services reduce consumer risk and increase buyer confidence, creating a higher perceived value than many private-party transactions. Overall, the study demonstrates that used vehicle prices are determined by much more than mileage or age and are influenced by numerous economic factors that shape both consumer demand and market equilibrium.

title: Informative blocking, the core, and majority stability

detail.title: Informative blocking, the core, and majority stability
detail.abstract: The core treats blocking as a feasibility test. This paper adds an informational requirement: a multi-member coalition informatively blocks only if it can standard-block and each member's assent raises that member's participation probability. The resulting Informative Blocking Core depends on residual payoffs and message--action relations and lies between the standard core and the imputation set. Under payoff responsiveness, a multi-member standard block is informative exactly when remaining after the others leave is strictly worse for every member. In simple majority games with $n$ players, under the zero-cost boundary benchmark, payoff responsiveness and majority-compatible residual payoffs, including canonical equal-surplus residual division, imply that an imputation survives exactly when its support has at most $\lceil n/2 \rceil + 1$ members; for even $n$, this is equivalent to support being contained in a minimal winning coalition. A threshold extension nests this benchmark: negative cutoffs weakly enlarge the surviving set, with the resulting sets decreasing to the zero-cost set as the cutoff rises to zero, whereas every positive cutoff eliminates all imputations for $n \geq 4$. In superadditive three-player games under payoff responsiveness and canonical equal-surplus residual division, equal two-player coalition surpluses over stand-alone payoffs make every imputation survive, whereas any imbalance places the Informative Blocking Core strictly between the core and the imputation set. More generally, payoff responsiveness and canonical equal-surplus residual division guarantee that every vertex imputation survives in any finite superadditive game with at least two players.

title: Cost-recovery of Grid-Scale Battery Energy Storage Systems in China’s Evolving Electricity Market
affiliations: , 3rdRail Inc., , University of California, Berkeley - Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab), CUNY - Baruch College and University of California Berkeley

detail.title: Cost-recovery of Grid-Scale Battery Energy Storage Systems in China’s Evolving Electricity Market
detail.abstract: Grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) are playing an increasingly critical role in supporting renewable integration and power system flexibility in China’s ongoing electricity market, yet whether emerging market mechanisms can provide sufficient revenues to sustain large-scale storage investment remains uncertain. Here we develop a two-stage mixed-integer optimization framework in which a representative 50 MW/100 MWh BESS acts as a price-taker in energy markets and a price-maker in regulation markets. Applying it to nine province-year cases across Shandong, Guangdong, and Shanxi from 2022 to 2024, we evaluate whether revenues from energy and regulation markets, combined with capacity payments, can support cost recovery. Under baseline conditions of 80% participation rate and 5% forecast error, co-optimizing participation in day-ahead and real-time markets raises revenue by $30–78/kW-yr relative to sequential strategies. Energy-market revenue alone can recover the annualized capital cost of $68.06/kW-yr in four of nine cases, although profit margins narrow through 2022–2024 and disappear in lower-volatility markets such as Guangdong. The newly introduced capacity payment ($8.96/kW-yr) lifts total revenue to $56–149/kW-yr and enables cost recovery in seven of nine cases, but it remains insufficient for the weakest case. The current mileage-only regulation tariff contributes little ($2–5/kW-yr). Replacing it with a two-part tariff at a 20% price-cost margin (i.e., Lerner index of 0.20) adds an additional $43–62/kW-yr and enables cost recovery in all nine cases, with results remaining robust across margins of 10–30%. Our findings show that the economic viability of grid-scale BESS in China is determined primarily by the energy market, while the capacity payment provides an important but limited complement, and regulation revenues remain constrained. Market reforms that move beyond the mileage-only regulation tariff by properly valuing both regulation capability and mileage could close the remaining cost-recovery gap, accelerate BESS deployment, and support the transition to a reliable low-carbon power system.

title: FCFE and the Equity Cash Flow: An Elementary Proof that they Yield the Same Equity Value

detail.title: FCFE and the Equity Cash Flow: An Elementary Proof that they Yield the Same Equity Value
detail.abstract: The most widely used valuation textbooks, among them those of the CFA Institute and Aswath Damodaran's Investment Valuation, state that the value of equity is obtained by discounting the free cash flow to equity (FCFE) at the required return on equity, and they present the FCFE formula without any derivation. That is, they do not explain why discounting this flow and not another yields precisely the value of equity. Pablo Fernández uses the equity cash flow (ECF), defined as the money actually distributed, to reach the value of equity as well, discounting it at the required return on equity. Fernández is one of the few authors, if not the only one, who derives the equity cash flow (ECF) rigorously from the balance-sheet identity, making clear why discounting this flow (and not another) yields the value of equity. The two flows, FCFE and ECF, differ by the change in the cash balance of the period, so that the two formulations lead to the same equity value only if the present value of the stream of cash increments is zero. This note proves, through an elementary development, that this present value vanishes when the excess cash earns the discount rate required by the shareholder, and it obtains the general expression for the case in which cash earns a different rate. That expression reproduces, as particular cases of a single line of algebra, Damodaran's rule of adding excess cash to the value of operations and Fernández's observation that hoarding poorly remunerated cash destroys value for the shareholder. The contribution lies not in the novelty of the result, known in the literature, but in the brevity and transparency of the derivation that unifies both perspectives.

title: The Sands Governing Theorem: Pre-Governing Conflict as a Necessary Condition for Long-Term State Legitimacy

detail.title: The Sands Governing Theorem: Pre-Governing Conflict as a Necessary Condition for Long-Term State Legitimacy
detail.abstract: We propose the Sands Governing Theorem: a governing class that has not been forged by pre-governing conflict-whether directly experienced or inherited within living institutional memory-lacks the legitimacy, resilience, and experiential wisdom necessary for stable long-term governance, and the state it governs will tend toward political instability in proportion to the conflict deficiency and inversely to the strength of inherited institutional memory. The paper develops the theorem formally, identifies the two variables (Conflict Deficiency Score and Institutional Memory Strength) that determine outcomes, examines historical cases across five centuries, and distinguishes the theorem from related propositions in Ibn Khaldun, Machiavelli, Hegel, and Taleb. The theorem is proposed as a testable framework for assessing the long-term stability of states, particularly post-conflict states and states undergoing generational leadership transitions.

title: Risk Behavior in Large Language Models: An Empirical Comparison of Three Models on Choices13k
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Risk Behavior in Large Language Models: An Empirical Comparison of Three Models on Choices13k

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve the recruitment of human participants or the collection of new human-subject data. It used a publicly available dataset and AI model outputs generated through API queries.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: As AI systems get increasingly integrated into risky environments such as finance or marketing, understanding how these models resolve probabilistic decisions is important. Behavioral sciences have created frameworks to evaluate human decisions, such as prospect theory, yet the extent to which these have been observed in AI remains heavily underexplored. This study evaluates three different OpenAI models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-nano and gpt-5.4-nano) on 350 A-or-B binary gambles taken from the Choices13k dataset, repeating each problem 10 times under 4 different personas (machine, human, loss-averse, and risk-taking) for a total of 42,000 decisions over models, personas, and samples. Each choice done by the model is compared to human choice rates and expected value (EV) between the two options provided. Risk behavior proved to be highly model dependent rather than uniform between the three; gpt-4o-mini selected B more often than humans (mean B-rate of 0.68-0.71 under the machine, human, and risk-taking personas, against a human average of ~0.51) while gpt-4.1-nano and gpt-5.4-nano preferred A heavily (B-rates of ~0.02 and ~0.13-0.16 under the machine and human personas, rising only to 0.30 and 0.42 under risk-taking). Personas did shift behavior in the expected direction for every model, but never closed the mean gap with human choice (below 0.33), and for gpt-4o-mini in particular, loss-averse and risk-taking actually widened it. Problem-by-problem correlation with human choices was modest at best (reaching a maximum of r = 0.52 uncorrected for noise in the human baseline values) and declined sharply for the loss-averse persona. Sensitivity to expected value was near-zero for gpt-4.1-nano for all personas, but gpt-5.4-nano tracked expected value around as well as gpt-4o-mini under neutral (human and machine) personas while still choosing Option A for most problems. These findings show that, across the models tested, risk preferences were model-specific (rather than shared), loosely connected to human data or expected value, and moved by persona and prompt. The two nano models defaulted to Option A on almost every problem. This variability across models and different framings could have consequences for automated systems that are given control over capital or important decisions, and makes a clear case for continued human oversight for such automated systems.

title: Monetary Warrant Closure Capacity: Measuring the Epistemic Quality of Monetary Policymaking
affiliations: Georgetown University

detail.title: Monetary Warrant Closure Capacity: Measuring the Epistemic Quality of Monetary Policymaking

contentType.other: Manuscript submitted for publication (not yet accepted)

detail.abstract: This paper asks a question conventional monetary-policy frameworks largely take as given: when should a central bank deliberate? It develops Monetary Warrant Closure Capacity (MWCC) to evaluate the epistemic and institutional conditions supporting policy judgment and when changing conditions warrant reconsideration. Empirical validation shows that stronger warrant-closure capacity is systematically associated with lower forecast errors. Monte Carlo (MS) simulations reveal a nonlinear relationship between scheduled reconsideration frequency and institutional loss: sparse calendars generate substantial losses, while marginal stabilization gains diminish as meetings become more frequent. Under the baseline specification, 8 meetings minimize simulated loss, while equivalence analysis identifies 6 as the smallest regular schedule statistically comparable to 8, robust to narrowing the equivalence margin from 10% to 5%. Dynamic simulations show that the value of additional reconsideration depends on policy inertia, while the break-even cost for reducing meetings from 8 to 6 rises from approximately 0.20% to 0.59% of mean Fixed-8 stabilization loss. The paper therefore endogenizes monetary-policy reconsideration: the appropriate meeting frequency depends on institutional learning, stabilization opportunities, and deliberation costs rather than on a universally optimal calendar.

title: Decision-Centred Modelling (DCM): A Governed Modular Architecture for Infrastructure Planning Under Deep Uncertainty

detail.title: Decision-Centred Modelling (DCM): A Governed Modular Architecture for Infrastructure Planning Under Deep Uncertainty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests that could have influenced the research, analysis, interpretation, or preparation of this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patients, animals, personal data, or primary data collection requiring ethics approval. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was developed in the broader context of doctoral research at Auckland University of Technology.

detail.abstract: Long-horizon infrastructure decisions often involve consequences that propagate beyond the physical boundaries of the system being modelled. Facility-level technology choices can create regional network effects, infrastructure exposure, policy interactions, and cross-scale costs that are significant to comparing alternatives, yet these consequences frequently fall outside the analytical scope of models bounded by a single physical system. The resulting gap is not only computational; it is also methodological, concerning how decision objectives, evidence, models, and uncertainty are organised when consequential effects cross analytical boundaries. This paper introduces Decision-Centred Modelling (DCM), a governed modular architecture for infrastructure planning under deep uncertainty, organised as a decision-learning process. DCM begins from the decision objective, identifies the consequences that matter for comparing alternatives, reviews the available data, models, and methods, and selects modelling approaches according to data availability, modelling maturity, and decision relevance. The framework does not prescribe a single modelling method. Instead, it standardises the artefact interface: heterogeneous modules may use synthetic profiles, optimisation, process simulation, power-system modelling, supply-chain models, emulators, or expert-informed assumptions, provided their outputs are expressed as governed, versioned, and traceable artefacts. The framework combines three design commitments: a decision-first boundary principle, a modular thin-waist artefact architecture, and robustness-oriented evaluation using regret, satisficing rate, and win rate. A bounded proof of concept demonstrates the approach through a site-to-region industrial process heat decision in New Zealand, showing how granular site-level analysis can be transformed into exchangeable artefacts, linked to a regional grid-interface screen, and evaluated across an ensemble of plausible futures. The proof of concept makes a regional infrastructure consequence visible and evaluable within a single traceable comparison, revealing it to be threshold-triggered, absent in some futures and consequential in others, a structure that a site-boundary comparison cannot represent. The numerical results are illustrative and reflect simplified, low-to-medium maturity modules; they are not presented as calibrated operational guidance for the real facility. The contribution is therefore methodological: DCM provides a governed way to make decision-relevant consequences visible, traceable, and progressively refinable as evidence and modelling capability improve.

detail.abstract: International Labour Organization (ILO) and directorates of employment of various countries have mapped out strategies that would enhance fair recruitment exercise between recruiters and potential migrant workers. However, some recruiters take advantage of migrant workers' experiences and economic hardship to deny them their rights and privileges. This paper, adopting the content analysis approach of the qualitative research method, evaluates the video content that showcases some of the traumatic experiences of migrant workers who thought before leaving their countries of origin that their new work environment would meet their needs and aspirations. Also the researcher utilized survey design of quantitative research methodology to ascertain the level of awareness created so far in the public to intimate the masses about the rudiments of fair and unfair recruitment exercises. Majority of the respondents are Nigerians. One of the objectives of this survey is to sample the opinions of some workers who engage in internal or interstate migrations across Nigeria, and to evaluate their experiences about fair and unfair recruitments. The population of the survey is 50 participants who filled an online Microsoft Form that contained the questions of the survey. The researcher discovered that there are traces of forced labour from the video content evaluated in this study. Answer to question number 8, from the survey conducted also reveals that 32 respondents, representing 65% of the population have not heard about Fair recruitment, as such, there is a need for ILO to create more awareness on the tenets of fair recruitment and the rights of migrant workers. The researcher further recommends that more campaigns should be carried out through the secondary schools and tertiary institutions, media and social media platforms, by organizing or instituting short-and long-term courses, and sensitization programmes for prospective migrant workers.

detail.abstract: The current account balance of the Russian Federation’s balance of payments in Q1 2026 amounted to $12.2 bn, a 34% decrease from the corresponding figure for Q1 2025. The financial account deficit (excluding reserve assets) narrowed to $14.5 bn, compared with $16.8 bn a year earlier. The decline in net capital outflows was driven by a reduction in purchases of foreign assets. The ruble exchange rate weakened by 3.9% over the quarter (to Rb81.3 per dollar), but strengthened to Rb74.9 per dollar in April. The average ruble exchange rate is expected to be Rb75–85 per dollar in 2026.

title: When Deterrence Fails: Lessons From the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War
affiliations: O.P JINDAL GLOBAL UNIVERSITY

detail.title: When Deterrence Fails: Lessons From the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War
detail.abstract: One of the most complicated conflicts in Eurasia, the Nagorno-Karabakh dispute between Armenia and Azerbaijan, devolved into full-blown war in 2020, ending its so-called "frozen" status. However, a closer look at the historical underpinnings of this conflict, along with the thirty-year gap between the first and second wars, reveals a more complex picture of deterrence between the two nation-states in the region. As such, this essay elucidates the history of this conflict and how it has informed Armenia and Azerbaijan's strategic rationales; the nature of the 2020 war; and what the failure of deterrence witnessed during said conflict may mean for deterrence as a framework in the 21st century.

reference: CESifo Working Paper No. 12890
title: The Dynamic Consequences of Inflow-driven Sudden Stops
affiliations: University of Namur and

detail.title: The Dynamic Consequences of Inflow-driven Sudden Stops
detail.abstract: This paper studies the macroeconomic effects of sudden stops using a newly constructed database that expands country coverage to 137 economies and extends the sample to 1985Q1–2025Q4. We document a new wave of sudden-stop episodes in the 2020s, partly reversing the apparent decline observed after the post-global-financialcrisis. Local-projection estimates show that sudden stops are typically preceded by economic expansions and followed by persistent output losses lasting up to two years. The contraction is driven mainly by sharp declines in investment and consumption, while net exports rise because imports contract more strongly than exports. The results reveal two distinct transmission mechanisms. Sudden stops in net external financing operate through forced external adjustment and import compression, with larger and more persistent effects under pegged exchange-rate regimes. By contrast, gross-inflow sudden stops operate through financial conditions: leverage rises, credit conditions tighten, asset prices fall, and investment declines. This financial transmission of gross-inflow sudden stops also differs across country groups, reflecting differences in financial structure. Developing countries are more exposed to increases in financing costs, whereas advanced economies display stronger debt deflation and asset-price effects.

title: When Does Party Convergence Persist under Alienation-Based Abstention?
affiliations: and

detail.title: When Does Party Convergence Persist under Alienation-Based Abstention?
detail.abstract: In the standard Downsian model, two office-seeking parties converge to the median voter. However alienated voters may abstain and turn out only for a party within their tolerance radius. For single-peaked voter distributions, convergence survives but relocates to a central voter, the median of the electorate that participates at the convergent platform. However single-peakedness of the voter distribution is an empirically contested assumption. So we first characterize purestrategy equilibrium for any continuous voter distribution. For general distributions, purestrategy equilibrium can fail to exist or be non-unique, and existence of equilibrium need not persist as the tolerance radius of the voters increases. In order to resolve these issues, we propose a fundamental object: centripetal structure for which there is a single anchor platform toward which competition always pulls. We show this structure produces convergence at equilibrium under alienation based abstention. Our main result concerns the emergence and persistence of this new structure as the tolerance radius increases. Even though equilibria for office-seeking parties themselves can vanish and reappear as the radius grows, once centripetal structure emerges, it persists as long as the midpoint voter is not alienated. Moreover, the centripetal structure always emerges, and this structure classifies equilibrium completely when parties are policy motivated.

title: Gender Disparities in Access to Nephrology Care in North India: A 10-Year Analysis of Tertiary Care Utilization

detail.abstract:
Background: Sex- and gender-related inequities in access to specialist kidney care remain insufficiently characterised in low- and middle-income countries despite the substantial burden of chronic kidney disease (CKD). We evaluated differences in utilisation of tertiary nephrology services by sex over a 10-year period in North India.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study using electronic health records from a high-volume tertiary nephrology referral centre in North India. All nephrology visits between Jan 1, 2010, and Dec 31, 2020, were included. Patient-level data were linked with district-level demographic and socioeconomic indicators from the 2011 Census of India. The primary outcome was utilisation of nephrology services by sex. Secondary outcomes included utilisation of kidney replacement therapies (haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, and kidney transplantation), post-transplant survival, temporal trends, and geographical patterns of access.

Findings: A total of 492,857 nephrology visits from 104,512 unique individuals were analysed. Women accounted for 152,136 (30.9%) visits and 35,254 (33.7%) unique patients. The lower representation of women was consistent across administrative divisions and throughout the study period, including after a marked expansion in service utilisation in 2014 (30.9% after vs 31.1% before; p=0.24). Women were also less likely than men to receive kidney transplantation. Among 1,205 transplant recipients, 151 (12.5%) were women; transplantation rates among patients receiving nephrology care were 2.45% for women and 6.86% for men (p<0.0001). Post-transplant survival was similar between women and men (log-rank p=0.38). Districts located farther from the study centre contributed fewer patients, whereas greater female socioeconomic advantage at the district level was associated with higher utilisation by women.

Interpretation: Women had consistently lower utilisation of tertiary nephrology services over a decade despite comparable post-transplant survival, suggesting that inequities occur primarily before access to specialist kidney care is achieved. Strategies that improve timely referral, equitable access to diagnostic and therapeutic services, and financial protection may help reduce sex- and gender-related inequities in kidney care in resource-constrained settings.

title: Weak Supervision at Rare-Event Priors: A Lift Threshold for Sign Degeneracy

detail.abstract: Label models of the Snorkel lineage take the polarity of each labeling function as given and estimate only a magnitude around it. At a rare-event prior that estimate cannot carry the polarity. For coverage c, lift ℓ and declared polarity p, the moment E[λy] equals p·c·(πℓ−(1−π))/(πℓ+(1−π)), so its sign turns over at ℓ* = (1−π)/π whatever the coverage. At a prior of 0.8185 % the threshold is a lift of 121.2; the strongest function in our register reaches 7.99. The sign such a model reports is a fact about the class balance, not about the function. In post-hoc synthetic sweeps, the conditionally correct sign instead of the declared one is worth 1.0 points of precision on a 5-function register and 48.4 on a 50-function one: writing more functions enlarges the surface of the one assumption nobody checks. In the same sweeps reversal needs no confounder; it all but disappears when functions are independent (0.5 % reverse), so correlation is its precondition, not an aggravating factor. The register came out of a pre-registered comparison on SEC filings, read exactly once, where four weak-supervision stages do not separate from one frozen rule at a budget whose registered detectable difference is 27.4 percentage points: the design cannot decide it, and said so in advance. A pre-registered placebo failed and is reported as such. We release it with the scored panel as a labeling-function benchmark in a regime existing suites do not pose as rare-event detection at an alert budget.

title: Does Federal Preclearance of State Election Laws Make a Difference? Examining the Effects of Shelby on the Minority Voting Gap and Countermobilization
affiliations: University of Colorado Boulder and University of Missouri - Economics

detail.title: Does Federal Preclearance of State Election Laws Make a Difference? Examining the Effects of Shelby on the Minority Voting Gap and Countermobilization
detail.abstract: In Shelby County v. Holder (2013), the Supreme Court suspended federal preclearance restrictions on changes to election laws in several states with a history of racial or ethnic discrimination and disparities in voting. We analyze the impact of this decision by estimating the triple difference in minority versus non-minority turnout in affected and unaffected states before and after Shelby. The end of federal preclearance does not appear to have detrimental effects on minority voter turnout or registration. We also show that revised federal preclearance procedures in the proposed John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act are not better targeted at states where minority voting may have retrogressed after Shelby. Finally, we do not find support for the hypothesis that countermobilization among minority voters mitigates or confounds what would otherwise have been an increase in the minority voting gap post-Shelby.

title: Re-Engineering Infrastructure Procurement: A Dynamic Life-Cycle Cost Analysis (LCCA) Framework Integrating Accelerated Depreciation and Stochastic Climate Risks into Public Asset Valuation

detail.abstract: The critical fiscal deficit in United States infrastructure asset management is largely driven by a systemic failure in long-term capital allocation strategies. Traditional public procurement pathways under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) prioritize minimized short-term capital expenditures (Capex), frequently resulting in the selection of low-cost vendors whose upfront savings are heavily wiped out by catastrophic operational expenditures (OpEx) over multi-decade horizons. This research establishes a novel, comprehensive financial engineering framework that re-engineers' legacy Life-Cycle Cost Analysis (LCCA) into a standardized, dynamic economic model. The proposed framework mathematically endogenizes both accelerated physical asset depreciation and stochastic climate-induced risk distributions directly into the dynamic Net Present Value (NPV) and Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) equations of smart public infrastructure. By utilizing advanced econometric modeling alongside a high-throughput 10,000iteration Monte Carlo simulation engine, this study provides a turnkey digital toolkit for state Treasurers and municipal chief financial officers. The model demonstrates a scalable capacity to achieve deep, sustainable long-term fiscal conservation, optimizing asset-liability management, stabilizing long-term municipal debt service requirements, and safeguarding American taxpayer wealth against compounding macroeconomic and environmental shocks over a fixed 30-year operational lifecycle.

reference: CESifo Working Paper No. 12892
title: Financing the Scalable Stage: Technology, Donations, and Earned Revenue in the Performing Arts

detail.title: Financing the Scalable Stage: Technology, Donations, and Earned Revenue in the Performing Arts
detail.abstract: This paper studies how digital distribution changes the financing mix of a nonprofit performing-arts organization when audience access becomes scalable but live production remains labor intensive. The organization chooses quality, live ticket prices, and digital access to maximize quality-adjusted service subject to break-even; a donor then contributes after observing earned revenue and the mission supported by each donated dollar. The model yields three results. First, higher live-production wages raise the contribution share but reduce donations, production, and mission output. Second, for a fixed digital strategy, better distribution technology lowers the contribution share while raising donations because earned revenue and audience reach increase the mission supported by each donated dollar. Third, the organization commercializes digital access when the monetization gain exceeds the donor-valued loss from narrower access. The commercialization threshold rises with Baumol pressure and falls as digital access becomes easier to monetize. Numerical experiments with endogenous quality, ticket prices, and commercialization generate open, mixed, and commercial regimes. Donations can therefore rise even as their share of operating resources falls, while digital distribution helps finance the labor-intensive live core.

title: Optimizing Public Infrastructure Financing in the U.S.: A Financial Engineering Framework Utilizing Green Bonds and Carbon Credit Arbitrage to Reduce the Cost of Capital
affiliations: Ain Shams University Cairo

detail.title: Optimizing Public Infrastructure Financing in the U.S.: A Financial Engineering Framework Utilizing Green Bonds and Carbon Credit Arbitrage to Reduce the Cost of Capital

detail.abstract: The massive structural funding deficit plaguing United States public infrastructure, exacerbated by the compounding macroeconomic pressures of persistent core inflation and elevated interest rates in 2026, demands an immediate paradigm shift in public capital efficiency. Traditional municipal financing models, which rely almost exclusively on regressive tax mechanisms and direct federal grants under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), are increasingly inadequate to cover substantial cost overruns and higher debt servicing burdens. This research introduces a novel, structurally integrated financial engineering framework designed to systematically minimize the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) for large-scale U.S. public infrastructure assets. The core mechanism of the proposed framework achieves this by synergizing high-efficiency Green Bond issuances with a dynamic Carbon Credit Arbitrage model. By doing so, it effectively establishes a multilayered quantitative pricing engine that allows state Departments of Transportation (DOTs) and local municipalities to monetize verified environmental externalities into highly liquid, upfront fiscal assets. Unlike existing qualitative sustainable finance literature, this study develops a predictive optimization model that calculates the precise empirical thresholds of the "Greenium" (the yield discount on green debt) while simultaneously factoring in the volatility of both voluntary and compliance carbon credit markets. Applied across a simulated portfolio of U.S. mass transit and clean energy grid expansions, the framework demonstrates a highly scalable capability to compress municipal borrowing yields by 150 to 300 basis points. Ultimately, this research provides an actionable, market-driven blueprint that safeguards American taxpayer funds, preserves long-term Debt Service Coverage Ratios (DSCR), and accelerates the deployment of strategically vital, climate-resilient national infrastructure.

title: Feedback And Learning in Higher Education: A Field Experiment with Exam Retrievals
affiliations: University of Bath - Department of Economics

detail.title: Feedback And Learning in Higher Education: A Field Experiment with Exam Retrievals

declarations.ethicsApproval: Approval code from the University of Bath Social Sciences Research Ethics Committee: SSREC S17-204

detail.abstract: Graded examination scripts often contain much information that could inform student learning, yet this information may never reach students. This is either because institutional regulations do not allow access to exam scripts (as in the case of final exams in the UK) or because students tend to not retrieve scripts when they already know their grades. What would students learn if they retrieved exam scripts that would otherwise remain uncollected? This question is investigated with a four-year field experiment with first year university students. In this experiment students receive their midterm exam grades but only receive detailed feedback by retrieving their script. A randomly selected group of students receives reminders to retrieve their script and suggestions on how to use it for revision for the final exam. We find that the effects of retrieving exam scripts are on average small and insignificant but vary with ability. Students with the highest university entry scores benefit substantially from retrieving their scripts while the benefits to students with lower entry scores are at best small and not statistically significant. These results can be explained by two key features of detailed feedback: that at least some prior study is necessary for it to be minimally effective and that it becomes more effective with better academic preparation. Because higher ability students tend to have better academic preparation, they benefit more from it.

title: Shadow Banking Regulation, Credit Supply Volatility, And the Effectiveness of Monetary and Macroprudential Policies in China
affiliations: School of Finance, Nankai University, Sun Yat-sen University and Guangdong University of Technology

detail.title: Shadow Banking Regulation, Credit Supply Volatility, And the Effectiveness of Monetary and Macroprudential Policies in China
detail.abstract: Building on an empirical analysis of stylized facts about the macroeconomic effects of China's shadow banking regulation, this study develops a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model including an explicit financial intermediary sector, and estimates this model on China data using macroeconomic time series to reveal how comprehensive shadow banking regulation can smooth credit supply fluctuations and strengthen the effectiveness of China's monetary and macroprudential policies. The results demonstrate that microprudential regulation curbs shadow banking's countercyclical expansion, enabling macroprudential policy to alleviate credit shortages via partial reintermediation. Coordinated policies foster countercyclical commercial bank lending, mitigating tensions between monetary countercyclicality and inherent credit procyclicality. Macroprudential subsidies endogenously curb self-fulfilling shadow bank runs, enabling better balance between economic stabilization and financial stability. Welfare analysis confirms that the coordination framework yields lower aggregate welfare losses, particularly when macroprudential policy appropriately weights the output gap. This study deepens the understanding of shadow banking regulation by quantifying how it limits the sector's impact on economic fluctuations and financial stability across different economic regimes, thereby contributing to a more coherent policy coordination framework.

reference: CESifo Working Paper No. 12891
title: Neighborhood Change and Local Economic Activity
affiliations: Rutgers University and University of Rome Tor Vergata - Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title: Neighborhood Change and Local Economic Activity
detail.abstract: We study how neighborhood change shapes local business demographics and employment. We use the regeneration of London public housing into mixed-income housing as a natural experiment that led to a large influx of more affluent households. In a difference-in-differences design comparing nearby businesses to those located farther away, we find that regenerations shift business composition – in both counts and employment – away from small local shops and toward larger general retail establishments and dining services that cater to the new residents. While we find no effect on total local employment on average, employment does increase in the areas most disadvantaged at baseline, suggesting that neighborhood change can expand local employment opportunities in these areas.

title: Unexpected Gross Profit and Cross-Sectional Stock Returns
affiliations: Sichuan Normal University, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Economics & Finance, University of Hawaii at Manoa - Shidler College of Business and Shanghai Jiao Tong University - Antai College of Economics & Management

detail.title: Unexpected Gross Profit and Cross-Sectional Stock Returns
detail.abstract: In this study, we define unexpected gross profit (GAP) as the difference between the current level of gross profit and its expected value, estimated using a moving average over the preceding eight quarters. With Fama-MacBeth t-statistics of 8.32 under ordinary least squares and 2.72 under weighted least squares, GAP emerges as one of the strongest predictors of individual stock returns, comparable to standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) measures. Moreover, GAP exhibits low correlations with both SUE and the revenue surprise measure, while providing incremental predictive power. Using the newly developed instrumented principal component analysis (IPCA) framework, we find that the predictive ability of GAP is primarily attributable to its role as a proxy for systematic risk (beta) rather than mispricing (alpha).

title: Reference Health, Medical Spending, and Investment Decisions
affiliations: Deakin University, Deakin University - Deakin Business School, University of Hamburg - Faculty of Economics and Business Administration and University of Zurich

detail.title: Reference Health, Medical Spending, and Investment Decisions
detail.abstract: We propose a dynamic economic model of medical spending, consumption, and risky investment including reference values in health and their adaptation to decaying health, which are found empirically relevant to the demand for medical care. Calibrating the model using Health and Retirement Study data yields gradually adapting health reference values for both genders which closely replicate observed medical spending and shares of risky investment. Including projection bias, meaning inability to fully anticipate the health reference value adaptation, significantly improves our model’s replication of observed choices for less wealthy individuals.

title: Market Risk Premium Expectation: Combining Option Theory with Traditional Predictors
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - Olin Business School, University of North Carolina  (UNC) at Wilmington,  and Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: Market Risk Premium Expectation: Combining Option Theory with Traditional Predictors
detail.abstract: We propose a state-dependent framework that integrates option-implied information with macro-financial variables to explore the out-of-sample predictive ability for the market excess return. By allowing economic conditions to influence the tightness of option-implied bounds, the approach transforms static measures into flexible bounds that adapt to changing market environments. Empirically, the resulting state-dependent bound (SDB) improves out-of-sample performance both statistically and economically. Relative to the Martin bound, the SDB increases the Sharpe ratio by over 150% and delivers utility gains exceeding 200 basis points per year. The framework also extends naturally to the cross section of stock returns.

title: Oil Price Uncertainty and Sovereign Spreads of OilImporters

detail.title: Oil Price Uncertainty and Sovereign Spreads of OilImporters
detail.abstract: This paper examines how global oil price volatility affects sovereign spreads in oil-importing countries. Using data from 35 emerging economies, I first establish a positive empirical relationship between oil price volatility and spreads. I then develop a sovereign default model where oil prices follow a stochastic volatility process estimated via Bayesian MCMC methods. The model reveals that spread responses to oil price changes are highly state-dependent. During high volatility periods, spreads respondthree times more sharply to price fluctuations than during normal times. Debt levels amplify this sensitivity—more indebted economies experience larger spread increases. Importantly, governments strategically borrow more during high volatility periods when oil prices are expected to rise, effectively using debt as insurance against future import costs and higher borrowing rates. These findings highlight oil price uncertainty as aquantitatively important macroeconomic risk for oil-importing nations.

title: Stablecoin Flows, Dollar Convenience Yields and Exchange Rates
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology,  and Tsinghua University, School of Economics and Management

detail.title: Stablecoin Flows, Dollar Convenience Yields and Exchange Rates
detail.abstract: We study how U.S. dollar–denominated stablecoins affect U.S. Treasury convenience yields, exchange rates, and financial market stability. We first find that a one-standard-deviation inflow into dollar stablecoins raises the U.S. Treasury convenience yield by 4 bps. The effects are more pronounced when transaction fees are lower, transaction activity is higher, and stablecoins command a larger convenience premium. To address endogeneity, we instrument stablecoin flows using shocks to crypto-market demand. Consistent with the effect of the convenience yield on the FX market, we find that stablecoin inflows are associated with a dollar appreciation in the short run, and that the stablecoin market size is negatively associated with the dollar's excess returns in the long run. These results support a convenience-yield-based view in which stablecoins generate a novel crypto-related demand channel for the U.S. dollar. We further show that dollar stablecoins transmit volatility from crypto markets to the FX and Treasury markets.

title: Narrative Contagion on a Network of Themes: Exact Tipping Thresholds, Spectral Stability, and Hysteresis

detail.title: Narrative Contagion on a Network of Themes: Exact Tipping Thresholds, Spectral Stability, and Hysteresis
detail.abstract: This paper models socially transmitted narratives as a bounded prevalence field over a measurable space of themes: the state is the fraction of the population carrying each theme, an element of the order interval . A discrete-choice microfoundation with retention and imperfect attention yields a monotone nonlinear operator that preserves prevalence in  theme by theme. It proves the existence of least and greatest stationary narratives, and we show that the stationary state is unique for every communication profile and every admissible semantic network if and only if , where  is conformity,  the attention probability, and  retention. Above this exact virality threshold, aligned communication generates two stable homogeneous states separated by an unstable tipping state. The stationary set admits a closed-form fold representation, which yields explicit communication thresholds and an exact hysteresis width, independent of the adoption threshold and — at full attention — of memory: retention and depletion of the susceptible pool offset exactly. Local stability is characterized mode by mode: at a homogeneous state the linearization is , so the Perron mode has the largest amplification factor and is the first to lose stability, while the decay or amplification of heterogeneous thematic shocks is governed by the spectrum of the semantic network. The fold geometry also yields exact one-period intervention thresholds — including a retention limit beyond which no single-period communication pulse can dislodge an entrenched narrative — thereby providing closed-form comparative statics for tipping, persistence, and communication interventions in a networked belief system.

title: Beyond Demolition: An Integrated Spatial, Structural, and Utility-Resilience Framework for Earthquake Risk Reduction in Historic Unplanned Cities -The Case of Old Dhaka

detail.title: Beyond Demolition: An Integrated Spatial, Structural, and Utility-Resilience Framework for Earthquake Risk Reduction in Historic Unplanned Cities -The Case of Old Dhaka

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known personal, financial, or professional conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper. No external funding was received for this work. The author has no financial or advisory relationships with any organizations, technology companies, or government agencies that could be perceived as having influenced the study design, interpretation of findings, or policy recommendations presented herein.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve primary data collection, experiments, or interventions with human participants, patients, or animals. The research is based entirely on a structured narrative synthesis of publicly available peer-reviewed literature, international agency reports, and published statistics. Therefore, formal ethics committee approval was not required. All sources cited are properly attributed in the references.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted without external funding. The author's institutional affiliation provided access to library resources and academic databases but did not provide financial support for the research or publication.

detail.abstract: Old Dhaka, the four-hundred-year-old core of Bangladesh's capital, sits on moderately active seismic ground while carrying some of the densest and most structurally fragile building stock in South Asia.
