title: The Friendship Paradox: Causal Evidence of Its Behavioral Consequences
affiliations: University of London - Royal Holloway College, University of Malaga, Stanford University - Department of Economics and Max Planck Institute for Behavioral Economics

detail.title: The Friendship Paradox: Causal Evidence of Its Behavioral Consequences
detail.abstract: We provide a first causal analysis of the behavioral consequences of the friendship paradox—the fact that people’s friends in a network have more connections than average. We find that people’s behavior is biased by their network position: they do not best respond to what they should infer the average behavior of the population to be, but instead simply to the average behavior of their friends. Moreover, we find that they fail to learn to overcome such a bias when relocated within the network, varying their observational environment. In these games of complements, the friendship paradox generates a systematic upward distortion in actions, increases behavioral dispersion, and persists despite learning opportunities.

title: Who Chooses to Judge? Endogenous Participation and the Limits of Bridging in Crowd
affiliations: and Georgia State University - Department of Computer Information Systems

detail.title: Who Chooses to Judge? Endogenous Participation and the Limits of Bridging in Crowd
detail.abstract: Crowd-based governance systems depend not only on how individual judgments are aggregated but also on which individuals choose to contribute those judgments. We examine this participation problem in X’s Community Notes, a crowd fact-checking system that uses a bridging algorithm to identify support across evaluators with contrasting rating histories. Using ratings of the same notes generated through two participation pathways—ordinary endogenous participation and randomized platform requests—we assess whether voluntarily produced judgments generalize to a broader evaluator sample. Our primary sample includes 9,853 notes, 2,660,703 endogenous ratings, and 706,135 platform-sampled ratings. Endogenous evaluators rate the same notes 0.0400 points less favorably, on average, than platform-sampled evaluators. We develop an evaluator-note selection framework and apply an exact symmetric decomposition to distinguish differences in relational composition from differences in conditional judgment within aligned and opposed evaluator-note relations. Endogenous participation produces a more aligned relational composition, which alone would make endogenous assessments more favorable. However, this compositional advantage is more than offset by substantially more critical conditional judgment, concentrated primarily within opposed evaluator-note relations. The conditional-judgment component also corresponds much more closely to cross-pathway differences in Community Notes helpfulness scores than does relational composition. These findings show that bridging across observed perspectives does not eliminate selection in the production of algorithmic inputs. More broadly, crowd-based platforms must evaluate both which perspectives participate and whether the judgments expressed within those perspectives generalize beyond voluntary contributors.

title: Agentic AI in the Age of Autonomy with Concepts and Case Studies
affiliations: Manisa Celal Bayar University, Muğla Sıtkı Koçman University - Department of Artificial Intelligence and International VISION University

detail.title: Agentic AI in the Age of Autonomy with Concepts and Case Studies
detail.abstract:
Artificial Intelligence is entering a new era in which systems are no longer limited to generating predictions or assisting users with isolated tasks. Agentic AI represents this transformation by enabling intelligent systems to perceive their environments, reason over complex objectives, plan multi-step actions, utilize external tools, collaborate with humans and other agents, and continuously adapt to changing conditions. As autonomous capabilities mature, Agentic AI is rapidly becoming one of the defining research and application areas of contemporary artificial intelligence.
This edited volume, Agentic AI in the Age of Autonomy with Concepts and Case Studies, has been prepared to provide a comprehensive perspective on this emerging paradigm. Rather than focusing solely on technical advances, the book brings together interdisciplinary contributions that examine the architectural foundations of agentic systems, human-agent collaboration, governance, domain-specific applications, and future research directions. The diversity of the chapters reflects our belief that the future of autonomous AI will be shaped not only by technological innovation but also by responsible design, societal acceptance, and practical deployment across different sectors.
The book begins by establishing the technical foundations of Agentic AI, explaining the layered architectures, reasoning mechanisms, orchestration strategies, and collaborative models that enable autonomous intelligent systems. It then explores issues of trust, governance, ethical responsibility, and social acceptance, highlighting the importance of balancing autonomy with transparency, accountability, and human oversight.
Building upon these conceptual foundations, the following chapters examine how autonomous AI agents are transforming software engineering from passive development tools into collaborative teammates, while also reviewing the growing role of AI agents in education through current architectures, opportunities, and pedagogical challenges. The educational perspective is further extended through the presentation of SymDevAI Edu, a supervised Agentic AI ecosystem that demonstrates how autonomous agents can support K-12 learning environments in real-world settings.
The volume continues with practical case studies illustrating the adoption of Agentic AI across diverse application domains. These include intelligent destination management supported by tourism dashboards, the interpretation of radiological images through large language models as decision-support systems in healthcare, neuro-symbolic autonomous governance for financial execution, and the coordination of autonomous swarm drones for adaptive wildfire prediction and disaster response. Together, these chapters demonstrate that Agentic AI is evolving beyond a theoretical concept into a versatile technological paradigm capable of addressing complex real-world challenges.
As editors, we hope that this book will serve as a valuable resource for researchers, graduate students, practitioners, policymakers, and technology leaders seeking to understand both the opportunities and the challenges presented by increasingly autonomous intelligent systems. By combining theoretical perspectives with practical implementations, this volume aims to encourage interdisciplinary collaboration and inspire future research on trustworthy, explainable, and human-centered Agentic AI.
Finally, we would like to express our sincere gratitude to all chapter authors for sharing their expertise and contributing their valuable research to this volume. We also extend our appreciation to the Izmir Academy Association Publishing House for its continuous support in promoting open-access, interdisciplinary scientific publications through the Future Tech Horizons e-book series. We hope this book contributes to the ongoing global dialogue on the responsible development and deployment of autonomous intelligent systems.

title: Resilytics: A Decision-Intelligence Platform and Revenue Durability Index for Small and Medium Businesses

detail.title: Resilytics: A Decision-Intelligence Platform and Revenue Durability Index for Small and Medium Businesses
detail.abstract: Small and medium businesses (SMBs) in emerging markets generate rich transactional data but rarely convert it into forward-looking decisions. Business-intelligence dashboards describe what happened; they do not tell a founder what is about to break. We present Resilytics, a decision-intelligence platform designed for Indian SMBs operating between ₹50 lakh and ₹50 crore in annual revenue. The system ingests raw sales data through a canonicalschema pipeline into a multi-tenant star-schema warehouse, computes a portfolio of key performance indicators, and condenses them into a single interpretable measure-the Revenue Durability Index (RDI)-composed of five risk dimensions: growth, stability, concentration, geographic spread, and operational balance. An intelligence layer adds explainability through percomponent contribution and sensitivity analysis, drift detection, forecasting, Monte Carlo shock simulation, and a policy engine that ranks concrete actions. A hybrid AI copilot combines deterministic tools with a large language model behind a validated intent-plan-tool pipeline, so that every answer remains grounded in the tenant's own warehouse data and the system degrades gracefully to deterministic-only operation. We describe the architecture, the RDI methodology, the guardrail design of the copilot, and our validation approach on a synthetic two-phase benchmark dataset covered by 377 automated tests. We report engineering lessons on silent LLM degradation and test-fixture integrity, and we discuss limitations and the path to field validation with pilot deployments.

title: The Two-Layer Economy of Intelligence III: The Internal Limits of Diminishing Returns — The Saturation of Scaling Laws and the Horizon of AI Capital

detail.title: The Two-Layer Economy of Intelligence III: The Internal Limits of Diminishing Returns — The Saturation of Scaling Laws and the Horizon of AI Capital
detail.abstract: The first two installments of this series established a two-layer economy of intelligence—a commoditizing Base Layer and a scarcity-preserving Apex Layer (Paper I)—and traced electricity cost as an external, physical constraint shaping that structure (Paper II). Both rest on an unstated premise: that Apex-Layer actors can perpetually renew their technical lead by continuing to pour in compute. This paper (Paper III) interrogates that premise from within, against one of the most widely observed empirical regularities in AI research—scaling laws—which imply diminishing returns: performance rises with compute, parameters, and data, but the marginal cost of each increment grows. We proceed not by original quantitative causal inference (the core data are proprietary to AI labs) but by (a) organizing the published scaling-law literature (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Caballero et al., 2023; Snell et al., 2024) and (b) reconsidering Paper I's premises through classical factor theory. Our position is that diminishing returns does not invalidate Paper I's central thesis but transforms the basis on which Apex-Layer power rests. We identify two asymmetries—a supply side, where rising acquisition costs raise entry barriers and entrench incumbents (read through the Specific Factors Model and differential rent), and a demand side, where inelastic frontier-task demand persists—and analyze them through the ambiguity decomposition (Krogh & Vedelsby, 1995), correcting an earlier draft's misattributed reliance on the Hong-Page theorem. Comparing Google, leading Chinese firms, and Anthropic, we distinguish a two-layer-integration path from a purification path. We are explicit throughout about the limitations: lab-reported figures, the metaphorical extension of a squared-error identity to generative outputs, and a preliminary, secondary-source firm comparison.

detail.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents are transforming software systems from passive AI-assisted tools into active, goal-oriented software teammates capable of perceiving context, maintaining memory, planning tasks, selecting tools, and executing multi-step workflows. This chapter examines this transformation by distinguishing autonomous AI agents from prompt-driven applications, conversational chatbots, workflow automation, and conventional software components. It presents a structured six-layer agentic architecture comprising perception, memory, reasoning and planning, action, orchestration, and governance, providing an architectural perspective for integrating autonomous agents into software engineering environments. The chapter further explores multi-agent collaboration patterns in software development, IT operations, and data analysis, with particular attention to task decomposition, contextual memory, tool execution, coordination, and conflict resolution. To demonstrate the practical application of these concepts, a multi-agent Software Quality Companion is presented, integrating specialized agents for code review, test generation, architectural consistency analysis, technical debt monitoring, and orchestration. The chapter also examines systemic risks associated with increased autonomy, including controllability failures, unreliable actions, objective misalignment, security vulnerabilities, privacy risks, coordination failures, and excessive user reliance. A governance framework is proposed based on policy and permissions, action gating, observability, and continuous evaluation. Finally, the chapter discusses evaluation criteria covering review quality, productivity, reliability, operational safety, human oversight, maintainability, and architectural trust. The analysis highlights that successful adoption of autonomous agents depends not only on model capabilities but also on disciplined software architecture, explicit authority boundaries, measurable performance criteria, and auditable governance mechanisms.

detail.abstract: This paper calls into question a common set of assumptions about the use of artificial intelligence in administrative law in Canada. While some assume that AI may be useful for assisting a decision-maker where core rights are affected, the prevailing view is that it cannot be relied upon to make final decisions, due mainly to functional limitations: AI cannot give reasons and its outcomes are fraught with bias and opacity that cannot be overcome. The prevailing view, however, took shape in response to earlier, more limited forms of AI. Large language models can be used in a way that mitigates earlier concerns to a significant degree—but both scholarship and policy have yet to absorb this. Experiments canvassed in this paper involving appellate court decisions show that when prompted to draw primarily on party materials, AI can produce a reasoned decision comparable in quality to that of a human, calling for a reassessment of AI’s possible role in administrative law and a shift of concern from underlying technical processes to the quality and cogency of reasons that AI can provide.

title: Personalized Bundle Design: A Hypergraph-based Approach with Psychological Distance Awareness
affiliations: , Beihang University (BUAA), Beihang University (BUAA) and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: Personalized Bundle Design: A Hypergraph-based Approach with Psychological Distance Awareness
detail.abstract:
Product bundling, as a widely adopted marketing strategy that presents a portfolio of products as a single offering, has become pervasive in $e$-commerce platforms due to its substantial economic benefits. Beyond serving as a promotional tactic, bundling has increasingly become a way to deliver more personalized experiences and enhance consumer satisfaction, giving rise to the so-called Personalized Bundle Design (PBD) strategy and bringing substantial research challenges. In essence, the utility of a bundle depends on complex yet implicit product relations, which consumers evaluate as a whole rather than the summation from a set of individual products. Meanwhile, consumers' bundle preferences are heterogeneous in different contexts and shaped through long-term purchase experiences, making bundle-level utility difficult to learn. These challenges are further compounded by the scarcity of genuine bundle data, which drown in tremendous noisy purchase transactions. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework: Hypergraph-based Personalized Bundle Design (HyperPBD). 
HyperPBD moves beyond pairwise relation modeling by constructing a product hypergraph, enabling the representation learning of higher-order product relations that better reflect latent but denoised bundling intentions. It further introduces a psychological distance-aware utility function, grounded in Construal Level Theory, to learn how consumers’ long-term purchase experiences shape their context-aware heterogeneous cognitive processes for bundles. Finally, it shifts bundle design from product-level prediction to bundle-level optimization via an adversarial learning framework, which enables direct learning of bundle design from consumers' set-level feedback. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that HyperPBD greatly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in two business scenarios of bundling. The essential roles of psychological distance–aware utility learning and adversarial bundle-wise optimization are justified by ablation studies. We further adopt an LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation framework to assess the rationality and creativity of designed bundles, showing that HyperPBD not only captures functional compatibility but also exhibits creativity by situating bundles within experiential and emotional contexts.

title: The Digital Euro as a Complementary Means of Payment: An Empirical Analysis of Consumer Acceptance
affiliations: FOM University of Applied Sciences for Economics and Management and

detail.title: The Digital Euro as a Complementary Means of Payment: An Empirical Analysis of Consumer Acceptance
detail.abstract: The European Central Bank (ECB) is preparing the potential issuance of a digital euro as a complementary, publicly issued means of payment for consumers in the euro area. Whether such a retail central bank digital currency (CBDC) will be adopted, however, depends decisively on consumer acceptance. This paper examines the determinants of consumer acceptance of the digital euro on the basis of an exploratory online survey conducted among more than 500 respondents in the German-speaking area. Four hypotheses derived from a systematic literature review are tested using a binomial test and ordinary least squares regressions. The results do not support the conjecture of a majority rejection of the digital euro: only 28.7 percent of valid responses indicate rejection of future use. Technology affinity and a positive assessment of privacy and security are positively and significantly associated with acceptance, whereas age shows no measurable effect. Descriptive findings reveal substantial information deficits, a strong preference for accessing the digital euro through the respondent's principal bank, and a clear demand for a uniform European payment solution. Benchmarking the results against the Eurosystem's public consultation and a representative Bundesbank survey confirms the central role of privacy, security, and cost-free usage. The findings support an intermediated distribution model and privacy-by-design as prerequisites for broad adoption.

title: Quantum-Resilient Cloud Communication: A Systematic Literature Review and Taxonomy of Protection Mechanisms
affiliations: Dharmsinh Desai University

detail.title: Quantum-Resilient Cloud Communication: A Systematic Literature Review and Taxonomy of Protection Mechanisms
detail.abstract: Cloud computing is now the default way organizations deliver scalable computing resources, distributed services, and real-time communication across public, private, hybrid, and multi-cloud environments [1]. That reliance raises the stakes for cloud communication security: confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and availability are no longer nice-to-haves but baseline requirements for critical business operations [1], [9]. Today, almost all of that security rests on classical public-key cryptography-RSA, Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), and Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange [13]-[16]. These schemes have held up well against classical attackers for decades. Quantum computers are a different story. Shor's algorithm and Grover's algorithm have already shown, at least theoretically, how a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could undermine the mathematical assumptions these systems depend on [5], [6]. This has pushed a wave of research into quantum-resilient security: post-quantum cryptography (PQC), quantum key distribution (QKD), hybrid cryptographic frameworks, cryptographic agility strategies, Zero Trust architectures, and more advanced key management [2]-[4], [8], [9], [17], [18]. The problem is that this work is scattered. Most studies zoom in on one technology at a time rather than asking how these pieces fit together into a coherent defense for cloud communication [8]-[12]. This paper works through that gap with a systematic literature review of quantum-resilient protection mechanisms for cloud communication channels, synthesizing current research, classifying existing approaches, and surfacing both trends and unresolved challenges [8]-[12]. From that synthesis, we propose a multi-dimensional taxonomy that organizes protection mechanisms along cryptographic, architectural, operational, and migration lines. We then go a step further and show how AOP/OOP software design principles can support cryptographic agility, modular security management, and scalable deployment of quantum-safe cloud services [21]-[24]. The paper closes with open research issues and future directions for securing cloud communication in the post-quantum era [9]-[12].

title: From Tacit Experience to Explicit Intelligence: A Human-AI Collaboration Mechanism and Knowledge Externalization Pathway for Data-Scarce Organizations
affiliations: Independent Researcher, Independent Researcher and

detail.title: From Tacit Experience to Explicit Intelligence: A Human-AI Collaboration Mechanism and Knowledge Externalization Pathway for Data-Scarce Organizations
detail.abstract: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) and AI agent technologies, many small and medium-sized enterprises and expert-intensiveorganizations are seeking to integrate AI into high-value knowledge work. However, their core capabilities often do not exist in large-scale structureddatasets that can be directly used for model training. Instead, these capabilities are embedded in the experience-based judgments, problem-framing approaches, risk identification abilities, resource selectionpreferences, and critical decision-making patterns developed by a limitednumber of experts through long-term practice. Existing approaches to AI adoption have primarily emphasized data infrastructure, model capabilities, or the efficiency improvement of individual tools. However, they provide relatively limited explanations for a more fundamental question: under conditions of limited historical data, highly tacit knowledge, and non-reducible governance responsibilities, how should organizations design human-AI collaboration mechanisms that enable AI togenerate immediate value within individual projects while continuously accumulating reusable organizational intelligence through cross-project interactions? Building upon theories of hybrid intelligence, human-centered andtrustworthy AI, and organizational knowledge creation, this paper proposes a project-centered human-AI collaboration mechanism. Theproposed mechanism consists of two interconnected layers: a CognitiveInfrastructure Layer and a Six-Chain Collaboration Pipeline Layer. The former focuses on capturing the formation, application, and refinement of expert judgment through structured records of participants, projects, andsix-chain events. The latter decomposes project collaboration into six interconnected chains—the Problem-Framing Chain, Cognition Chain, Logic Chain, Resource Chain, Decision Chain, and Execution Chain—allowing task execution, knowledge externalization, responsibility traceability, and capability evolution to occur within a unified structure. Furthermore, this paper proposes three complementary mechanisms: theProject–Six Chain–Memory Loop, the Progressive Delegation Pathway, and the Evidence Triad Governance Mechanism. These mechanisms suggest that AI should not be designed as a one-time replacement systemfor experts, but rather as a collaborative infrastructure that enables expert judgment to be reused across time, projects, and individuals. The contribution of this paper lies in integrating human-in-the-loop approaches, tacit knowledge externalization, organizational memory, and the evolution of AI agent capabilities into a unified conceptual framework that is discussable, implementable, and empirically testable. Theframework provides a theoretical foundation for future empirical researchinapplication scenarios including generic drug development, employment compliance, ESG reporting, B2B proposal development, and high-valueconsulting services.

title: Legal, Ethical, and Human Oversight Aspects of Human-Centered Remote Maintenance and Asset Management using XR and AI Tools

detail.abstract: This chapter examines the legal and ethical dimensions of human oversight in AIand XR-enabled remote maintenance and asset management, using Pilot 2 of the Horizon Europe XR5.0 project as a case study. Developed by Schmidt + Haensch in partnership with Maintastic and integrated into the Maintastic SHARE platform, the pilot integrates generative AI and explainable AI within an extended reality environment to support technicians in diagnosing and resolving issues on complex laboratory instruments remotely. Applying the Assessment List for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (ALTAI), the analysis assesses how the system operationalizes human-in-the-loop and human-in-command principles, ensuring that AI functions solely as an assistive tool while technicians retain full decision-making authority. The chapter further evaluates the pilot's compliance with data protection, cybersecurity, and AI governance requirements under the GDPR and the AI Act, highlighting robust safeguards such as data minimization, privacy by design, and cited, verifiable AI outputs, alongside remaining gaps in formal security testing and bias monitoring. The findings illustrate how effective human oversight can be embedded into industrial XR systems through a combination of technical design, organizational safeguards, and regulatory compliance, offering practical lessons for trustworthy human-centered AI deployment in Industry 5.0.

title: The Tokenization of Real World Assets: A Qualitative Analysis of Investor Perceptions, Adoption Barriers and the Trust Paradox
affiliations: FOM University of Applied Sciences for Economics and Management and

detail.title: The Tokenization of Real World Assets: A Qualitative Analysis of Investor Perceptions, Adoption Barriers and the Trust Paradox
detail.abstract: Despite the economic potential attributed to the tokenization of real world assets (RWAs), including fractional ownership, reduced illiquidity discounts and accelerated settlement, actual investor adoption remains limited. This paper examines which factors promote or inhibit investors' willingness to invest in tokenized RWAs. Drawing on ten semi-structured expert interviews with blockchain investors and traditionally oriented investors in the German-speaking region, analyzed by means of structuring qualitative content analysis, the study shows that market access (31% of coded statements) and efficiency (23%) dominate the perceived potential, while complexity and platform-related trust concerns (each mentioned by 80% of respondents) as well as regulatory uncertainty (70%) constitute the central barriers to adoption. Three findings extend the theoretical debate. First, perceived usefulness in the Technology Acceptance Model requires differentiation by adopter group: traditional investors conceive of usefulness as process efficiency, blockchain investors as market access. Second, loss aversion proves to be reference-point dependent, as blockchain investors frame non-participation in an anticipated future market state as the relevant loss. Third, a trust paradox emerges: although blockchain technology set out to substitute institutional trust with technical mechanisms, investors explicitly demand established institutions, clear accountability and regulatory anchoring. The results point to hybrid market structures rather than full disintermediation and consolidate into a three-tier investor concept that prioritizes institutional legitimation, visibility and education, and usability.

title: The HR Software Loophole: How the Industry Has Escaped Liability for Employment-Related Harms
affiliations: University of Oregon - School of Law

detail.title: The HR Software Loophole: How the Industry Has Escaped Liability for Employment-Related Harms
detail.abstract:
Corporate employers rely on human resources (“HR”) software for tasks like applicant selection, timekeeping, payroll, benefit management, and productivity monitoring.  When that software causes or contributes to wage theft or employment discrimination, employers have been largely unsuccessful at obtaining indemnification or contribution from software companies. This article reveals how software-related actors have evaded liability under both state and federal law through (1) statutory coverage limitations under the Fair Labor Standards Act (“FLSA”) and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act (“Title VII”); (2) case law precluding indemnification under FLSA and Title VII; (3) judicial enforcement of limitation of liability provisions in software contracts; and (4) judicial application of the economic loss doctrine to tort claims. 

Because HR software companies rarely incur liability for their role in employment law violations, they have little incentive to invest in precautions that would reduce the likelihood of harm. Closing any of the loopholes described above would force software companies to internalize the costs the software imposes on workers.

title: Biographical Templates and Temporal Narratives in Digital Consumer Interaction

detail.title: Biographical Templates and Temporal Narratives in Digital Consumer Interaction
detail.abstract:
This manuscript revisits and extends early work by Smith (2005, 2006) on digital consumer
interaction. The original model proposed that online behaviour is shaped by biographical
templates, temporal narratives, cognitive drivers, goals, adaptations and socio-technical
conventions. Using the 2006 MSc dissertation as primary empirical research and the 2005
IADIS paper as a position statement, this manuscript integrates those findings with later
developments in narrative cognition, biographical practice theory, brand biography research and
socio-technical interaction studies. The analysis demonstrates that Smith’s early model
anticipated several major theoretical shifts. A revised integrated framework is proposed for
understanding digital consumer behaviour in 2026.

title: Executable Sustainability Taxonomies in Trade, Procurement, and Structured Finance: Design Features for Transaction-level Implementation
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Executable Sustainability Taxonomies in Trade, Procurement, and Structured Finance: Design Features for Transaction-level Implementation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial interests in the framework described in this paper. The author is exploring potential non-commercial and commercial applications of the STES framework; at the time of writing, no such venture exists and no funding has been received from any party for this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual, theory-building study involving no human participants, no personal data, and no primary data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Sustainability taxonomies, product-carbon-footprint standards, and disclosure regimes determine what may be characterised as green or transition-aligned, yet they do not determine what happens when a specific commercial delivery is financed, procured, or pooled. This paper develops the Sustainability Transaction Execution Standard (STES), a proposed governance and data architecture that translates existing measurement evidence into contractual conditions and finance-workflow inputs. The central contribution is the identification and formalisation of a distinct execution layer in sustainable-finance infrastructure, analytically separable from the measurement and exchange layers that have received extensive scholarly attention. STES does not propose new measurement science and does not replace ISO 14067, Environmental Product Declarations, the GHG Protocol, WBCSD PACT, CBAM, or jurisdictional taxonomies. It occupies a distinct execution layer: linking an assured Delivery Pathway Model to a commercial transaction through disclosed delivery linkage, then mapping the resulting evidence to agreed procurement, financing, and reporting consequences.

The framework rests on a two-unit architecture: emissions are measured and assured at the Delivery Pathway level—a Production Pathway for goods, a Service Delivery Pathway for services—while legal and financial execution occurs at the invoice, purchase-order, delivery, usage record, or receivable level. A separate Linkage Quality tier (L1–L4) prevents an assured model from being indiscriminately attached to transactions, and an automated data-integrity layer applies source-system capture, version controls, quantity conservation, and multi-record reconciliation, reserving human review for exceptions.

Drawing on transaction-cost economics, principal-agent theory, incomplete-contracts theory, and trade-finance doctrine, the paper proposes a parsimonious Core Execution Gate—eligibility × evidence confidence—expanded by five contextual dimensions (Activity, Data, Ambition, Place, Terms). The paper derives seven testable propositions, specifies model-level assurance, proxy governance, a pre-assurance holding model, contractual liability allocation, a procurement RFx execution taxonomy, and a Transition Commerce Stack combining ordinary liquidity with procurement rebates, model-upgrade support, offtake-linked milestones, and blended-finance risk sharing.

The methodology uses integrative theory building and abductive reasoning, framed as a conceptual design and research-agenda article. Comparative analysis spans the EU, Singapore, Japan, and ICC digital-trade infrastructure as maximum-variation contexts. The paper identifies operational failure points—entity-level ESG ratings unable to resolve intra-firm production variance, CBAM/PCF data not commercially reusable, manual ESG forms producing errors and fraud exposure, SME evidence incompleteness, documentary finance unable to verify physical truth, and costly manual due diligence for green receivables—and maps each to a specific STES design response.

Key design features include: (i) model-level rather than invoice-level assurance, following financial-statement audit logic; (ii) a pre-assurance holding model (T0–T2) preserving liquidity during evidence development; (iii) automated quantity conservation preventing duplicate claims across buyers; (iv) segregation of duties across plant operations, sustainability teams, finance, IT, verifiers, and governance bodies; (v) role-based confidentiality disclosure; and (vi) CBAM and Scope 3 interoperability through purpose-of-calculation, boundary, and methodology-version fields.

The paper addresses commercial viability through the Transition Commerce Stack, recognising that per-invoice rate discounts of 10–50 basis points rarely fund measurement infrastructure. It specifies free-rider mitigations for model-development costs, SME minimum-viable evidence pathways achievable with basic digital tools, and an anchor-buyer pilot model for resolving the coordination problem. Governance requirements—registry, conformance testing, benchmark stewardship, dispute resolution, and rule evolution—are specified with candidate institutional hosts.

STES is advanced as a conceptual design proposition. It does not claim to reduce financing costs, lower emissions, or improve credit quality. Its most credible empirical setting is repeat, data-rich trade in CBAM-exposed and buyer-mandated supply chains, where measurement costs are already sunk and an execution layer can render existing data commercially actionable. The paper specifies falsification conditions for each proposition and a phased pilot protocol suitable for controlled testing within 18–24 months.

title: MOUNTAIN ENTREPRENEURSHIP IN COMMERCE: CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES. EUROPEAN MOUNTAIN SERIES ANALYSIS (5)
affiliations: Centre for Mountain Economy of the Romanian Academy, CBM International University, Centre for Mountain Economy of the Romanian Academy, Universitatea din Oradea, , Centre for Mountain Economy of the Romanian Academy, Centre for Mountain Economy of the Romanian Academy and University of Oradea

detail.title: MOUNTAIN ENTREPRENEURSHIP IN COMMERCE: CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES. EUROPEAN MOUNTAIN SERIES ANALYSIS (5)
detail.abstract: This study analyzes the economic performance and entrepreneurial dynamics in mountain commerce in Europe during 2021-2022, using 28 economic indicators (I1-I28). The results highlight a series of mixed trends, showing signs of resilience but also major challenges. The sector demonstrated notable stability, maintaining the number of active enterprises (I1) and recording an increase in the business survival rate (I6-I9). Additionally, there was an improvement in productivity (I25-I27), indicating that many businesses adapted to market demands. Dependence on seasonal employment (I21) remained a major limiting factor, and some segments of the sector recorded low revenues (I19-I20), reflecting economic challenges in certain areas. Despite these challenges, the sector continued to show signs of adaptability and long-term growth potential. Progressive digitalization (I24) and the implementation of eco-friendly practices (I25) offer significant opportunities for development. detail.abstract:
Fraudulent digital transactions are a systemic challenge across e-commerce, banking, and welfare
programs in the United States. Card-not-present (CNP) fraud, chargebacks, and misuse of EBT
systems collectively cost billions annually (Federal Trade Commission, 2023; U.S. Government
Accountability Office, 2025; USDA Food and Nutrition Service, 2023). Existing solutions such as
OTP, 3DS, and encryption address technical vulnerabilities but impose costs on freelancers,
merchants, and governments.
This white paper introduces CivicSentra, a cross-rail fraud-prevention model combining real-time
edge risk scoring with a specified federated learning plane intended to let banks, merchants, and
government agencies share protective intelligence without centralising raw transaction data.
A Phase 0 reference implementation of the scoring rules has been evaluated against synthetic EBT
transaction data, and the results are reported in Section 8. Of the model’s four stated claims, two
were tested and neither held as written: measured scoring latency was 637 milliseconds against a
sub-30 millisecond design target, and the measured savings-to-cost ratio at field-realistic fraud
prevalence was 1.99:1 to 2.86:1 rather than the 20–80× previously projected. The remaining two —
federated learning and graph-based fraud ring detection — were never implemented and are
reported as untested. The evaluation’s principal finding concerns the model rather than the
implementation: because the spend-baseline feature normalises against current balance, a quantity
under an attacker’s control, false positives concentrate on households that have already been
defrauded, and no threshold setting corrects it. Section 9 sets out the remediation programme.
CivicSentra is informed by the author’s direct experience in banking IT security and by
measurement rather than projection: every figure reported in Sections 8 and 9 is computed by the
evaluation harness released with the reference implementation. The model is presented as a
sustainable response to a problem of growing urgency in the United States.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Paper accepted for presentation at the “28th International Conference on Harbor, Maritime and Multimodal Logistic Modeling & Simulation (HMS 2026). The conference version is scheduled to appear in Procedia Computer Science.

detail.abstract: Critical maritime chokepoints face ongoing intensifying risks where shocks such as geopolitical uncertainty can affect their service reliability and operations. Although Digital Twin (DT) technologies can monitor and contribute to decision-making, existing maritime DT studies have focused mainly on coordination applications, leaving a gap for computationally efficient decision support. This paper proposes a conceptual DT framework for maritime disruption management that utilizes an AI-accelerated decision-support mechanism. This framework simulates a virtual representation of chokepoint operation conditions, including demand, capacity, and disruption intensity. A feedforward neural-network surrogate that was trained to approximate benchmark optimization outputs using a weighted loss function prioritizes performance in high-disruption and high-capacity stress scenarios. Proof-of-concept simulation using synthetically generated disruption scenarios demonstrate stable training behavior, decreasing optimality gap, and reduced computation time compared with an offline benchmark optimization model. We distill that surrogate-based decision engines may improve the responsiveness of future maritime DT systems where future work will focus on the actual evaluation of the framework using real maritime data, further refinement of the surrogate decision engine, and validation of its operational outputs through empirical data and real-life scenarios.

detail.abstract: Organisations are delegating work to artificial agents faster than the institutions governing those decisions can respond, and the returns are asymmetric: the cost saving arrives in full and at once, while the quality it costs returns capped, lagged, or not at all. A rational manager facing that ledger will automate past the point at which the work is worth most to the people it serves. This paper asks what a governance instrument would have to look like to hold that line, and tests candidates in a calibrated economy of 6,696 US home health agencies, six governance regimes, twenty model periods and 1,024 sensitivity draws. Uncertainty is propagated, never tested. The organising idea is the Human Irreducibility Criterion, which sorts tasks by the ground on which human labour is retainedcapability, constitution, or accountabilityof which only the first decays as machines improve. Under laissez-faire the human task-minute share leaves the value-maximizing zone in every draw, at a deployable task-minute share of 0.2926 [0.2434, 0.3192] against a calibrated start of 0.4929: the overshoot is the initial condition, not a future risk. A category-aware floor holds the highest value in 91.7% of draws, but its real advantage is predictabilityits intervals are 5.89× narrower on Pretium and 12.24× narrower on realized quality. A category-blind floor never buys value: better than doing nothing in 0.7% of draws, worse in 31.9%. The payment adjustment required to hold the zone exceeds its statutory cap in every draw. With the calibrated feedback channels on, the realized share rests below the zone in 83.4% of draws and above it in essentially none. The zone has two edges doing different jobs: a lower boundary below which withdrawing human work destroys more value than it saves, and a sweet spot beyond which added human work no longer pays for itself. Governing composition means naming which work is protected and on what ground, not how much.

title: The -ing of Web 2.0: How Users Defined the Social Media Era
affiliations: and Vassar College

detail.title: The -ing of Web 2.0: How Users Defined the Social Media Era
detail.abstract: The standard history of Web 2.0 is built on nouns such as Facebook and Twitter. The history treats platforms as primary cultural artifacts. The most significant remnants of the social web are user-generated gerunds. The-ings formatting turned fleeting digital actions into durable social phenomena. The gerunds are a bottom-up folksonomy of social behavior. Participants coined the terms when platform-issued language failed the complexity of networked life. Each gerund encodes a technical function and a social scene of motive and power. The gerund is what Archaeobytology calls a Vivibyte. A Vivibyte is a living artifact that reveals how individuals inhabited designed systems. The linguistic stratigraphy stretches from the optimism of early friending through the attention-economic machinery of liking. The record continues through the algorithmic opacity of shadowbanning and the despair of doomscrolling. The stratigraphy arrives at Cory Doctorow's concept of enshittification as the final sign of platform decay. The gerunds are the linguistic record of a civilization learning what the social shift meant to live inside external frameworks.

title: Does ChatGPT Help You Sell More? Effects of Large Language Models on Review Homogeneity and Product Sales

detail.title: Does ChatGPT Help You Sell More? Effects of Large Language Models on Review Homogeneity and Product Sales
detail.abstract: We investigate how large language models reshape the semantic homogeneity of online reviews and how such changes affect product sales through three complementary studies that combine an experiment and large-scale observational panel data analyses. Study 1 demonstrates that AI-generated reviews are semantically more homogeneous than authentic human-written reviews in a controlled setting, a finding that replicates across multiple publicly available datasets. Study 2 analyzes nearly 5 million Amazon Electronics reviews from January 2021 to August 2023 to examine how the semantic homogeneity of reviews changed following the introduction of ChatGPT. Using a year-over-year difference-indifferences design, we find that review semantic homogeneity increased significantly after ChatGPT's introduction, with larger effects among products that historically received fewer reviews. Study 3 combines the Amazon review data from Study 2 with historical product sales rankings to examine how the semantic homogeneity of reviews influences marketplace performance. We find an inverted U-shaped relationship between review semantic homogeneity and product sales. Moderate semantic homogeneity improves product sales, whereas excessive homogeneity reduces them. A counterfactual analysis suggests that approximately 53% of Amazon Electronics products would benefit from the ChatGPT-induced increase in semantic homogeneity, holding the semantic homogeneity of competing products constant. These findings contribute to the emerging literature on generative AI and online reviews by showing that LLMs reshape review ecosystems beyond the characteristics of individual reviews.

detail.title: Technological Change and its Influence on Social and Entrepreneurial Relationships
detail.abstract: The 21st century has transformed human existence, significantly affecting communication, especially in education. This research analyzes the impact of technology on relationships among students at Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Ghana, focusing on social and entrepreneurial aspects. The study utilized qualitative methods, including a survey of 121 students and interviews with 21, revealing extensive use of communication platforms like WhatsApp, Instagram, and Telegram for social networking and academic collaboration. Technology has facilitated seamless connectivity, enabling students to share resources and coordinate group work despite geographical barriers. Entrepreneurially, students engage in diverse ventures, leveraging digital tools for business growth, enhancing advertising, and reaching broader markets. However, challenges include overdependence on technology leading to reduced face-to-face interactions, emotional isolation, and potential misinterpretations in communication. Cybersecurity threats and the influence of social media on self-esteem further complicate this digital landscape. The reliance on informal language in academic settings has also been noted. The study advocates for the establishment of university-specific platforms to bolster student entrepreneurship and emphasizes the importance of digital literacy training. These findings illustrate the dual nature of technology's impact, emphasizing the need for a balanced approach to foster productive relationships and sustainable entrepreneurial success within the evolving digital dynamics of university life at KNUST.

detail.abstract: Public transport systems are essential for urban mobility, economic development, and environmental sustainability in developing countries such as Bangladesh. However, the sector continues to face persistent challenges including low service quality, overcrowding, delays, and declining passenger satisfaction, all of which negatively affect ridership intention. This study examines the impact of the Service Marketing Mix (7Ps) on Ridership Intention in Bangladesh's public transport system, with Customer Satisfaction as a mediating variable. Using a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design, primary data were collected from 249 public transport users through a structured 35-item questionnaire measured on a five-point Likert scale. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, and bootstrapped mediation analysis (PROCESS Macro, Model 4; 5,000 resamples, 95% bias-corrected confidence intervals). The instrument demonstrated high internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.873). Promotion (M = 3.78) and Product/Service Quality (M = 3.59) were the highest-rated 7Ps dimensions, while Ridership Intention items scored moderately (M = 2.93-2.97). Customer Satisfaction significantly and SERVICE MARKETING MIX AND RIDERSHIP INTENTION 2 partially mediated the relationship between Service Marketing Mix and Ridership Intention (indirect effect β = 0.160, 95% CI [0.073, 0.261]), and all four hypotheses were supported. The findings extend the 7Ps framework to a developing-country public transport context and offer practical guidance for transport authorities seeking to strengthen ridership through targeted service improvements.

title: The Relational Blind Spot: A Conditional Framework of Unrealized Value Creation in Customer Relationships
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Relational Blind Spot: A Conditional Framework of Unrealized Value Creation in Customer Relationships

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Both authors are employed by Sparkner AG; beyond this affiliation, the authors declare no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Research on value creation in customer relationships is fragmented across theoretical traditions — the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities, the relational view, relationship marketing, behavioral and systems perspectives — each explaining one level of a phenomenon none explains in full (cf. Lepak, Smith, & Taylor, 2007). We integrate these literatures not by cataloging their convergence but by specifying a conditional structure. The relational blind spot — a persistent organizational state in which a firm fails to perceive and mobilize the use value of its customer relationships beyond their realized exchange value — occurs when five conditions hold jointly: value asymmetry (substance), calibration (structure), experience binding (cognition), delegation (organization), and self-reinforcement (persistence). Necessity and sufficiency operate at two levels: the conjunction defines the construct, and what is tested is its perimeter — each condition's necessity through boundary and contrast predictions, joint sufficiency through a sixth-exit test, in which a firm meeting all five conditions that nonetheless moves would break the structure. From this structure we derive nine falsifiable propositions, including a core prediction: exogenously breaking exactly one of the three blindness conditions shifts the firm's perceived opportunity field measurably. We introduce three measurement constructs — a four-logic relationship profile, a six-dimensional relationship value radar, and a structural module capturing organizational embedding (the "O" in VRIO) — each delimited against existing B2B scales. A research agenda built on condition-breaker designs specifies how the framework can lose.

detail.abstract: For a personal injury law firm on Google, the Knowledge Panel that renders when the firm's brand name is queried is almost always a Google Business Panel: a place-template entity surface backed by the firm's Google Business Profile, not a person-template entity backed by the firm's Wikipedia article. The completeness of that Business Panel governs how the firm appears in the local pack, the map surface, AI Overviews for local-commercial queries, and every downstream AI answer engine that draws on Google's local entity graph. This paper introduces the Google Business Panel Completeness Index (GBPCI), a nine-attribute composite score, and reports the first large-N baseline audit of GBPCI across 1,005 top-ranking US personal injury law firms covering 51 US markets. The nine attributes are (1) Google Business Profile presence, (2) address populated, (3) phone populated, (4) website populated, (5) any Google Business category assigned, (6) a specific personal-injury category assigned (rather than a generic legal-services category), (7) star rating shown, (8) review corpus of ten or more reviews, and (9) multi-location presence (more than one office place entity returned). We find that 95.9% of the 1,005 firms return a Business Panel entity when the firm brand is queried, and that the mean GBPCI is 7.05 / 9 with a median of 8 / 9. Attribute-level prevalence exposes the three areas of the vertical's collective missed opportunity: 43.0% of firms use a generic Google Business category rather than the specific Personal injury attorney category, 33.8% have fewer than ten reviews, and 49.9% operate as a single-office firm. GBPCI does not correlate with SERP rank in this sample (Spearman-0.011, p = 0.73) nor with the Schema Completeness Index reported by the companion structured-data paper (Spearman +0.036, p = 0.26), evidence that on-page schema hygiene and off-site Business Panel completeness are governed by two distinct decision loops inside the firm. We situate the findings inside Google's own patent record on local-business ranking (US-8312010-B1), category-density (US-2014074820-A1), and sentiment-based review ranking (US-9317559-B1), and offer a prioritized recommendation set for firms and their SEO teams targeting Business Panel quality as an AI Visibility surface.

title: When Government Has the Data but Cannot Make a Determination: Institutional Computability in Administrative Systems

detail.title: When Government Has the Data but Cannot Make a Determination: Institutional Computability in Administrative Systems

detail.abstract:
Public agencies increasingly seek to make eligibility, exemption, prioritization, and service determinations using information already available in administrative systems. These efforts are often evaluated as problems of data availability or predictive accuracy. Yet an institution may possess information relevant to a determination without being able to use that information to produce the determination it is authorized to make.

This article introduces Institutional Computability as a framework for diagnosing this gap between administrative information possession and institutional decision capacity. The framework distinguishes an underlying state, administrative observations of that state, the representations constructed from those observations, the subset of representations admissible to an authorized determination process, and the institutional computation producing a determination.

It develops a practical reconstruction protocol for locating six distinct structural limitations: information insufficiency, administrative representation non-instantiation, representational fidelity loss, representational incompatibility, administrative under-specification, and determination ambiguity. Ex parte Medical Frailty exemptions within Medicaid work requirement systems illustrate the approach.

The framework redirects administrative data practice from asking only whether government possesses relevant information toward asking whether that information can become a sufficiently faithful and admissible representation on which an authorized operation is defined and capable of producing a unique determination where one is required. This distinction offers policymakers and public administrators a practical diagnostic for improving data-enabled decision systems without defaulting to additional data collection or predictive modeling.

detail.abstract: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) is commonly examined as philanthropy, reputation management or consumer-facing communication. Less is known about how multinational technology companies embed CSR in market-development activities in institutionally and technically developing business-to-business markets. This article examines how SAP SE's CSR activities were perceived to support its strategic marketing and competitive positioning in Ethiopia's emerging enterprise-software market. It draws on an interpretivist qualitative case study based on semi-structured interviews with 11 informed participants and documentary evidence. The analysis identifies a hybrid CSR portfolio comprising charitable giving, collaboration with local non-governmental organisations, university-oriented software education, employee volunteering, social-sabbatical initiatives and a digital-skills partnership with an international development organisation. The findings indicate different degrees of strategic embedding. Charitable giving primarily generated visibility and goodwill, whereas NGO collaboration strengthened local credibility, knowledge and relational access. University education, professional training and skills-based volunteering were more closely connected to SAP's technological competencies and contributed to market education, professional-capacity development and enterprise-software ecosystem formation. These mechanisms supported stakeholder familiarity, legitimacy and favourable conditions for competitive positioning. Participants nevertheless questioned the developmental breadth, measurement and motives of some initiatives. The study therefore does not attribute SAP's market outcomes to CSR alone: product capabilities, pricing, organisational demand, technical readiness, implementation partnerships and competition also mattered. The article conceptualises embedded CSR as a relational and market-enabling form of strategic marketing whose value arises through stakeholder relationships, legitimacy, knowledge transfer and ecosystem development rather than promotion alone.

title: Digital Identity Optimization (DIO): A Conceptual Framework for Entity-based Visibility in the Age of AI-mediated Search
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Digital Identity Optimization (DIO): A Conceptual Framework for Entity-based Visibility in the Age of AI-mediated Search

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing personal, financial, or institutional interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
The emergence of AI-driven search and answer engines has fundamentally disrupted the logic of digital visibility. Traditional Search Engine Optimization (SEO), built on keyword-document matching, and AI Optimization (AIO), focused on answer-engine citation, provide increasingly insufficient responses to a landscape in which artificial intelligence recommends entities rather than ranks pages.

This paper theorizes Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) as a third-generation framework for digital visibility. Building on Beránek’s (2026) foundational manifest, it defines DIO as the systematic optimization of an entity’s digital identity—its distributed digital representation across human and machine interpretive systems—so that AI systems, search engines, and human audiences can consistently, correctly, and confidently identify, understand, and recommend that entity.

The paper develops the framework along three analytical axes: (1) comparative complexity of SEO, AIO, and DIO; (2) differential value across stakeholder profiles; and (3) multilateral digital identity structures. For large multi-product corporations, the latter is developed as a brand–category/segment–product model; other entity types may exhibit analogous but different structures.

Conceptually, DIO is presented as a bottom-up discovery rather than a top-down fabrication. It crystallizes a latent intersection of psychology, semiotics and post-structuralist thought, branding, SEO, structured data, knowledge graphs, and AI retrieval. Practically, it requires alignment across three domains: human-facing interpretation, pre-AI technical representation, and AI-mediated reconstruction.

title: The Economic Consequences of Insecure Property Rights
affiliations: Hebrew University of Jerusalem - Faculty of Law and Hebrew University of Jerusalem

detail.title: The Economic Consequences of Insecure Property Rights
detail.abstract: Secure property rights support efficient allocation and investment, yet their effects in affluent urban markets remain understudied. We examine Jerusalem properties built on church-owned land under 99-year leases approaching expiration, creating substantial legal and political uncertainty. Using all residential transactions from 2004–2024, we compare nearby properties with secure and insecure rights within the same blocks. Insecure rights reduce transaction likelihood by about 20 percent and prices by 10–15 percent on average, revealing large costs of legal uncertainty. A present-value framework implies that market participants assign a substantial, but far from certain, probability to losing rights.

detail.title: Deregulation and Investment Spillovers in Multi-Product Production Settings
detail.abstract: This paper studies how the removal of price regulation was associated with changes in quality, efficiency, and welfare in the Belgian bread and cake industry. In the summer of 2004, price controls on bread were abolished. Because most firms in this industry produce both bread and cakes, the reform provides a useful setting in which to examine both direct changes in the deregulated market and spillovers to a related product line. We use detailed firm-product-level information on values and physical quantities to estimate product quality, technical efficiency, marginal costs, markups, and welfare. We find that deregulation was associated with substantial improvements in both quality and efficiency. Welfare increased through gains in consumer surplus and producer surplus, and the gains were not confined to bread. We also find evidence of spillovers to cake production, suggesting that deregulation encouraged technological upgrading that affected firms' broader production process.
